90-tyoaika-kuljetusala.title: "90 working hours" in road haulage: what 90 hours really means
90-tyoaika-kuljetusala.description: "90 working hours" is not a Working Hours Act rule. In haulage, 90 h is the two-week driving limit; working time is capped by 80 h, 60 h and 48 h limits.
90-tyoaika-kuljetusala.html:
Key takeaways

  • "90 working hours" is not a concept in the Working Hours Act: the current Finnish Working Hours Act (872/2019) contains no rule allowing working time to be agreed to exceed the contractual hours by 90 hours over a four-month period.
  • In road haulage, 90 hours is a driving time limit: under the EU driving and rest time regulation 561/2006, total driving time over any two consecutive weeks may not exceed 90 hours.
  • Under the collective agreement for the truck sector, regular working time is 80 hours per two-week period; hours above that are overtime, with the first 12 hours paid at time and a half (+50 %) and the rest at double time (+100 %).
  • Working time including overtime may average no more than 48 hours a week, and a driver within the scope of the driving and rest time regulation may work no more than 60 hours in any calendar week (Working Hours Act, section 18).
  • Besides driving, a driver's working time includes loading, unloading, terminal work and maintenance, so the working time limit is often reached before the driving time limit.

People searching for "90 working hours" are often looking for a rule that does not exist: the Finnish Working Hours Act (872/2019) has no 90-hour flexibility over a four-month period. In road haulage, the figure 90 comes from the EU driving and rest time regulation, which caps driving time over two consecutive weeks at 90 hours. Working time, meanwhile, is limited by the 80-hour two-week period in the collective agreement for the truck sector, the drivers' 60-hour weekly cap and the 48-hour average. Below you will find a worked example and rostering guidance to keep you within the limits.

What does "90 working hours" mean in law?

There is no 90-hour rule in the Working Hours Act. The Working Hours Act 872/2019, in force since the start of 2020, replaced the old Working Hours Act 605/1996, and neither of them allows working time to be agreed to exceed the contractual hours by an average of 90 hours over a four-month period. In road haulage, 90 hours is a driving time limit: total driving time over two consecutive weeks may not exceed 90 hours (Regulation 561/2006, Article 6).

The provisions and their purpose

A driver's hours are limited by three different sets of rules. The driving and rest time regulation 561/2006 limits driving time: no more than 9 hours a day (10 hours twice a week), 56 hours a week and 90 hours over two consecutive weeks. The Working Hours Act 872/2019 limits total working time: working time including overtime may average no more than 48 hours a week over four months, and a driver within the scope of the driving and rest time regulation may also work no more than 60 hours in any calendar week (section 18). The collective agreement sets regular working time and overtime pay.

The limits exist for road safety and to keep drivers from burning out: the driving time limit prevents excessively long driving stints, and the working time limit stops loading, unloading and waiting from stretching the week unreasonably. Employer and driver cannot agree between themselves to depart from these limits. A national collective agreement may extend the reference period for the 48-hour average (Working Hours Act, section 34), and the collective agreement for the truck sector uses the calendar year as the reference period (section 11, point 2).

What can be agreed in the employment contract?

The driving time and maximum working time limits cannot be overridden by an employment contract. There is room for agreement in how regular working time is arranged: under the collective agreement for the truck sector, regular working time is 80 hours per two-week period (period-based working time, Working Hours Act section 7), and overtime always requires the driver's consent (Working Hours Act section 17). Write the applicable collective agreement, the regular working time and the pay basis into the employment contract, so that rostering and payroll are lawful.

Once the working time terms are correctly set out in the contract, it makes sense to track them in the same place as the jobs. RAHTIS is designed for small haulage firms where the owner does the planning: https://www.rahtis.eu/fi.

How does "90 working hours" differ from the "40" and "75" working time figures?

The three figures mean different things. 40 hours is regular weekly working time under the general working time rules: no more than 8 hours a day and 40 hours a week (Working Hours Act, section 5). 75 is not a statutory limit in road haulage; it usually refers to a 7.5-hour working day, i.e. a 37.5-hour week, which is regular working time under many office-sector collective agreements. 90 hours, on the other hand, is the driving time limit for two consecutive weeks under Regulation 561/2006, not a working time limit.

FigureWhat it refers toPeriodTypical use
40Regular weekly working time under the general rules (Working Hours Act, section 5)One weekOffice work, fixed day work
75Not a statutory limit; usually a 7.5-hour working day (37.5 h a week)One dayOffice-sector collective agreements
90Driving time limit (Regulation 561/2006, Article 6)Two consecutive weeksDrivers within the scope of the driving and rest time regulation

Why the figures get mixed up

The confusion arises because all three concern the same question: how much a driver may drive or work. In a small haulage firm, tachograph driving times, the two-week pay period and the weekly rota run side by side, and driving time is easily confused with working time.

A rule of thumb: compare driving time with 9, 56 and 90, and total working time with 80 (the two-week regular working time in the collective agreement), 60 (the weekly cap) and 48 (the average). A single week may run to, say, 55 hours, as long as the 60-hour weekly cap and the 48-hour average hold and hours above 80 in the two-week period are paid as overtime. In haulage, peaks come irregularly, and that is exactly why the two-week period is practical: hours from a busy week can be balanced out with a quieter one.

When does the 90-hour limit apply?

The 90-hour driving time limit applies whenever a transport operation falls within the scope of the driving and rest time regulation 561/2006: as a rule, goods transport in vehicles over 3.5 tonnes and, from 1 July 2026, international transport in vehicles over 2.5 tonnes as well. The limit applies to every period of two consecutive calendar weeks and cannot be overridden by agreement. It also applies to self-employed drivers, because the regulation limits driving, not employment.

What the employer must record

The employer must keep working time records of each driver's hours worked, overtime hours and the overtime pay made for them (Working Hours Act, section 32), and must give the driver a driver's logbook, for which a tachograph may be used instead (section 31). The work roster must be notified in writing no later than one week before the start of the period it covers (section 30).

In road haulage, the collective agreement changes the statutory starting points, so first check whether your firm applies the collective agreement for the truck sector (between the employers' federation ATL and the transport workers' union AKT). Even a one-lorry firm should put the employment contract in writing as soon as it hires: it should state the regular working time, the pay basis and the applicable collective agreement. Fix the two-week periods in advance, for example always starting on a Monday, and track the 48-hour average over whichever reference period applies to you. That way balancing out hours is based on a plan, not on random peaks.

How are hours calculated in a two-week period?

Worked example: a two-week period

Take the basic case: the driver is covered by the collective agreement for the truck sector, so regular working time is 80 hours per two-week period. In the first week the driver drives for 50 hours and does 8 hours of loading and other work, giving 58 hours of working time. In the second week driving may total no more than 40 hours, because driving time over the two weeks may not exceed 90 hours. The driver drives for 30 hours and does 6 hours of other work, 36 hours in total.

Working time for the period is 58 + 36 = 94 hours. Regular working time is exceeded by 14 hours: the first 12 are paid at +50 % and the next 2 at +100 %. Driving time is 50 + 30 = 80 hours, below the 90-hour limit, and each week stays under the 60-hour weekly cap. Driver B drives 56 + 34 hours and uses up the full 90-hour driving limit. In the first week, on top of 56 hours of driving, there is room for only 4 hours of other work before the 60-hour weekly cap is reached.

Overtime and shift allowances in the same calculation

Over a longer period, you check the average: 48 hours a week means no more than about 835 hours of working time, including overtime, over a four-month period (about 17.4 weeks). If a driver regularly works 94-hour two-week periods, the average is 47 hours a week, so the limit is close. All time spent working counts, including hours falling on a Sunday or at night.

Overtime and evening and night allowances do not change how the limits are calculated, but they are linked to it: hours above 80 in the two-week period are overtime paid at the higher rate, and evening and night allowances are paid separately under the collective agreement for the hours that qualify. So record three figures for every shift: driving time, other working time, and hours falling in the evening or at night. With these kept apart, checking the period is a matter of simple addition, not guesswork.

How does the 90-hour driving limit affect driver rostering?

Driving time limits and working time limits have to be planned together. Regulation 561/2006 limits daily driving time to nine hours (ten hours twice a week), weekly driving time to 56 hours and driving time over two consecutive weeks to 90 hours. In domestic distribution and terminal work, the working time limit is usually reached before the driving time limit, whereas on long international runs the driving time limit bites first.

Combining driving and rest times with the working time cap

A driver's actual working day is longer than the hours spent driving: loading, unloading, terminal work and maintenance all count as working time. When planning the week, add up driving and other work and compare the total with the 60-hour weekly cap and the 48-hour average, and compare driving time separately with the 56-hour and 90-hour limits. That way you can see which one constrains you first.

A 56-hour driving week is only possible if other work in the same week is no more than 4 hours, because a driver may work no more than 60 hours in a calendar week. Driving the following week is then limited to 34 hours. In domestic distribution, less driving time accrues, but terminal work and loading fill working time quickly, so the 60-hour weekly cap and the 48-hour average are reached before the driving time limits. The planner's job is to know which limit binds first and to allocate shifts accordingly.

How dispatch tracks the running totals week by week

Keep the running totals visible every Monday: for each driver, driving time and working time in the two-week period, driving time remaining before the 90-hour limit, and the working time average since the start of the reference period. When driving time approaches 90 or weekly working time approaches 60, move jobs to a driver with spare capacity or shorten the days. That way you avoid breaching a limit purely through poor planning.

What are the most common mistakes in applying the 90-hour limit?

The most common mistake is to think that 90 hours is a working time flexibility that can be written into the employment contract. It is not: 90 hours is the two-week driving time limit, and the working time limits always apply on top of it. Work beyond regular working time is overtime or additional work, and it must be paid for.

The second mistake is counting only driving time: driving time can stay below 90 hours even though working time exceeds the 60-hour weekly cap. The third is calculating overtime pay wrongly, for example by paying all hours above 80 in the two-week period at +50 %, even though after 12 hours the rate is +100 %. The fourth is relying on a paper notebook: without working time records you cannot prove the running total, nor spot an error until the driver claims compensation.

How to put mistakes right afterwards

The fix is to recalculate the actual working time for the period, pay any missing overtime retrospectively and document the procedure for future periods. The Finnish occupational safety and health authorities require employers to keep reliable records of each employee's working time and to retain them so that the basis for pay can be verified. For drivers, tachograph data supplement the working time records but do not replace them.

If the error is only discovered after the period has ended, the unpaid overtime must be paid retrospectively. An example: a driver has been underpaid by 2 hours of overtime in every two-week period. There are 26 periods a year, so the missing overtime adds up to 52 hours per driver, and 624 hours in a firm with 12 drivers. A driver can claim the pay within two years of the end of the calendar year in which the right to it arose (Working Hours Act, section 40). A regular check every Monday is cheaper than a lump-sum payout after the event.

How does a working time system help you comply with driving and working time limits?

A working time system has three jobs: calculate working hours and overtime for the two-week period automatically, import driving times directly from the tachograph, and warn you before the 60-hour weekly cap, the 48-hour average or the 90-hour driving limit is reached. Tracking on paper or in Excel usually falls apart at the point, midway through the period, when you need to know how many hours each driver has left.

What RAHTIS covers and what it doesn't

RAHTIS brings dispatch, the freight exchange and driver management together in one place, so rostering and driver details stay in a single view. The driver report calculates hours from the recorded shifts and, when a pay model based on the collective agreement for the truck sector has been selected for the driver, overtime for the two-week period; the report can be exported as PDF, Excel or CSV. To be honest: RAHTIS does not read tachograph files and does not track the 90-hour driving limit, the 60-hour weekly cap or the 48-hour average. The report is an aid for internal payments, not payroll, so make sure statutory tracking comes from your tachograph software and your payroll.

Selection criteria for a small haulage firm

Ask for these three features before you buy: a per-driver report of two-week periods and the 48-hour average, import of tachograph data (vehicle unit and driver card) without manual re-keying, and an alert before a limit is reached, not after. If the system requires a separate licence per driver, ask for the total cost at the scale of 12 lorries before you commit.

FAQ

Can I use the "90 working hours" rule if it isn't mentioned in the employment contract?

No, because no such rule exists. The Working Hours Act does not allow working time to be agreed to exceed the contractual hours by 90 hours over a four-month period. Hours above regular working time are overtime, which requires the driver's consent and is paid at the higher rate, and total working time is limited by the 60-hour weekly cap and the 48-hour average. Check your sector's collective agreement first and write the regular working time into the employment contract as soon as you hire.

How many hours a month is "90 working hours"?

90 hours is a two-week driving time limit, not a monthly working time. Driving may total no more than 90 hours in two consecutive weeks and no more than 56 hours in a single week, so monthly driving time depends on how the weeks fall within the month. Working time is limited by the average: 48 hours a week is about 209 hours a month (48 × 4.35 weeks), including overtime. An individual month may differ, as long as the average over the reference period adds up and no week exceeds 60 hours.

Does a driver's driving time count as working time?

Yes, but driving time alone is not the whole of working time. Working time also includes loading, unloading, terminal work and maintenance, so hours driven are always fewer than total working time. Compare driving time with the 56-hour and 90-hour driving limits, and the sum of driving and other work with the 60-hour weekly cap and the 48-hour average. Whichever limit is reached first is the one that decides.

Does unused driving time carry over to the next period?

No. The 90-hour limit applies to every period of two consecutive weeks, so driving time left unused in a quiet week does not raise the limit for the following weeks, and weekly driving time is capped at 56 hours in any case. As for working time, hours above 80 in the two-week period are paid as overtime in that period's pay, and a short period cannot be offset against overtime in the next one.

Does the 90-hour limit also apply to subcontracted haulage?

Yes. The working time and rostering of a subcontractor's drivers are the subcontractor's responsibility, and the subcontractor answers for their lawfulness, but the 90-hour driving limit applies to every driver within the scope of the driving and rest time regulation, including subcontractors' drivers and self-employed drivers. A self-employed driver's working time is also limited by the Act on the Working Time of Self-Employed Drivers in Road Transport (349/2013). So before you start working together, make sure the schedules you give a partner can be driven within the limits.

alihankinta-pienkuljettajalle-vaihe-vaih.title: Subcontracting for small hauliers, step by step
alihankinta-pienkuljettajalle-vaihe-vaih.description: Get subcontracting under control in a 1–12 lorry firm: freight exchange search, quote, POD and payment tracking in one workflow, without the paper notebook.
alihankinta-pienkuljettajalle-vaihe-vaih.html:
Key takeaways

  • When subcontracting, you carry out the haulage on behalf of another company and invoice that client, not the end customer.
  • The POD, i.e. the signed consignment note, is the most important document, because without it the invoice often goes unpaid.
  • The contract should set out the payment term, the division of liability and penalties for late delivery tied to a specific time.
  • Four metrics are enough: punctuality, payment time, empty running share and a comparison of subcontractors on the same route.
  • One tool that combines load search, POD and payment tracking removes most of the manual record-keeping.

In practice, subcontracting means finding freight on a freight exchange or from your own customers, quoting, completing the job and then invoicing with a POD attached. This guide covers the whole chain, from posting your availability to payment tracking, for a small firm of 1–12 lorries that does its own dispatching and invoicing. Subcontracting is the quickest way to fill a lorry when your own customer base is not enough, which is why managing it is a core skill for every owner-driver.

What exactly does subcontracting mean?

In road haulage, subcontracting means carrying out transport on behalf of another company: the client sells the job to its customer, and you do it with your own vehicle and driver. The client invoices the end customer; you invoice the client. The same model works the other way round, too, when you can't cover a booking and buy it in from another haulier.

Subcontracting vs your own fleet work

Your own fleet work means your own customers and your own haulage contracts. Subcontracting is a faster way to keep the lorry full: you look for loads on a freight exchange such as TIMOCOM, or take bookings directly from a larger haulier. The risk is lower, but so is the margin, and you often have to wait for payment from the client rather than the end customer. Your own customer often pays within 14 days, whereas a subcontracting client may stretch payment to 30–45 days unless the contract says otherwise. For a small operator this difference is critical for cash flow, which is why negotiating the payment term is part of the bread and butter of subcontracting.

Who is the subcontractor and who is the client

The subcontractor carries out the haulage and is responsible for its own driving, its driver and their working time. The client looks after the customer relationship and pays the agreed price. The interface lies where the invoice and the consignment note change hands. RAHTIS handles both directions in one place, and you can apply to join straight away.

The client is also responsible for customer communication and for any compensation claims if the subcontractor is late. The subcontractor, for its part, is responsible for ensuring the vehicle is legal, insurance is in order and the driver is qualified. Keeping these two roles apart matters, because both liabilities and costs are split differently from those with your own customers.

How does the subcontracting process work, step by step?

Step 1: post your availability and search

Start by posting your own vehicle availability on a freight exchange such as Trans.eu or TIMOCOM. Include the route, vehicle type, capacity and when the vehicle is free. At the same time, browse return loads for your route to keep empty running to a minimum. Keep your search up to date: a load found in the morning is usually better than what's left in the afternoon.

Update your search at least twice a day, because many clients publish new loads overnight or early in the morning. If you run a regular route, make the search recurring so that you see loads on that route automatically without browsing by hand.

Step 2: quote and confirmation

When you find a load, quote quickly but check first: mileage, waiting times, loading times and unloading. Price on real costs, not wishful thinking. Always get the confirmation in writing, even if you agreed it by phone first. A written confirmation can be a simple email stating the route, price, loading and delivery addresses and the schedule.

Make sure the written order confirmation (rate confirmation) also arrives before the job, not after delivery. If the client doesn't send it in time, insist that the job doesn't start without it: without a rate confirmation you have no written proof of the agreed price, and in a dispute it's your word against theirs, which leaves you in a weak position.

Step 3: transport and POD

Stay in touch with the client during the job and collect the POD (the signed consignment note) as soon as the goods are unloaded. The POD is the most important document, because without it the invoice often goes unpaid. If the delivery point won't give you a signed paper copy, ask for a digital acknowledgement or at the very least a photo of the unloaded goods and the recipient's name. Send the POD to the client the same day, not a week later: fast delivery also speeds up invoicing and payment. If the client uses its own TMS, check whether you can upload the POD directly to their portal so the paperwork doesn't get lost in an email thread.

Step 4: invoicing and payment tracking

Once you have the POD, send the invoice with the consignment note, the quote confirmation and any extra charges attached. Track the payment term actively: note who pays and when. RAHTIS keeps the job, POD and invoice together and shows which invoices are overdue, so you don't need to keep a paper notebook of who owes what. The RAHTIS API documentation explains how the system connects to other tools if you want to export the data to your own systems.

Invoice within 24 hours of receiving the POD at the latest, because the longer you leave it, the more likely payment is to be late. Show the due date and late-payment interest on the invoice: in business-to-business trade the law entitles you to late-payment interest and €40 compensation for collection costs when payment is late.

What are the most common subcontracting challenges?

For a small haulage firm, subcontracting problems come down to four things: late deliveries, dispatch run on paper, separate logins to freight exchanges, and nobody knowing who is paying when.

Late delivery: what it costs

When a subcontractor's lorry arrives late, the cost doesn't stop at the driver's day. Your own customer raises a claim, you have to enforce the penalty clause against the subcontractor, and trust is lost. Without a shared schedule and event tracking, you only find out about the delay when the customer rings. In RAHTIS the delivery status is visible in a single view, and through the API the status can also be shared with the customer (API documentation).

The true cost of a late delivery is higher than a single claim: next time the job goes to another subcontractor, and a bad reputation spreads quickly in a trade where clients all know each other. That is why tracking late deliveries systematically matters: if one subcontractor is repeatedly late, the next request for quotation goes to someone else first.

Separate freight exchanges and a paper notebook

The typical set-up: TIMOCOM, Trans.eu and Teleroute, each with its own login, an outdated TMS and a notebook for recording who owes what. Every search and request for quotation takes three logins, the trail of a load is lost as soon as the paperwork changes hands, and when every subcontracted load lives in its own email thread, nobody remembers a week later which client the load belonged to and at what price it was agreed. The problem with a paper notebook isn't just lost information; it's also that nobody can say at the end of the month how much subcontracting was done, what the average payment time was or what share was empty running. Comparing payment times by client also becomes guesswork, even though that is exactly the information that decides who gets the next load and from whom you should demand payment up front. Without these figures you can't negotiate better rates or spot loss-making routes, which is why consolidating into one tool removes half of this work and brings the monthly figures back into view without separate bookkeeping: when the same tool shows searches, PODs and unpaid invoices in one view, the monthly review takes minutes rather than hours, and decisions are based on figures rather than memory.

How do digital tools make subcontracting easier?

One view across several freight exchanges

Without tools, looking for subcontracted work means logging into each broker's site separately: TIMOCOM, Teleroute and Trans.eu each sit in their own tab, and quotes and messages end up scattered. A TMS in which you record the jobs taken from exchanges brings them together in one view, where you can compare freight, route and return load without switching between five logins. When the same tool handles both your own customers' traffic and exchange subcontracting, you have one place that tells you who is doing what, and where. This visibility matters especially when a driver is on the road and you have to decide whether to take a new load from your own customer or from subcontracting. Without a single view the decision is guesswork, and guesswork leads either to empty running or to overbooking.

Real-time tracking and fewer jobs left uninvoiced

Another tangible benefit is real-time tracking, i.e. knowing where each load and vehicle is right now. Once vehicles and drivers have been entered into the system, every load moves visibly from quote to POD and invoicing, following the workflow described above: the rate confirmation comes in, the POD is requested on completion, the invoice goes out and the payment term is tracked. This reduces waste, because empty running and the search for a return load become visible in good time and no load is forgotten when invoicing. RAHTIS is built for exactly this: trailer, container and load leave on time, and the phone stops ringing (RAHTIS).

In fairness: no tool replaces a subcontractor's own reliability, and real-time tracking doesn't work if drivers don't update their status. The tool reduces manual work, not responsibility. The driver still has to enter their status in the system, and if they forget, tracking shows the last known position, not the actual one. That's why it's important to agree a clear routine with drivers: status is always updated at loading and unloading, not "sometime in the evening at the hotel". Building the routine takes a week, but after that tracking works without daily reminders.

How do you choose the right subcontractor?

There are three criteria: reliability, working time discipline and vehicles. Always ask for evidence of previous jobs and check that the subcontractor's operator licence details and insurance are in order before the first load. Also check that the subcontractor has valid CMR insurance covering carrier's liability on international journeys.

Ask for a copy of the insurance certificate and check the cover. Remember that under Article 23 of the CMR Convention the carrier's liability is limited to 8.33 SDR (Special Drawing Rights) per kilogram of gross weight, roughly €10 per kilogram: if a 1,000 kg consignment is worth €50,000, compensation is still only about €10,000. If you have promised your customer wider liability than this, you bear the difference, so for valuable goods agree a declaration of value (Article 24) or cargo insurance separately. That's why checking insurance is just as important as checking the driver's licences.

Driving and rest times and driver workload

A driver's hours are not just the subcontractor's problem: under Article 10 of Regulation (EC) No 561/2006, clients and principal contractors must also ensure that agreed transport schedules respect the driving and rest time rules. The rules can be found in the EU's EUR-Lex legislation database, and with every job it's worth asking the subcontractor to confirm that the schedule fits within the driver's driving and rest times. If they can't confirm it, the load doesn't go to them.

Keeping an eye on driving times isn't just bureaucracy: if the subcontractor's driver exceeds the limits and is caught at a roadside check, the vehicle can be held for the rest period, the delivery can be delayed, and you answer to the end customer. A realistic schedule is therefore risk management as well as compliance. Ask for the confirmation in writing, by email for example, so you can check it quickly before handing over the load.

Cutting late-night admin and getting a real-time picture

Many small hauliers find return loads on exchanges such as Trans.eu or TIMOCOM (Trans.eu), but cutting late-night admin takes more: a real-time picture of where your own and subcontracted vehicles actually are. In RAHTIS (rahtis.eu/et) you can see the status of your own vehicles in a single view, so subcontracted capacity is only brought in when you don't have your own. Fuel consumption is shown in RAHTIS from the fuel card report, driver entries and GPS, but technical condition monitoring, such as tyre pressures, stays with the vehicle's own telematics. Cutting late-night admin doesn't mean you won't work evenings; it means that in the morning you already know which loads have been delivered and which are waiting, with no guesswork. If three vehicles are on the road and one becomes free tomorrow, you can see at a glance whether to take a subcontracted job or wait for a load from your own customer.

Which tools suit a small haulage firm?

For a small operator three things are decisive: availability of loads, invoicing and payment tracking in the same package, and a price that stays reasonable as the fleet grows. Below is a comparison on those criteria.

Where RAHTIS falls short

To be honest: the RAHTIS offer desk is its own freight exchange where shippers publish jobs, but it doesn't pull in loads from TIMOCOM, Teleroute or Trans.eu and is nowhere near their size, so if you're only looking for loads, searching a larger exchange is an essential addition. If your business is international contract haulage with large operators, a Transporeon-type integration may be more relevant. RAHTIS is strongest when you do your own dispatching and invoicing, source subcontracted work from an exchange and want "who owes what to whom" to be clear without a scrap of paper. RAHTIS's strength is managing the whole picture: when you know where the vehicle is, what it's carrying and when the invoice falls due, you can make decisions faster than a competitor hunting for information in five different places.

Which contract terms deserve attention in subcontracting?

Three terms matter most: the payment term, the division of liability and penalties for late delivery.

On payment, hold out for 14 days or less, and agree late-payment interest and reimbursement of collection costs. Also state who pays the freight exchange and broker fees, so that a scrap of paper headed "who owes what" isn't your only record. Check, too, whether the price includes VAT or whether it's added separately, and whether the rate is per kilometre or a fixed price per job. Writing these details down saves explanations later, when the invoice arrives and the total doesn't match what was expected.

On liability, specify whether the subcontractor's liability insurance covers the full carrier's liability, and agree how the excess is split. Include a requirement that drivers hold a valid driving licence and Driver CPC, and that driving and rest times are complied with. Also define who is responsible for loading and unloading: if the subcontractor's driver has to unload alone and it takes three hours, who pays for the waiting time? Agree waiting times in advance: for example, two hours included in the price, then €30–50 per hour after that.

Penalties for late delivery should be tied to a specific time, not to a "reasonable delay", with the exceptions defined: congestion, weather and unloading delays at the customer's end. For example: "For delays of more than 2 hours beyond the agreed time, excluding force majeure, the subcontractor shall pay 5% of the haulage price per hour or part thereof." This is precise, measurable and easy to apply in a dispute. The alternative, "reasonable compensation", leads to endless negotiation in which each party interprets what is reasonable from its own point of view.

Tie the terms to practice: require the POD and rate confirmation for every job and attach them to the invoice, whatever tool you use. Without attachments an invoice is just an invoice; with them it is proof of performance, and proof speeds up payment.

How do you track and measure subcontracting?

Tracking needs only four metrics, and most of them come straight from job and invoice records without any extra work.

Punctuality: how many collections and deliveries were on time. When every job is logged in the system, the percentage calculates itself at monthly level. The target is above 95%: if it's lower, either the subcontractors or your own drivers need a word. Punctuality is also a bargaining chip: when you can show a subcontractor that their punctuality is 80% while others manage 96%, the next request for quotation goes to someone else without lengthy explanations.

Payment time: how many days pass from sending the invoice until the money arrives. RAHTIS tracks the due dates of unpaid invoices, so you can see at a glance who is late paying. An average of more than 30 days means either your contracts are too loose or your clients are struggling to pay. Under 14 days is a realistic target if you've chosen your clients carefully and your contracts include late-payment interest.

Empty running: how many kilometres you drive without a load. When searching freight exchanges (Trans.eu, TIMOCOM, Teleroute), always check for a return load before quoting, and measure empty running as a percentage of total distance. The target is under 15%: over 20% means route planning is lacking or subcontracted jobs are too often taken one way without a return load. Every percentage point of empty running comes straight off your profit margin, so this is a figure worth knowing precisely.

Subcontractor comparison: compare subcontractors' prices and punctuality against each other on the same route. If one is consistently more expensive than the rest, the next request for quotation goes to someone else first. In the same way, compare your own prices with the market: if subcontractors are offering the same route 20% cheaper, either your costs are too high or your price is too low to compete.

These four figures tell you which subcontractors are worth keeping and which of your own customers pay slowest. A monthly review is enough: there's no need to track them daily, but knowing these figures at the end of the month makes the difference between being able to negotiate better terms or not.

FAQ

How much does subcontracted haulage pay on a freight exchange in Finland?

On a freight exchange, the price is set by competitive bidding, so there is no fixed list price. The margin left to the client is typically thinner than on your own customer contracts. The price depends on mileage, waiting and loading times, and unloading. Always price on real costs and agree in writing in advance who pays the freight exchange and broker fees.

Can I manage subcontracting without a TMS if I have fewer than 5 lorries?

You can start without a separate TMS, but the typical set-up is then TIMOCOM, Trans.eu and Teleroute, each with its own login, plus a notebook for recording who owes what. Every search takes several logins, and the trail of a load is lost when the paperwork changes hands. One tool that combines load search, POD and payment tracking removes much of the manual work.

How do I invoice subcontracted jobs and keep track of unpaid invoices?

Once you have the POD after unloading, send the invoice with attachments: the consignment note, the quote confirmation and any extra charges. Without the POD the invoice often goes unpaid. Note who pays and when, and track the payment term actively. RAHTIS shows which invoices are overdue, so the paper notebook becomes unnecessary.

Do I need a separate contract with each subcontractor?

Yes, and three terms matter most: the payment term, the division of liability and penalties for late delivery. Hold out for a payment term of 14 days or less, agree late-payment interest and reimbursement of collection costs, and define how the excess is split. Tie penalties to a specific time rather than a reasonable delay, and require the POD and rate confirmation for every job, to be attached to the invoice.

How do I avoid empty running and find a return load?

Check return loads for your route before you quote, and keep your own availability posted on the freight exchange with the route, vehicle type, capacity and time the vehicle becomes free. A load found in the morning is usually better than what's left in the afternoon. When you measure empty running as a percentage of total distance, you can see whether it is coming down.

cmr-rahtikirjan-hallinta-digitaalisesti.title: Managing CMR consignment notes digitally, step by step
cmr-rahtikirjan-hallinta-digitaalisesti.description: Managing CMR consignment notes digitally: e-CMR fields, electronic signatures, carrier's reservations and archiving, with a checklist.
cmr-rahtikirjan-hallinta-digitaalisesti.html:
Key takeaways

  • e-CMR is legal in Finland under the 2008 Additional Protocol to the CMR Convention for carriage between countries that have joined the Protocol, provided the system guarantees the authenticity and integrity of the document and the identification of the signatory.
  • The carrier's reservations go in box 18 at loading and the consignee's remarks next to its receipt in box 24, before signing, because an entry added afterwards loses its evidential value.
  • In Finland, consignment notes are kept as accounting records under the Accounting Act: vouchers and other material for at least six years, books and financial statements for ten, and the original electronic data is a safer archive than a PDF copy alone.
  • The electronic signature is tied to the signatory's name, role, time and location, which settles disputes over the time of delivery and shortens insurance investigations.
  • Start the switch on a single regular route and keep paper CMRs as a fallback for when the consignee insists on paper or the destination country hasn't joined the Additional Protocol.

Moving the CMR consignment note from paper to digital can be done on carriage between countries that have joined the Additional Protocol, in three steps: choose an e-CMR-compatible system that covers the mandatory particulars of the CMR Convention, introduce the driver's electronic signature, and record reservations and remarks (boxes 18 and 24, damage and discrepancies) so that they keep their evidential value in a dispute or an insurance claim. This guide goes through the fields, the signature, the reservations and the archiving obligations with a practical checklist.

What is a CMR consignment note and which of its fields are mandatory?

The CMR consignment note is the document for international road carriage that evidences that the carrier has taken over the goods and that a contract of carriage exists. Its content is defined by the CMR Convention, and the same content applies in every contracting state, whether the note is on paper or electronic.

Key fields under the CMR Convention

Under Article 6 of the Convention the mandatory particulars are: place and date of the note, the sender, the carrier and the consignee, the place of taking over and the place designated for delivery, the description of the goods, the number of packages and their marks, the gross weight, the carriage charges, instructions for customs formalities, and a statement that the carriage is subject to the CMR Convention. The time the driver takes over the goods and the driver's signature, along with the consignee's receipt on delivery, complete the document. The text of the CMR Convention is available on the UNECE website, and the Additional Protocol permits an electronic version.

What the consignment note proves and what it doesn't

The CMR proves the goods were taken over and in what quantity, but it proves neither the quality of the goods nor who owns them. The carrier's reservations are recorded in box 18 and the consignee's remarks next to its receipt in box 24, and they determine liability afterwards. That is why the fields are best filled in carefully at loading, not afterwards from a spreadsheet. In RAHTIS, the job that holds the signature and the scanned CMR appears directly in dispatch and invoicing (https://www.rahtis.eu/fi).

Is the electronic CMR (e-CMR) legal in Finland and the EU?

Yes, between countries that have joined the Additional Protocol. The electronic consignment note under the CMR Convention is governed by the 2008 Additional Protocol, which allows paper to be replaced by an electronic document provided the system guarantees the authenticity and integrity of the document and the identification of the signatory. Finland ratified the Additional Protocol in 2019, so e-CMR is legal for carriage between Finland and the other countries that have joined; there are more than 40 of them, including Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Estonia, Germany and Poland. If the country of loading or delivery hasn't joined, a paper CMR is needed. In practice, the parties to the carriage need to agree to the use of the electronic method.

The Additional Protocol and its requirements

The Additional Protocol does not prescribe any particular software; instead it sets requirements: the transport data must be tamper-proof, signatures must identify the signatory and carry a timestamp, and the data must remain available throughout the journey. If the system goes down or the data cannot be handed to the authorities at a roadside check, the method does not meet the requirements.

When to keep a paper copy as a fallback

When the customer or consignee doesn't use e-CMR, or when you're heading to a country that hasn't joined the Additional Protocol, a paper CMR note is still the safest backup. Many small firms start e-CMR on one regular route to a country that has joined and keep paper forms in the cupboard for other cross-border work. If you're weighing up the switch, you can sign up for a RAHTIS trial at https://www.rahtis.eu/sv/apply and test how your own workflow copes with an electronic signature and a scanned consignment note.

How is the consignment note signed digitally during the journey?

The driver's signature on a mobile device

The driver signs the CMR on a phone or tablet at loading. In practice an electronic signature means a fingerprint, a PIN code or a signature drawn on the screen, tied to the driver's ID and a timestamp. Finland ratified the e-CMR Additional Protocol in 2019, so a signature made under it is as valid as a handwritten one on carriage between countries that have joined Finland's treaty series (Finlex).

The consignee's signature and the moment of delivery

The consignee signs on the same device or on their own device, to which the driver sends a signature request. The moment of delivery is recorded in the system to the second, which settles disputes about when the goods were delivered. If the consignee refuses to sign electronically, the driver can revert to paper or record the discrepancy directly in the system.

What the signature must include

The signatory's name, role (sender, carrier or consignee), time and location are stored with the signature. This makes it possible to prove afterwards who signed and when. In RAHTIS, the signature is saved with the signatory's name, and the scanned consignment note and photos, with where they were taken, are available through the API, so they can be linked directly to invoicing and job status tracking (https://www.rahtis.eu/fi/api-docs). The signature does not replace reservations, but it locks them into the document unchanged.

How are CMR reservations (damage, discrepancies) recorded digitally?

Boxes 18 and 24: reservations and remarks recorded electronically

Box 18 is the carrier's reservations box: it records shortcomings found when taking over the goods in the number of packages, their marks or the apparent condition of the goods and packaging. At unloading, the consignee records any damage or shortage it finds next to its receipt in box 24. With an electronic CMR the entry is made directly in the system during the journey, and it is timestamped. In the RAHTIS driver app, damage is photographed and marked during the inspection step, so the entry stays attached to that job rather than in a paper notebook.

Damage checklist: photo, description, witnesses

To preserve evidential value, follow the same routine every time:

StepWhat to record
1. PhotoClose-up of the packaging and goods, with the timestamp visible
2. DescriptionWhat is damaged, where and how badly
3. WitnessesConsignee's name and signature before the load is handed over
4. ReservationText in box 18 (loading) or 24 (unloading) before signing

If the consignee refuses to sign, record that on the consignment note as well.

When the entry must be made before signing

The reservation is recorded before the consignment note is signed. An entry added after signing loses its evidential value, because the other party has not seen or confirmed it. In an electronic system this boils down to one practical rule: inspect the load, record the reservations and photos, and only then sign. In the RAHTIS API (https://www.rahtis.eu/en/api-docs) the damage photos and the CMR are in the job's documents, so the client can see them too without a separate phone call.

How long must a digital CMR be kept and how should it be archived?

Retention periods in Finland and the EU

In Finland, vouchers and other accounting material, which include consignment notes and transport documents, must be kept for at least six years from the end of the year in which the financial year ended, and the books and financial statements for ten years from the end of the financial year (Finlex, Accounting Act 1336/1997, chapter 2, section 10). The CMR Convention itself sets no retention period. In the other Nordic and EU countries retention periods typically range from five to ten years, so always check the requirement in the customer's country before deciding how to archive. An electronic CMR is kept for the same number of years as a paper one.

Archiving: PDF, original data or both

A PDF copy on its own is the weakest option: its signature data cannot be verified later. It is safer to keep the original electronic document in a system that keeps the metadata and signatures unaltered. Many hauliers do both: the system holds the data, and PDFs are saved at year end as a backup.

In practice, archiving is best linked to the same place as dispatch and invoicing, so that years' worth of records don't end up scattered across different services. RAHTIS keeps the scanned consignment note, the damage photos and the signature on the same job, and you can find out more or request a demo at https://www.rahtis.eu/ru/apply.

What should you check before switching from paper to digital consignment notes?

Choosing a system from a small firm's point of view

Test the system on one of your own empty runs and jobs before committing: how many clicks does it take to create a consignment note, and does it work on a phone at the depot without a network connection? Ask for a written price per company, not per user – in a 1–12 vehicle firm, per-user pricing quickly doubles the cost. Make sure the system supports CMR reservations and archiving as standard, not as an add-on module.

Training drivers and customers

For drivers, one practice run is enough: signing, attaching a photo and recording a discrepancy. Tell customers and consignees in advance that acknowledgement will be by link or app, and keep the paper option available for the first few weeks. Start with one regular route, not all jobs at once.

RAHTIS, honestly: where it's enough and where it isn't

RAHTIS handles consignment note management as part of dispatch and invoicing: the job is published, the driver updates the status, and the signature, photos and scanned consignment note are saved on the job in one place. It does not issue an e-CMR under the Additional Protocol and is not an e-CMR archive, nor does it merge several freight exchange logins into a single sign-on: jobs come from your own customers and from RAHTIS's own load board. If you need a load board and your own fleet management in one place, it is enough; if you need an official e-CMR, you will need a separate e-CMR service for it.

How does the digital consignment note link to dispatch and invoicing?

When the consignment note is digital, the same data can live throughout the job: order, dispatch, receipt and POD form a single chain that dispatch, the driver and invoicing all look at simultaneously. A paper CMR requires copying and re-keying at every stage, and errors arise precisely at those handovers.

The consignment note as part of the job life cycle

In practice, a job moves through statuses: published, assigned, collected, delivered, POD received, invoiced. When the consignment note is part of the system, the arrival of the POD can trigger the invoice directly, and an available drop trailer or return load shows up straight away without phone calls. The electronic signature is a precondition here, because the driver's and consignee's confirmation reaches the system immediately rather than waiting for the paper to come back to the office. The eIDAS Regulation provides a common EU framework for electronic signatures, on which confirmations between systems can be relied upon (EUR-Lex, eIDAS Regulation).

Documenting drop trailer and freight exchange jobs

On jobs taken from a freight exchange, the order, consignment note and POD are often in three different places. A digital chain keeps them in the same work queue, so documents can be traced even through a subcontracting chain. In RAHTIS the consignment note, POD and invoicing are built from the same job data, but to be honest: if your customer specifically requires paper, the system doesn't remove that obligation; it supports both side by side.

Summary: moving from paper to digital CMR

Break the switch into five steps. First, make sure the system you choose meets the requirements of the e-CMR Additional Protocol and covers the mandatory particulars. Second, try the signature on a single job before a wider roll-out. Third, make reservations part of the driver's routine so that damage and discrepancies are recorded during the journey. Fourth, sort out archiving: the digital CMR is kept in the system, but backups and the retention period are your responsibility. Fifth, link the consignment note to dispatch and invoicing, and the paper shuffle disappears altogether.

An honest note about our own system: RAHTIS handles job tracking and documents in one place and takes the signature in the driver app, but it does not issue an e-CMR under the Additional Protocol, so for that you need a separate service. Start small, measure the hours saved each week, and only expand once paper and digital are running side by side without problems.

FAQ

Can a driver sign a CMR without a network connection or a smartphone?

Most systems support an offline mode: the signature and entries are stored on the device and synchronised later. If the driver has no smartphone at all, the options are a paper CMR note or confirming the driver's ID on an office device. Test the offline function on your own route before committing, because the signal often drops at depots and ports.

Will customs or an insurer accept a digital CMR instead of a paper one in a dispute?

Yes, if the carriage is between countries that have joined the Additional Protocol and the system meets its requirements: the document is tamper-proof, the signatures show the signatory and a timestamp, and the data can be handed over at an inspection. In a dispute, what decides the matter are the reservations, the photos and the to-the-second timestamps that e-CMR records automatically. Insurers value photos and a precise time of delivery because they shorten the investigation.

What do I do if the consignee refuses to sign electronically and insists on paper?

Go back to the paper form for that delivery and record the discrepancy in the system so the chain stays traceable. Tell the customer in advance that acknowledgement will be by link or app, and keep the paper option available for the first few weeks. Start with one regular route so that briefing consignees stays manageable and discrepancies don't pile up.

Can one consignment note cover a trailer swap or a drop trailer job with several vehicles?

A CMR is tied to a single contract of carriage, but changing tractor units doesn't prevent that: a change of driver or trailer is recorded as an entry on the same document. On a drop trailer job with several vehicles, each leg needs its own receipt and signature. Check how your system handles multi-leg journeys before bringing such jobs into the digital chain.

How much does introducing an e-CMR system cost a small haulage firm?

The price depends on the pricing model, so ask for it in writing per company, not per user: in a 1–12 vehicle firm, per-user pricing quickly doubles the cost. Other cost items are driver training, for which one practice run is enough, and any add-on modules such as archiving. Test the system on one of your own empty runs before committing, so that you only pay for a solution that works.

consignment-note-cmr-opas.title: CMR consignment note: a guide for small hauliers
consignment-note-cmr-opas.description: The CMR consignment note explained box by box: who fills it in, who signs it, and how a correctly completed note speeds up invoicing and the POD chain.
consignment-note-cmr-opas.html:
Key takeaways

  • The CMR consignment note is the key document for international road carriage; it evidences the contract of carriage and the taking over of the goods, and serves as proof of delivery for invoicing.
  • The carrier's signature binds them to what the note says, so the number of packages, their marks and condition must be checked before signing.
  • The consignee's signature is the POD that releases the invoice; without it payment is delayed and the burden of proof shifts to the carrier.
  • On the most common form layout, box 18 holds the carrier's reservations and box 24 the consignee's receipt, so empty boxes shift the risk of a dispute onto the carrier.
  • The electronic e-CMR is a legal alternative to paper in Finland for carriage between countries that have joined its Additional Protocol, but it only works if the consignee is on the system too.

The CMR consignment note is the document for international road carriage that evidences the contract of carriage, the taking over of the goods and the terms of carriage, and its entries decide the division of liability between the sender, the carrier and the consignee. This guide covers the legal basis of the CMR Convention, the numbered boxes 1–24 of the most common form layout one by one, and what each party's signature means in law.

What is a CMR consignment note and why is it mandatory?

The CMR consignment note is an international document for the carriage of goods that proves the carrier has taken over the goods and that a contract of carriage exists. At the same time it is the proof of delivery on which you invoice the customer.

The CMR Convention and Finland

The 1956 CMR Convention has bound Finland since 1973, as well as Sweden, Norway and Denmark; it defines the content of the consignment note and the parties' liabilities in the official text of the CMR Convention (UNECE). When you carry goods for reward across a border and the country of loading or delivery is a contracting state, the CMR applies: the contract is confirmed by a consignment note, and its entries and signatures determine who bears liability for damage and delay.

When a CMR consignment note is not required

For purely domestic journeys the CMR is not mandatory: a domestic consignment note under the Finnish Road Transport Contracts Act or another delivery document is enough. On international journeys an electronic e-CMR can replace paper when both the country of loading and the country of delivery have joined its Additional Protocol; Finland ratified the Protocol in 2019. In RAHTIS the signature and the scanned consignment note are saved on the job, and data protection is described in the RAHTIS privacy notice.

Who fills it in, who signs it and who is liable?

The sender's responsibility

The sender fills in the key details of the consignment note: the parties, a description of the goods, the weight and the delivery address. By signing, the sender confirms that the information given is correct and is liable for any errors in it. If the details of the goods are incomplete, the sender bears the consequences.

The carrier taking over the goods

The driver's signature means the carrier has taken over the goods and checked what is apparent: the number of packages, their marks and numbers, and the apparent condition of the goods and packaging. Hidden defects cannot be detected, and under Article 17 of the CMR the carrier can be relieved of liability for damage caused by the inherent nature of the goods or defective packing. When you collect a load, check the boxes before you sign, because your signature binds you to what the note says.

The consignee's signature and the POD

The consignee's signature is the proof of delivery (POD): it proves the goods have been delivered and accepted. Without it, invoicing stays open and you may be left waiting weeks for your money. The RAHTIS driver app takes the consignee's signature on screen and scans the consignment note onto the job, so you know immediately which delivery is complete and which needs a phone call (RAHTIS API documentation).

CMR form boxes 1–12: the parties and the goods

The top half of the form shows who is sending, who is receiving, where the goods travel from and to, and what was loaded onto the vehicle. These boxes determine who can bring a claim and to whom the proof of delivery belongs. The numbers follow the most common form layout; some layouts number the boxes differently.

Boxes 1–4: sender, consignee and right of disposal

Box 1 records the sender and box 2 the consignee. Box 3 is the place of delivery of the goods, and box 4 the place and date of taking over the goods, i.e. loading. The right of disposal is not a box on the form: under Article 12 of the CMR the sender may change, for example, the place of delivery or the consignee until the second copy of the consignment note is handed to the consignee, unless the sender has stated on the note that the consignee holds this right from the start.

Boxes 5–12: attachments and details of the goods

Box 5 records the documents attached to the consignment note, such as customs documents. Boxes 6–10 describe the goods: marks and numbers, number of packages, method of packing, nature of the goods and statistical number. Box 11 is the gross weight in kilograms and box 12 the volume in cubic metres. The electronic CMR holds the same particulars, and the UNECE e-CMR guide explains how the Additional Protocol works; the countries that have joined it include Finland, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Estonia, Germany and Poland.

Why the top half deserves care: box 3 says where the goods are to be delivered, and if the sender changes the place of delivery during the journey, ask for the change in writing. Boxes 6–12 serve as evidence of quantity and condition at the time of taking over, so a missing number of packages or gross weight shifts the dispute onto the carrier. Box 5 ties the customs paperwork to the consignment note: under Article 11 of the CMR the sender is liable for missing or inadequate documents, but an attachment that isn't listed makes that harder to show. In RAHTIS the order details are the same for the driver, the shipper and the API, and you can explore the API in the Finnish-language RAHTIS API documentation.

CMR form boxes 13–24: instructions, charges, reservations and signatures

Boxes 13–24 cover the sender's instructions, payment terms, the carrier's details, reservations and signatures. They are short, but this is where most after-the-event disputes arise, because the boxes are often filled in in a hurry at the loading bay.

Boxes 13–15: instructions, payment and cash on delivery

Box 13 holds the sender's instructions, such as customs and other formalities and handling instructions like temperature requirements. Box 14 is the instruction for payment of carriage (carriage paid or carriage forward), and box 15 is cash on delivery, the amount to be collected from the consignee before the goods are handed over. If the cash on delivery is not collected, the carrier is liable to the sender for it (Article 21). If carriage is invoiced later, state the payment instruction clearly so that the driver and invoicing have the same information.

Boxes 16–24: carrier, reservations and signatures

Box 16 records the carrier and box 17 any successive carriers. Box 18 holds the carrier's reservations and observations on taking over the goods, box 19 special agreements (such as a declared value or an agreed delivery time), and box 20 the amounts to be paid: carriage, supplementary charges, customs duties and other charges, and who pays them. Box 21 is the place and date the note was made out, boxes 22 and 23 are the signatures of the sender and the carrier, and box 24 is the consignee's receipt for the goods.

BoxContentTypical mistake
13Sender's instructionsVerbal instructions don't make it onto paper
14Instruction for payment of carriageBox left blank, who pays is disputed later
15Cash on deliveryAmount not collected before handover
18Carrier's reservationsPoor packaging or a broken seal not recorded
20Amounts to be paidCarriage or surcharges not entered, leading to a collection dispute

In RAHTIS the order details are the same for the driver, the shipper and invoicing, so they carry over to the consignment note without separate copying. The same chain also works for cross-border jobs, as shown in the German-language version.

Paper or electronic CMR consignment note?

Both paper and electronic consignment notes are legal. The electronic version rests on the 2008 Additional Protocol to the CMR Convention, which Finland ratified in 2019, and it can be used on carriage between countries that have joined the Protocol.

The legal status of e-CMR

The electronic consignment note (e-CMR) is made out under the Additional Protocol to the CMR Convention, and its electronic signature has the same legal effect as one on paper, provided the system guarantees the authenticity and integrity of the document. The problem isn't the law but the fact that the loader or consignee may not be on an e-CMR system.

What works in practice in the Nordic countries

For a small fleet, paper still works: the driver gets a signed copy, scans it and sends it to the office. It's slow, and paper gets lost. If your customers are subcontractors found through TIMOCOM or Trans.eu, ask in advance whether they accept e-CMR. RAHTIS saves the signature and the scanned consignment note on the same job for invoicing, but honestly: if the consignee insists on pen and paper, going electronic only gets you halfway.

What happens if the CMR consignment note contains an error or is missing?

A missing or incorrect CMR consignment note does not invalidate the contract of carriage, but it shifts the burden of proof onto you: if the goods are damaged, you have to show what you delivered and in what condition. In practice, missing paperwork shows up as late invoices and disputes over whether the goods arrived at all.

The most common mistakes on small hauliers' forms

Box 18 (carrier's reservations) is left blank even though the packaging was poor or the seal was broken. The consignee records the damage next to its receipt in box 24, and without a reservation of your own you carry the risk alone. Other typical ones: the description of the goods is written solely on the sender's say-so, package details are vague ("one load"), and box 20 is left blank, so surcharges go uninvoiced.

How liability limits relate to insurance

The liability limit of the CMR Convention (8.33 SDR per kilogram of gross weight of the goods lost or damaged, Article 23) does not replace your insurance, but the insurer assesses the claim precisely on the basis of what is written on the consignment note. A correctly completed form is the cheapest insurance evidence you will ever get.

How does the CMR consignment note fit into day-to-day driving and invoicing?

When you drive and invoice yourself, the consignment note is three documents in one: evidence of the contract of carriage, the proof of delivery and an attachment to the invoice. The structure of the form supports this: boxes 1–15 give the parties, the goods and the instructions, boxes 16–20 the carrier, reservations and charges, and boxes 21–24 the signatures. The 2007 model in the IRU's guidance on the CMR form numbers the boxes differently (reservations, for example, are in box 8), so check which layout you are using. Without the consignee's receipt in box 24 you have a journey, but no proof of delivery.

POD, rate confirmation and invoice in one chain

In practice, the POD, rate confirmation and invoice form a chain: the rate confirmation shows the price, the consignment note shows what was carried and box 18 the carrier's reservations, and the consignee's signature releases the invoice. When these three documents are together, the paper "who owes what" notebook becomes unnecessary. Clear handwriting pays: an illegible signature or a missing date is the most common reason for late payment.

Subcontracting from a freight exchange: whose CMR?

When you take a load from TIMOCOM, Trans.eu or Teleroute, the client usually provides its own consignment note on which you are entered as the carrier. Check box 16: your company must appear there if you want your own liability and your own invoice for the freight exchange booking. Keep a copy yourself: if the client disputes the delivery, your signature on the consignment note is your only evidence.

How does RAHTIS handle the consignment note and proof of delivery chain?

RAHTIS joins up the chain that currently lives on paper and in email: consignment note, POD and invoice. The driver takes the signature on screen in the app and scans the paper CMR to PDF, and the carrier closes the job without a separate upload; the shipper gets the consignment note and photos straight away. When you record the invoices you send, overdue ones show up directly, so the "who owes what" notebook goes. Jobs for your own customers and jobs taken from the load board run through the same pipeline.

What RAHTIS doesn't do (yet)

RAHTIS does not merge external freight exchanges: TIMOCOM, Teleroute and Trans.eu searches stay behind their own logins, and you carry the details of a load taken there across by hand; in RAHTIS, shippers publish jobs on its own load board. Nor does RAHTIS issue an e-CMR under the Additional Protocol: the paper consignment note travels with the goods and is scanned onto the job. And if you're thinking of switching from McLeod, RAHTIS isn't built on that scale; it's made for the day-to-day running of 1–12 vehicles.

FAQ

Can the sender or a broker fill in the CMR consignment note instead of the carrier?

Yes. The sender fills in the key details of the consignment note and is responsible for their accuracy. A broker or client may also provide a ready-made consignment note on which you are entered as the carrier. Your signature covers what you were able to check: check the number of packages, their marks and condition before signing and record any shortcomings as reservations, because your signature binds you to what the note says.

What is box 13 (sender's instructions) on the CMR and when is it mandatory?

Box 13 is reserved for the sender's instructions: customs and other formalities, and instructions on handling the goods during carriage. It isn't mandatory for every journey, but if the carriage involves customs formalities or the goods need special handling, such as temperature requirements or a specific unloading sequence, the instructions must be on paper. Verbal instructions don't appear on the consignment note, so an unrecorded instruction shifts the risk of a dispute onto you.

How many originals and copies of the CMR form are needed?

Under the CMR Convention the consignment note is made out in three original copies: the first goes to the sender, the second accompanies the goods to the consignee and the third is kept by the carrier. Form sets often include an extra copy for other purposes. For a small haulier, the most important ones are the copy that travels with you and the proof of delivery signed by the consignee. Keep a copy yourself, because if the client disputes the delivery, the signed consignment note is your only evidence.

Can a CMR consignment note be corrected afterwards if I spot a mistake?

A mistake can be corrected, but the correction must be agreed by all parties and be traceable. A private amendment made in pen without signatures loses its evidential value in a dispute. If you spot the mistake before signing, correct it immediately. If the consignee has already recorded reservations, add your own remark and ask for it to be confirmed.

Is a photographed POD without a signed CMR acceptable for invoicing?

A photo can support an invoice, but it does not replace a signed proof of delivery. Without the consignee's signature, invoicing stays open and the burden of proof shifts to you: you have to show what you delivered and in what condition. Best practice is to scan the signed paper and attach it to the invoice together with the photos.

dat-load-board-for-box-trucks-setup-guid.title: DAT Load Board for Box Trucks: Setup Guide
dat-load-board-for-box-trucks-setup-guid.description: Set up a DAT load board for box trucks: filter equipment type, read rate view per mile, and decide if the subscription beats free boards.
dat-load-board-for-box-trucks-setup-guid.html:
Key takeaways

  • Set DAT equipment type to Van or Straight Truck and skip Hotshot unless you tow a gooseneck.
  • Filter origin radius to 100-150 miles and destination radius to 200-300 miles to match box truck range.
  • Read DAT rate view as a per-mile range and compare it against your own cost per km before booking.
  • Check weight, pallet count, and remarks for liftgate or inside delivery needs before calling a broker.
  • For Nordic or Baltic lanes, a regional freight exchange usually beats DAT on fit and break-even cost.

A dat load board for box trucks only works if you configure it for your equipment: set equipment type to van or straight truck, filter deadhead to 150 miles or less, and read rate view as a per-mile range, not an average. This guide walks through those exact settings, then weighs DAT against free load boards so a one-to-twelve truck operation can decide if the subscription pays for itself.

How do you filter DAT load board searches for box truck equipment types?

Equipment type: van vs straight truck vs hotshot

DAT's search settings let you pick equipment types before anything else, and the DAT load board documentation covers the filter options in its help centre. For a box truck, start with "Van" if you run a straight box with a liftgate, and add "Straight Truck" as a second equipment type so you see both postings. Skip "Hotshot" unless you actually tow; those loads assume a gooseneck and a pickup with a trailer, and brokers posting there expect different weight ceilings.

Radius and lane filters that match a box truck's range

The filter that actually saves you time is the origin radius, because a box truck lives on short regional runs, not cross-country lanes. Set your origin radius to 100-150 miles and your destination radius wider, around 200-300 miles, which matches a same-day or next-day round trip without a forced overnight. Leave the length and weight fields alone unless a shipper specifies, since DAT posts dimensions per load rather than per equipment filter, and blank beats wrong. If you chase return loads to cut empty running, save the search once and let it persist; the same saved-lane logic applies whether you work DAT or a Nordic rahtipörssi like RAHTIS, where publishing a keikka once replaces re-entering it into every load board you are logged into.

What does DAT's rate view show for box truck lanes and how do you read it?

DAT's rate view pulls historical rates for a lane and equipment type, so you can see what straight trucks actually got paid on that lane before you spend a minute on the phone.

Spot rate vs contract rate on straight-truck lanes

Spot rates are one-off loads priced at the moment; contract rates are committed lanes at a fixed rate. On box truck lanes the gap matters less than on van lanes, but always check which one the rate view is showing. A posted load above the spot average is worth the call; one below it usually means the broker is fishing.

Reading per-mile averages against your cost per km

Convert the lane's per-mile average to per-km and hold it against your real cost per km: fuel, driver, insurance, depreciation. If a Helsinki–Tampere keikka pays under your cost line, no volume makes it worth running empty back. Rate view tells you the market price; only your own numbers tell you if it's a good job.

The same judgement applies on any rahtipörssi, not just DAT. If you're running Nordic freight, a combined TMS and freight exchange like RAHTIS keeps the rate, the CMR and the invoice on one job instead of three tools.

Which DAT workflow steps take a box truck load from search to booked?

From search to call: what to have ready

Filter to a straight truck or box truck equipment type, set your deadhead radius, and save the lane search so you can rerun it each morning. Before you dial, know three numbers: your rate per mile floor, what DAT's Rate View shows for the lane's recent spot rates, and whether the shipper will tarp or hand-load. Brokers ask for your MC number, insurance certificate, and references on the first call, so keep those in one file.

Booking, confirmation and the paperwork trail

Once you agree on a rate, get the rate confirmation in writing before you dispatch the truck, and check that it matches what you negotiated, including detention and lumper terms. The broker then sends the carrier packet; you sign, send insurance and W-9 back, and the load is booked. From there the trail is the signed rate con, the CMR or bill of lading at pickup, and the signed POD, which triggers your invoice. If you run Nordic freight, a combined TMS and freight exchange like RAHTIS collapses that paperwork into one flow: the job, the rahtikirja and the invoice follow each other instead of living in a notebook and three inboxes.

How do free load boards for box trucks compare on load volume and booking speed?

What free load boards give you and what they cost you in time

Free boards cost nothing up front and charge you in hours. You refresh manually, call brokers to ask rates because no rate data is shown, and re-enter the same load details into your spreadsheet, notebook and paper CMR. For one truck with steady direct clients, that trade can be fine. For a 4-truck outfit where you are dispatcher, accountant and safety guy at once, the refresh-and-call loop is where the day disappears.

DAT flips the trade: you pay a subscription and get rate view, saved lane filters and alerts that push loads to you, so booking speed comes from fewer manual checks rather than more phone calls.

Decision table: when DAT pays for itself

FactorFree load boardsDAT (paid)Combined TMS + exchange like RAHTIS
Box truck / pickup load volumeThin, varies by laneHighest, filtered by equipment typeNordic-focused; shippers publish directly
Rate dataNone; you ask by phoneLane rate view includedRates set by shipper on publication
AlertsRare or noneCustom per lane and equipmentJob-by-job follow-up built in
Booking speedSlow: refresh, call, confirmFaster via alerts and rate viewFastest when shipper and carrier share one system
Dispatch paperworkSeparate spreadsheet and notebookStill separate from the boardLoad, CMR and invoicing in one place

Honest shortcoming of our own product: RAHTIS does not match DAT's raw North American load volume, so if you chase US cross-border freight, DAT wins on supply. Where RAHTIS fits is Nordic freight, rahtipörssi loads and irtoperä backhauls, where the load board and your dispatch live in the same place instead of separate logins.

Is DAT worth the subscription for a single box truck or pickup operation?

Honest answer: probably not, unless you cross borders regularly. DAT's subscription tiers are priced for brokers and carriers chasing volume, and its rate data is strongest on North American lanes (DAT freight rates and subscription overview).
