For a one-truck operator in Finland, the break-even math is simple: if the subscription plus your time filtering loads costs more than the margin on one extra return load per month, it loses.

Break-even logic for a one-truck operation

Count what a paid board must produce: one booked return load per month that you would not have found otherwise. If you already have two or three regular clients, a notebook dispatch, and a freight exchange login, the marginal loads a US-focused board surfaces rarely justify the per-user cost of a paid board.

Regional alternative: Nordic and Baltic freight exchanges

Exchanges like Trans.eu or TIMOCOM cover the lanes you actually drive. A combined tool such as RAHTIS puts its own load board and dispatch in one place, so one login replaces the board-plus-TMS stack.

What load types should box truck operators avoid on DAT?

Overweight and trailer-shaped freight

DAT lets brokers post under any equipment type, so check the weight and pallet count before you call. A "partial" posting with 8 pallets or 15,000 lbs is a trailer load wearing a box truck label. If the commodity is dense, ask: steel, liquids, and packaged flooring regularly blow past straight-truck payload limits. Skip lanes where the rate only works with a 53-foot trailer's volume.

Hidden handling requirements: liftgate, inside delivery, appointment freight

The details that eat your margin live in the remarks, not the rate. A load with no liftgate flag that turns out to need one, or an inside delivery at a mall dock, can add an unpaid hour. Appointment-only freight is worse for a solo dispatcher: you hold the keikka slot while your options for a return load shrink. Read the full notes before booking, and price residential or jobsite deliveries as if the access will be bad.

How do you set up DAT alerts so box truck loads near your route reach you first?

Watch lanes and alert frequency

In DAT, a watch lane is a saved lane plus equipment filter. Set equipment to Straight Truck or Van, define origin and destination radius (50 miles around your usual route works for pickups), then choose push alerts so the load arrives on your phone the moment it posts. Speed matters: on lanes with heavy freight exchange volume, like the corridors covered by TIMOCOM's European freight exchange, the first carrier to call often takes the load.

Pairing alerts with your empty-running pattern

Set alerts on the return leg of your regular keikka before you leave the yard. If you know Tuesday ends in Turku, a watch lane from Turku north catches return loads while you are still driving, so the tyhjäajo home becomes a paid backhaul instead of dead miles.

What changes when your load board and dispatch live in one place?

RAHTIS against the same criteria: where it fits and where it does not

RAHTIS (rahtis.eu) runs the same test the earlier sections applied to DAT and the free boards. It is a combined TMS and freight exchange built for the Finnish and Nordic market: you publish a keikka once, carriers fill empty running with return loads, and you follow each job step by step instead of juggling separate logins. Where it does not compete with DAT is raw volume. DAT's US load count dwarfs anything a Nordic exchange can offer, so if your box truck work depends on high-volume spot markets, DAT remains the bigger pool. RAHTIS fits the opposite case: a small fleet working Nordic lanes, where one login for both rahtipörssi and dispatch beats three tools.

From paper CMR to tracked jobs and offers

The shift is concrete: the notebook tracking who owes what becomes a job record, the paper rahtikirja becomes a CMR note attached to the job, and offers sit next to dispatch in the same place. For a one-to-12-truck outfit, that is fewer tabs and fewer lost PODs, not a bigger load board.

FAQ

Can you use DAT load board for pickup trucks and hotshot loads?

Yes, but with caveats. DAT posts hotshot loads under the Hotshot equipment type, and those assume a pickup towing a gooseneck, not a cargo bed alone. Pickup operators without a trailer will find few matching postings, and box truck operators should skip Hotshot entirely since brokers there expect different weight ceilings and trailer-based pricing.

How many box truck loads are posted on DAT per day?

DAT does not publish a daily count broken down by equipment type, so no exact figure exists. What is known is that DAT's overall North American load volume is the largest among paid boards, and straight truck and van postings are a subset of that. Expect thin volume on narrow regional lanes and denser volume around major metro corridors.

Is a freight exchange like Trans.eu or Teleroute a better fit than DAT for Nordic box truck freight?

Usually yes. Trans.eu and TIMOCOM cover the lanes a Nordic box truck actually drives, with shippers and carriers already on them. DAT's rate data and volume are strongest on North American lanes, so its subscription rarely pays off for regional Finnish or Baltic work. A combined exchange and dispatch tool suits that market even better.

dat-load-board-pricing.title: DAT Load Board Pricing: What Each Tier Really Costs
dat-load-board-pricing.description: DAT One carrier plans list at $59–$339 a month, broker plans at $159–$449. What each tier costs, extra-user fees, and European alternatives.
dat-load-board-pricing.html:
Key takeaways

  • DAT One carrier plans list at $59/month for Standard, $149 for Enhanced, $169 for Pro, $259 for Select and $339 for Office; broker plans run $159-$449. DAT publishes no annual-billing discount.
  • The checkout price is a floor: sales quotes vary, and add-ons like extra seats and RateView push the real total higher.
  • DAT prices by plan, not truck count: the plan price covers one user, so solo dispatchers pay one base fee, but each extra user costs more.
  • DAT's lane coverage is strongest in North America and thin on Finnish domestic and Baltic cross-border freight.
  • European exchanges like Teleroute, TIMOCOM and Trans.eu cover European corridors and fit subcontracting workflows better for Nordic carriers.

DAT load board pricing runs from $59 per month for DAT One Standard to $339 for the Office carrier plan and $449 for the top broker plan, with extra users and add-on tools pushing the total higher. This breakdown covers each tier line by line, then compares the total cost against European freight exchanges like Teleroute, TIMOCOM and Trans.eu, so a Finland-based carrier running rahtipörssi loads can decide whether DAT is worth the budget at all.

How much does DAT load board cost per month in each tier?

DAT lists five carrier plans and three broker plans on its pricing page. At the time of writing (November 2026), the carrier plans cost $59 a month for DAT One Standard, $149 for Enhanced, $169 for Pro, $259 for Select and $339 for Office; the broker plans cost $159 for Express, $319 for Select Broker and $449 for Office Broker, and combined broker/carrier plans $339 or $469 (DAT One pricing). The page lists monthly prices only. Standard covers basic load search; Enhanced adds 15-day average lane rates; Pro adds 7-day lane rates, more search tabs and TriHaul routing; Select and Office show the best available lane rates, and Office adds workgroups for several users.

Published rates vs quoted rates

DAT's checkout price is a floor, not the final number. Sales regularly quotes different figures on the phone, and add-ons such as extra user seats or separate analytics products change the total. Treat any quote as negotiable and get it in writing before you commit.

Monthly vs annual billing math

DAT's pricing page lists monthly prices only and publishes no annual-billing discount; if sales offers a cheaper rate for a longer commitment, get it in writing, because it locks you in for the whole term. For a 1-12 truck operation testing whether DAT fits alongside your rahtipörssi logins, one month of Pro is the cheaper experiment; a longer commitment only pays off once you know you'll use it weekly. Whatever you sign, check how your data and documents are handled before uploading loads or CMR details, as with any platform (see, for example, how we document this at RAHTIS privacy).

What is the difference between DAT One Select, Pro, and Broker tiers?

DAT splits its carrier load board into five plans, and the gap between them is mostly about how many searches you can run side by side and how fresh the rate data is. The names change occasionally, but the structure holds: cheap entry plans, mid plans for owner-operators who live on the board, and top plans for fleets, with separate plans for brokers.

What the entry plans limit

Standard and Enhanced are the floor. Standard is aimed at partial-load operators and shows little rate data; Enhanced adds 15-day average lane rates but only two search tabs. That is workable if you run one truck and check the board once a morning. The moment you hunt return loads across several lanes or recheck rates mid-day, the limits bite, and with older rate averages you are negotiating partly blind.

When Pro pays for itself

Pro adds a third search tab, fresher 7-day lane rates and TriHaul routing, and Select moves up to the best available lane rates and ten search tabs; fresher rate data is the real reason carriers upgrade. If you subcontract from a freight exchange alongside your own clients, knowing the going rate on a lane before you quote is worth more than the tier difference. The same logic applies on this side of the Atlantic: TIMOCOM and Trans.eu both charge for rate and market data at higher access levels, so the pattern is not unique to DAT. A 4-truck outfit where one person dispatches, invoices and chases PODs should judge any tier by one question: does it cut a phone call or a notebook entry per keikka? That is also the test we built RAHTIS around, publishing a job once and following it to paid invoice. Where DAT falls short for Nordic operators is lane coverage: it is strongest in North America, thin on Finnish domestic and Baltic cross-border freight.

Broker and Office plan scope

The broker plans (Express, Select Broker, Office Broker) are for posting loads and finding carriers, with DAT's market-rate data; Office adds workgroups for several users. For a 1-12 truck carrier the broker plans are overkill; you are paying for features that only matter if you broker other carriers' freight.

Are there hidden fees like setup, add-on, or cancellation charges?

The headline monthly price is not the whole bill. Extra users cost extra (on the Select and Office plans DAT lists $169 a month per additional user), and DAT sells separate products such as RateView analytics next to the load board. What each rep bundles varies, which is why two carriers on the same tier can pay different amounts. DAT's own sales pages list the add-on products separately from the core membership (DAT sales page), so ask for a line-item quote before signing.

Cancellation and auto-renewal terms

DAT One plans are billed monthly and renew automatically. Per DAT's support pages, a cancellation takes effect on the next billing date and unused time is not refunded, so cancel before the cycle ends. If sales sells you a longer term, its own notice and cancellation terms apply; get them in writing at signup.

Budget the same way you would for a rahtipörssi subscription: base fee, add-ons, and the commitment period. If you also run a TMS like RAHTIS alongside a freight exchange, count the DAT add-ons against what those tools already cover so you are not paying twice for rates and document handling.

Is DAT pricing different for owner-operators vs fleets vs brokers?

Per-seat vs per-company pricing

DAT prices by membership tier, not by truck count, so a one-truck owner-operator and a twelve-truck carrier on the same plan pay the same base subscription. The plan price covers one user, and the cost scales when you add users: a dispatcher who is also the accountant and safety guy needs one login, but a second dispatcher or an office clerk means another per-user charge. Brokers pay more because the Broker tier adds features carriers never touch, like posting loads for carriers rather than searching for loads.

Why the 4-truck owner pays disproportionately

If you dispatch alone, per-seat pricing is actually in your favour: one seat covers the whole operation. The disproportionate cost is your time, not the invoice. Juggling a load board, a separate TMS and a paper rahtikirja book is the real per-user fee, paid in evenings. That is the problem a combined freight exchange and TMS like RAHTIS targets, with one place to find keikka, dispatch and invoice, and no per-seat penalty for being a one-person office.

How does DAT pricing compare to European freight exchanges like Teleroute, TIMOCOM and Trans.eu?

Coverage vs cost for Northern European lanes

DAT is built around US and Canadian lanes. A Finnish carrier moving port, terminal or irtoperä freight out of Helsinki, Turku or Hanko will find almost nothing to bid on there, so the monthly fee buys access you cannot use. Teleroute, TIMOCOM and Trans.eu all operate on European corridors, which is where your keikka traffic actually lives. If you also pull backhaul from a Nordic rahtipörssi, a US load board adds a second login without adding a single return load. Check the renewal terms before subscribing to anything: DAT subscriptions auto-renew, and the DAT site is where you find the account and billing terms that govern cancellation.

Subcontracting and offer-tab workflows

The European exchanges are built for the subcontracting chain: you post a load, carriers bid in the offer tab, you accept, and the freight exchange documents the assignment. That maps directly to how a small Finnish fleet covers overflow with subcontracting partners. DAT's workflow assumes you are the one searching for trucks, not handing loads to subcontractors, so its tier structure rewards a different job than yours.

Is DAT worth the price for a small carrier, or should the budget go to a TMS?

The stacked-tools cost trap

The subscription fee is only part of what a load board costs you. Add a separate TMS, a separate invoicing tool, and the hours you spend each week retyping the same load into three systems, and the real number is much higher. For a one-person dispatch office running 4-12 trucks, admin time is often the biggest line item, and it never shows up on a quote.

Where RAHTIS fits, and where it falls short

RAHTIS combines the freight exchange and the TMS: shippers publish a job once, carriers fill empty trucks and track the keikka step by step, with the rahtikirja and paperwork handled in the same place. That removes the separate load board logins and the paper notebook for who owes what.

Where it falls short: if your customers are North American brokers, RAHTIS does not replace DAT, and its exchange coverage is strongest in Finland and Northern Europe. If you need deep US market rates, you still need a DAT subscription on top.

Can you negotiate or get a discount on DAT membership?

DAT does not publish discount rates, but the subscription is sold through a sales team, and reps routinely have room to move on price if you commit to a longer term or ask directly. Committing to a longer term is the usual lever; month-to-month is the rate you pay for flexibility. What is fixed: the tier structure itself and the per-user add-ons, which rarely get discounted for a 1-12 truck operation.

European exchanges are no different here. Teleroute does not list prices either: its price depends on company size, number of users and the modules you need, and you get it after a demo (Teleroute membership). Whichever board you pick, compare written quotes, not list prices.

Which DAT tier fits which carrier profile?

If you run one truck and book everything from your phone, the entry tier covers the load board itself; you don't need broker features or extra seats. A 2-6 truck fleet with own clients plus freight exchange subcontracting needs fresh rate data and several search tabs, so Pro or Select is the honest fit; pay for an extra user only if a second person dispatches.

If you also broker loads or post freight for subcontractors, a broker or combined broker/carrier plan is unavoidable, since posting loads is broker-side functionality. But a Nordic carrier subcontracting via Teleroute, TIMOCOM or Trans.eu should ask a harder question first: does DAT access pay for itself at all, or is the budget better spent on dispatch and invoicing that runs the trucks you already have?

That's the same test we built RAHTIS around: publish once, follow the job, invoice without a paper notebook. Whatever board you pick, the TMS decision matters more than the tier.

FAQ

Does DAT charge per user or per company?

DAT charges by plan, not by truck: the monthly plan price covers one user, so a one-truck owner-operator and a twelve-truck carrier on the same plan pay the same base price. The cost scales with users, not trucks. A solo dispatcher who also handles invoicing needs one login, but adding a second dispatcher or office clerk means paying for another user (DAT lists $169 a month per additional user on Select and Office).

Can I use DAT load board from Finland or elsewhere in Europe?

Yes, you can subscribe and search from Finland, but the value is limited. DAT's lane coverage is strongest in North America and thin on Finnish domestic and Baltic cross-border freight, so a carrier running Helsinki, Turku or Hanko traffic will find little to bid on. European exchanges like Teleroute, TIMOCOM and Trans.eu cover those corridors instead.

What happens to my posted loads and rate data if I cancel DAT?

DAT One plans are billed monthly and renew automatically; per DAT's support pages, a cancellation takes effect on the next billing date, with no refund for unused time. Posted loads and searches end with access, so download anything you need before the billing period closes. If you signed a longer term with sales, check its cancellation terms.

Is there a free trial before paying for a DAT tier?

DAT's pricing page offers no free trial of the paid plans; a free DAT One account gives only limited access. The practical alternative is one month of a mid tier paid monthly: it tests whether the board fits your lanes without locking you into a long commitment while you evaluate it.

Do I still need a separate TMS if I have a DAT subscription?

Usually yes. DAT is a load board with rate data; it does not dispatch, invoice or track your paperwork, so most carriers stack a TMS or invoicing tool on top, retyping loads between systems. A combined freight exchange and TMS like RAHTIS covers find-load-to-paid-invoice in one place, though it does not replace DAT for North American customers.

kuljettajan-tyoaikojen-seuranta-lain-vaa.title: Recording drivers' working time to meet legal requirements
kuljettajan-tyoaikojen-seuranta-lain-vaa.description: Recording drivers' working time as Finnish law requires: log hours, overtime and breaks correctly and avoid inspection problems. Checklist and example included.
kuljettajan-tyoaikojen-seuranta-lain-vaa.html:
Key takeaways

  • Working time records must be kept until the limitation period for claims ends, i.e. two years from the end of the calendar year in which the right to compensation arose, so keeping them for three years is a safe practice.
  • Tachograph data alone is not enough as working time records; it has to be combined with timesheets and job orders.
  • Responsibility for recording always lies with the employer, even if the recording is done externally or by the driver.
  • Driver card data must be downloaded at the latest every 28 days and vehicle unit data at the latest every 90 days, and the downloaded data must be kept for at least one year.
  • Overtime must be recorded separately during the shift itself, because it feeds directly into the payslip and your readiness for inspection.

Recording drivers' working time in line with legal requirements means logging driving, other work, breaks and periods of availability for each driver in your working time records, in accordance with the Finnish Working Hours Act (872/2019) and EU Directive 2002/15/EC, and keeping those records for at least two years. This guide brings both pieces of legislation together into one checklist, with an example job, including empty running, loading and breaks, logged line by line.

What does the law require when recording drivers' working time?

Recording drivers' working time is based on two pieces of legislation, which set both the limits and the recording obligation. Below is a brief summary of each, and of who is responsible.

The Finnish Working Hours Act 872/2019

The working time of employed drivers is governed by the general Finnish Working Hours Act (872/2019, Finlex), which has its own sections for motor vehicle drivers: daily working time (section 9), the 60-hour weekly cap (section 18), breaks (section 24) and the driver's logbook (section 31). The Act requires the employer to keep records of hours worked, overtime hours and the overtime pay made for them (section 32), and to keep those records until the limitation period for claims ends. The Act came into force at the start of 2020 and replaced the previous Working Hours Act (605/1996). There is no separate drivers' working time act; the working time of self-employed drivers is governed by its own act (349/2013). As the provisions on drivers implement an EU directive, the requirements are in line with other Member States, but the detailed limits may differ.

EU Working Time Directive 2002/15/EC

Directive 2002/15/EC harmonises the working time rules for drivers across the EU. Finnish law was drafted on its basis, so the Directive's requirements are reflected directly in the domestic recording obligation. The Directive sets minimum requirements, such as maximum weekly working time and minimum break lengths, but leaves the details to national legislation. This means that if you run cross-border international traffic, you need to know both Finnish law and the corresponding rules in the destination country.

The employer's and the driver's responsibilities

Responsibility for recording lies with the employer, i.e. you, even if you also do driving work yourself. The driver's job is to report their working time correctly. When recording is in order, a single system holding the data is enough at an inspection, just as RAHTIS brings jobs and their details together in one place. The employer's responsibility also extends to making sure the driver understands their reporting obligation: if the driver doesn't report working time correctly, the penalty still falls on the employer. That is why it's important to give drivers clear instructions and a recording template that minimises human error.

What information must be entered in the working time records?

Mandatory information

For every shift, at least the following must be recorded for drivers' working time records to meet the legal requirements (Working Hours Act 872/2019 and Directive 2002/15/EC):

ItemExample
Driver's name and vehicle registration numberMatti M., ABC-123
Start and finish time of the shift06:00–18:30
Working time and overtime shown separately8 h regular working time, 3 h 45 min overtime
Breaks and their duration45 min break, 11:30–12:15
Periods of availability and standby3 h waiting at the loading point
Time off and daily rest18:30–06:00

Overtime must be recorded separately, because it is paid at an enhanced rate and counts towards the 48-hour maximum working time. Waiting at the loading point is working time when the driver must stay there at the employer's disposal (Working Hours Act, section 3), even if they aren't driving; if they are free to leave the truck, the collective agreement for the truck sector pays the time as waiting-time pay, but it does not count as working time. The records must also show the driver's working time arrangement and any exceptional arrangements that have been applied. For example, general working time (8 hours a day, 40 hours a week) and period-based working time (80 hours per two weeks) are recorded separately, because overtime is calculated differently for each.

Where the data comes from: tachograph, timesheets and other documentation

Tachograph data shows driving, breaks and other work, but it doesn't cover everything. Shift start and finish times, periods of availability and information reported by the driver come from the timesheet or a system entry. In practice you need three sources combined: tachograph printouts, the timesheet and the job orders. Driver card data gives precise times, but it doesn't tell you whether a period was loading, unloading or empty running. The job orders show what the driver was supposed to do, but not always when they did it. The timesheet or system entry is the glue that joins the two together and produces the statutory working time records.

A worked recording example for one shift

Monday: start at 06:00, drop trailer collected at 07:00, 45-minute break at 11:30, consignment note signed at destination at 16:00, load unloaded at 17:30, shift ends at 18:30. What gets recorded: 11 h 45 min working time (a 12.5-hour shift minus the 45-minute break), of which about an hour is waiting at the unloading point. Under general working time, the 3 h 45 min above 8 hours is overtime; under period-based working time, overtime is calculated at the end of the two-week period. When jobs and records run in the same system, as in RAHTIS, the job times and the records sit in the same chain (RAHTIS – Transportledning och lastbörs).

Broken down in more detail, the working day looks like this: 06:00–07:00 is other work: the pre-departure vehicle check, coupling the trailer and checking the freight documents. 07:00–11:30 is driving time, of which the tachograph records 4.5 hours of continuous driving. 11:30–12:15 is the statutory 45-minute break. 12:15–16:00 is driving time, including a short refuelling stop.

16:00–17:30 is unloading and waiting, of which unloading is other work and waiting is working time, because the driver has to stay on site. 17:30–18:30 is the return drive to the employer's yard and vehicle maintenance. This breakdown is what an inspector wants to see.

How long must working time data be kept?

Retention period for working time records

Working time records must be kept until the limitation period for claims ends, i.e. two years from the end of the calendar year in which the right to compensation arose (Working Hours Act, sections 32 and 40). This applies to all recorded data: hours worked, overtime and breaks. The EU Working Time Directive 2002/15/EC requires records to be kept of mobile workers' working time, and those records to be kept for at least two years after the end of the period they cover. In practice it is wise to keep the records for longer than the minimum, because a retrospective claim may come later. For example, a driver may claim overtime pay after the event, and without records you have no evidence of what happened. Keeping records for three years is a safe practice that also covers any late claims.

Retention period for tachograph charts and data

Tachograph printouts and downloaded digital data must be kept for at least one year. If the data is used as the basis for working time records, the same two-year retention obligation applies to it as well. Systematic electronic archiving removes the risk of paper charts going missing. RAHTIS does not archive tachograph files, but you can pass job times from it to other systems via its API (the interface specifications are in the API documentation). Digital data must be kept in its original format, i.e. .ddd and .v1b files must not be edited. If you edit the files, they lose their evidential value at an inspection. That is why it's important to download the card regularly and store the data in a locked archive that only authorised users can access.

What are the limits on working time, overtime and breaks?

Daily and weekly working time

The Working Hours Act (872/2019) sets its own limits for drivers, some of which are stricter than in other sectors. A motor vehicle driver's daily working time may not exceed 11 hours in the 24 hours following daily rest, and it may be extended to no more than 13 hours if the work cannot otherwise be organised (section 9); under the collective agreement for the truck sector, daily working time is limited by the agreement's rules on rest and breaks. Working time covers loading, unloading, maintenance and waiting during which the driver must stay on site, as well as driving. Working time including overtime may average no more than 48 hours a week over four months, and a driver within the scope of the driving and rest time regulation may work no more than 60 hours in any calendar week (section 18). The current Act has no separate annual overtime cap: overtime is limited by the 48-hour average. These limits are worth writing straight into your own checklist, so that recording drivers' working time in line with the law becomes routine rather than a separate project.

Overtime limits and compensation

Overtime is only permitted with the driver's consent and is recorded separately from regular working time. Overtime is paid at an enhanced rate or compensated with time off, so how it's broken down in the records feeds directly into the payslip. Under general working time, overtime is work beyond eight hours a day or 40 hours a week; under period-based working time in the collective agreement for the truck sector, it is work beyond 80 hours in the two-week period. For daily overtime, pay is increased by 50 per cent for the first two hours and by 100 per cent after that; for weekly overtime, by 50 per cent (Working Hours Act, section 20). In period-based working time, the first 12 overtime hours are paid at +50 per cent and the rest at +100 per cent, and the collective agreement may provide for better terms. Record overtime separately during the shift itself and don't leave it to be fixed in the monthly routine, because then the driver doesn't know what their pay is based on.

Breaks and rest periods

Under the driving and rest time regulation 561/2006, a break of at least 45 minutes must be taken after 4.5 hours of driving, and it may be split into two parts (first at least 15 minutes, then at least 30 minutes). Based on working time, the driver must also be given a break of at least 30 minutes for every 5.5 hours of work (Working Hours Act, section 24, and the collective agreement for the truck sector); Directive 2002/15/EC requires a 30-minute break when working time is 6–9 hours and a 45-minute break when it exceeds 9 hours. Daily rest must be at least 11 hours and weekly rest 45 hours. Daily rest may be reduced to nine hours no more than three times between two weekly rest periods. Weekly rest may be reduced to 24 hours, provided at least one regular 45-hour weekly rest is taken in any two consecutive weeks and the reduction is compensated by an equivalent period of rest taken en bloc before the end of the third week following. These exceptions must be recorded separately so that the inspector can see when reduced rest was applied and whether it complied with the rules.

How do you combine tachograph data with working time records?

The tachograph records the hours driven, but working time records need more: working time subject to monitoring, breaks and periods of availability must be derived from the card data and supplemented manually. For driving and rest times, the source data are on the card directly in line with Regulation (EC) No 561/2006, but records meeting the working time legislation only come into being once that data is combined with information on loading and other work. Regulation (EC) No 561/2006 sets driving and rest time limits that are separate from the working time limits. Under the Regulation, continuous driving time is limited to 4.5 hours, and daily driving time to 9 hours, extendable to 10 hours twice a week. These limits apply only to driving, whereas Working Hours Act 872/2019 covers all work, including loading, unloading and waiting.

Downloading the card and the vehicle unit

Download the driver card at the latest every 28 days and the vehicle unit at the latest every 90 days. Import the data into software that reads .ddd and .v1b files directly. RAHTIS does not read tachograph files, but you can bring job times into the same software via the RAHTIS API. That way the card data doesn't stay as PDF printouts but flows straight into your working time records. The card's memory is limited: when it is full, the oldest data is overwritten with new data, and anything not downloaded then has to be retrieved from the vehicle unit, if it is still stored there. That is why card downloads should be set as a calendar reminder, not left to the driver's discretion.

Interpreting anomalies: empty running, loading and waiting

The tachograph doesn't distinguish empty running from laden running, or loading from other work. Mark them yourself: empty running as driving, loading as other work, and waiting as either other work or availability, depending on whether the driver is free to use the time as they wish. Without a note, unclear periods are hard to explain at an inspection. For example, if the driver spends two hours at the loading point, the tachograph will show "other work", "availability" or "break/rest" depending on which activity the driver selected. If the driver selected break but was actually loading, the working time records end up wrong. Correct these anomalies in the monthly routine by comparing job orders with the card data.

Monthly routine for a small firm

Go through drivers' cards every month: compare the hours on the card with the records, correct anomalies and save everything before the start of the following month. The monthly routine is when you notice if a driver has recorded breaks that weren't taken, or if overtime is missing. Allow 30 minutes per driver for the routine. If there are many anomalies, retrain the driver on how to record. Don't leave corrections until the following month, because then errors pile up and become harder to fix.

What happens if recording is inadequate?

Inspections and authorities

Compliance with the Working Hours Act is supervised by the occupational safety and health authority, which since the start of 2026 has been the Finnish Licensing and Supervision Agency (Lupa- ja valvontavirasto; previously the occupational safety and health divisions of the Regional State Administrative Agencies, AVI); the police also check driving and rest times at roadside checks. At an inspection you may be asked for working time records, tachograph data and employment contracts. If records are missing or incomplete, that in itself is a breach of the law, even if the driver's working hours were otherwise within the rules. An inspection can lead to written notices or obligations with deadlines, and the matter may end up being put right afterwards by an employers' association or a lawyer, at greater cost. An occupational safety and health inspection may be announced in advance or unannounced. Unannounced inspections often target firms whose operations have attracted attention, for example through lots of overtime or short rest periods. That is why records must always be up to date, not just when an inspection looms.

Duty to correct and the driver's rights

Inadequate recording often ends up costing the driver: overtime, days off and rest periods aren't realised if they aren't recorded. The driver can claim compensation retrospectively within two years of the end of the calendar year in which the right arose (Working Hours Act, section 40), so a claim may cover periods almost three years in the past. Correct the records before an inspection, not during it. If a driver claims compensation after the event and you have no records showing that no overtime was worked, the burden of proof shifts to you. This means you may have to pay compensation even if the overtime was never actually worked. That is why the records protect both driver and employer.

How should working time recording be organised in a 1–12 vehicle firm?

Options: forms, spreadsheet and software

In a one-vehicle firm, a paper form or freely structured records will do, as long as the details for every 24-hour period can be found. From two vehicles upwards, paper starts to leak: shifts, tachograph printouts and allowances payable are recorded in different places, and a missing entry at an inspection is your responsibility. Remember too that tachograph data must be kept for at least one year under Regulation (EU) No 165/2014. A spreadsheet is enough if you record with discipline, but it won't remind you of missing entries or total up overtime for you. At three vehicles a spreadsheet becomes prone to human error: one forgotten overtime entry a month per driver adds up to 36 entries a year, and they're missing at the inspection.

Selection criteria, and RAHTIS measured against them

Choose a tool that meets three conditions: it records start and finish times, calculates the overtime limits for you and passes data to the finance side without re-keying. In RAHTIS, job entries, driver shifts and documents are in the same place, which reduces the number of loose forms. To be honest, RAHTIS is not a comprehensive HR system covering Working Hours Act 872/2019, nor does it replace tachograph data as the official source. When evaluating software, check three things: does it support the breakdown requirements of Finnish working time law, does it read tachograph file formats directly, and does it export to payroll? If all three are met, you'll save time every month.

Where RAHTIS doesn't help (yet)

Actual payroll, annual leave records and analysis of tachograph files are currently handled by other tools. RAHTIS's strength is managing jobs and transport, not serving as the final archive for statutory working time records. So combine RAHTIS entries with either a spreadsheet or a payroll program where the official records live. For example, you can export the hours from the RAHTIS driver report as a CSV or Excel file and import them into your payroll program, where overtime and compensation are finally calculated. This two-system model is common in small firms, and it works as long as the transfer is documented and repeatable.

Step by step: a checklist for setting up statutory recording

Steps 1–7

  1. Establish which rules apply to your company: employed drivers are covered by the Working Hours Act (872/2019) and the sector's collective agreement, self-employed drivers by Act 349/2013, and those driving within the scope of the driving and rest time regulation also by Regulation 561/2006.
  2. Decide how you will record: a spreadsheet, off-the-shelf working time software, or recording built into a system such as RAHTIS.
  3. Set the contractual working time for each driver and write it down.
  4. Introduce a recording template that captures working time, overtime, breaks and hours attracting pay supplements every day.
  5. Reconcile tachograph card data with the records at least once a week.
  6. Set the retention period to at least the limitation period, i.e. two years from the end of the calendar year in which the data was created.
  7. Review the records every month and correct gaps straight away.

Monthly recurring routine

Block out a fixed slot in the calendar: check hours exceeding the limits, sign off any corrections with the drivers and back up the data. The same routine every month keeps you ready for inspection without a separate project. Also review the rest periods drivers actually took: was the 45-hour weekly rest taken, and did the 11-hour daily rest comply with the rules? If rest was reduced, check whether the reduction was permitted and whether compensating rest was given. Record these checks as part of the routine so you have evidence of regular monitoring if an inspector asks for it.

FAQ

Can a tachograph printout be used as working time records on its own?

No. Tachograph data covers driving, breaks and other work, but not shift start and finish times, periods of availability or information reported by the driver. Records only come into being when card data is combined with timesheets and job orders. Unclear periods, such as empty running or waiting at the loading point, must be marked separately so they can be explained at an inspection.

What do I do if a driver forgets to record overtime or breaks?

Correct the gaps straight away in the monthly routine by comparing the card hours with the records and signing off the corrections with the driver. Missing entries can cost you in retrospective overtime pay or penalties. Responsibility for the records always lies with the employer, so introduce a fixed weekly routine in which card data and records are reconciled before the month ends.

Do the working time rules also apply to owner-drivers and light goods transport?

An owner-driver's working time is governed by the Act on the Working Time of Self-Employed Drivers in Road Transport (349/2013): working time may average no more than 48 hours a week and may not exceed 60 hours in any single week, there are separate rules on breaks and night work, and the owner-driver must have working time records or other reliable evidence covering the previous two years. The driving and rest time regulation applies to owner-drivers in the same way as to employed drivers. For light goods transport and where the line for commercial operation lies, check the legislation itself.

Do paper CMR consignment notes and tachograph charts have to be kept for the same length of time?

No. Tachograph charts and downloaded digital data must be kept for at least one year, but if the data is used as the basis for working time records, the two-year retention obligation applies to it too. Working time records must be kept until the limitation period for claims ends, i.e. two years from the end of the calendar year in which the right to compensation arose. The CMR Convention sets no retention period, but where a consignment note is an accounting voucher or an invoice attachment, the Finnish Accounting Act (1336/1997) requires it to be kept for six years from the end of the year in which the financial year ended, so in practice it has the longest retention period of these three types of document.

Can I make a subcontractor responsible for recording working time?

Not entirely. Responsibility for recording lies with the employer, and a missing entry at an inspection is your responsibility, even if the recording is done externally. A subcontractor or software can do the practical work, but the obligations, such as two-year retention and inspection readiness, stay with you. That is why an outsourced service should be documented and the data it produces checked regularly.

kuorma-auton-kuljettajan-palkka.title: HGV driver pay in Finland
kuorma-auton-kuljettajan-palkka.description: HGV driver pay in Finland: the collective agreement pay table, experience increments and supplements explained, with a worked example of gross and net pay.
kuorma-auton-kuljettajan-palkka.html:
Key takeaways

  • An HGV driver in Finland typically earns around €3,000–3,800 a month before tax.
  • The pay table of the HGV sector collective agreement (TES) sets the minimum wage, below which nothing can be agreed: the pay group depends on the vehicle, and years of service raise pay in steps.
  • Supplements, daily allowances and overtime pay can raise gross pay well above basic pay.
  • Posti follows the collective agreement for the communications and logistics sector, not the HGV agreement, so its pay levels can't be compared directly with other employers.
  • In the example, gross pay of €3,500 comes to roughly €2,550–2,650 net, and the employer's total cost is about €4,300.

An HGV driver's pay isn't a single figure but a sum: basic pay from the collective agreement (TES) pay table, evening, night and overtime supplements, and tax-free daily allowances. The collective agreement and the employment contract determine what a driver can earn, and Posti is covered by a different collective agreement. This article unpicks the structure and works out an example of monthly net pay.

What is the average pay for an HGV driver in Finland?

An HGV driver in Finland typically earns around €3,000–3,800 a month before tax. The exact figure depends on experience, routes driven and supplements, but the baseline is set by the HGV sector collective agreement (TES) between the Finnish Road Transport Employers' Federation (ATL) and the Finnish Transport Workers' Union AKT, whose pay tables set drivers' minimum wages.

When you're pricing jobs or hiring a driver, the collective agreement table is the figure you can't go below. Everything above it is up to you: experience supplements, night and Sunday work, and per-kilometre or per-route payments quickly push the total up.

The same logic applies to earning from your own work. If you count trips, supplements and unpaid invoices by hand, any review of pay levels is only ever half done. RAHTIS (rahtis.eu/fi) keeps the job, consignment note and invoice in one chain, so you know what each shift actually brought in.

How is an HGV driver's pay set under the collective agreement?

An HGV driver's pay isn't at the employer's whim: the sector's generally binding collective agreement (TES) sets minimum wages, and no lower wage may be agreed. If you run a firm with 1–12 vehicles, the pay table is the base to which you add experience pay, supplements and allowances.

What does the collective agreement pay table contain?

The pay table first groups drivers by vehicle (full-trailer and modular combinations, semi-trailers, rigid trucks, vans) and then, within each group, by years of service: under 4, 4–8, 8–12 and over 12 years. Pay is an hourly rate or a two-week period wage (80 hours), not a monthly salary. Below are the table rates for a semi-trailer (CE) driver from 1 June 2026; the monthly level is worked out from the period wage:

Years of serviceDescriptionTable pay from 1 June 2026
Under 4 yearsLowest service step€16.56/h (about €2,870/month)
4–12 yearsTwo middle steps: 4–8 and 8–12 years€16.73–17.24/h (about €2,900–2,990/month)
Over 12 yearsLong experience€17.57/h (about €3,045/month)

Always check the exact figures in the collective agreement table currently in force, as they are updated during the agreement period (next on 1 June 2027). International haulage has its own table, and a vocational qualification counts as eight months of service. In addition, drivers of HCT combinations, crane trucks and low-loaders, for example, get a 5% special supplement on the table rate without separate negotiation.

How does the collective agreement bind the employer?

The collective agreement is binding: an employment contract may not set terms that are worse than the agreement, even if the driver agrees to them. The minimum wage is a floor, not a ceiling, so market pressure often pushes pay above it. If you employ drivers, RAHTIS helps keep jobs and their profitability in order alongside pay: more information and the application form are at https://www.rahtis.eu/en/apply.

In practice, general applicability means that even an employer who isn't a member of the employers' federation has to comply with the terms of the collective agreement, provided the work done falls within the agreement's scope. You can check this on the website of SKAL (the Finnish Transport and Logistics association), which has up-to-date information on the agreements in force and their interpretation. If you don't want to risk disputes over interpretation, keep pay above the collective agreement table.

How much do experience and further training raise a driver's pay?

The collective agreement pay tables step up with years of service: pay rises as the driver's experience in the trade grows. In practice, at four, eight and twelve years the driver moves up to a higher pay row, and the effect shows directly in the hourly rate. According to the wage statistics of Statistics Finland, more experienced drivers' average earnings are clearly higher than the sector average (Statistics Finland wage statistics).

Additional certificates work in a different way. An ADR certificate for carrying dangerous goods, a crane or loader qualification and a category CE licence make a driver fit for work that would otherwise go unfilled. The collective agreement pays separate supplements for such work, for example 5% of the table rate for ADR transport of explosives, toxic, infectious and radioactive substances, so the certificate pays off for both driver and employer.

For an owner-driver, experience shows up through a different channel: as a seasoned professional you get more loads done and judge routes and return loads better. If you're planning to hire your first driver, put the experience requirement and additional certificates in the job advert and direct applicants to a detailed description of the work, for example via a freight platform.

Years of service don't accrue automatically: the driver must be able to prove previous work history with employment certificates. The collective agreement doesn't distinguish between domestic and foreign experience: all professional driving shown in employment certificates counts as service. So if you're hiring experienced drivers from the Baltics or elsewhere abroad, ask for their employment certificates at the application stage.

How much does Posti pay an HGV driver?

Posti follows the communications and logistics sector collective agreement between the Service Sector Employers Palta and the Post and Logistics Union PAU, together with its protocol on Posti, not the HGV sector agreement. In practice, this means a Posti driver's pay is set by that agreement's pay tables, and experience and area of work affect pay differently than for an ordinary haulier.

As a large employer, Posti also has its own supplement models: shift supplements, Sunday work enhancements and route-specific arrangements are set by its own agreement. So its pay doesn't tell you directly what you should pay your own driver.

When comparing pay, compare the whole package, not just basic pay. Work out your own pay level from your own collective agreement supplements and working hours, while making sure jobs and invoicing run without manual paperwork. RAHTIS helps keep track of who does what and who pays what, on our Latvian pages too (https://www.rahtis.eu/lv).

A particular feature of Posti's pay is the transparency and predictability of its supplements, whereas as a small operator you may have to negotiate each extra item separately. That can be an advantage when competing for staff, if you can offer a clear model in which the driver knows exactly what each route and shift will bring. A small operator's flexibility in agreeing terms can also work in your favour, as the pay structure can be tailored around that particular driver's strengths.

Which supplements and allowances make up an HGV driver's pay?

An HGV driver's pay isn't just the monthly salary: it includes supplements, daily allowances and mileage allowances, which can raise gross pay considerably. When you calculate a driver's pay yourself or compare costs when pricing a job, it's worth itemising these components separately.

How are supplements calculated?

Supplements are calculated as a percentage of the table rate or of average hourly earnings. Under the HGV collective agreement, the evening supplement (18:00–22:00) is 15% and the night supplement (22:00–06:00) 20% of the table rate, Sunday and public holiday work is paid at a 100% enhancement, and overtime pay is set by the agreement. Special supplements and the international haulage supplement also go into the same gross pay. In practice, this means two drivers on the same basic pay can receive different amounts each month if one of them drives nights and weekends.

The employer must keep records of all supplements and allowances so that they can be checked in payroll, in taxation and in any dispute over interpreting the collective agreement. Daily allowances and other travel expense allowances must be itemised separately, because up to the Finnish Tax Administration's maximum amounts they are tax-free, unlike pay. They are reported to the Incomes Register as a separate item and must not be hidden in the general pay total.

What is paid on international work?

On international work, the collective agreement's international haulage pay table applies, and a driver who has worked in international haulage at the same company for at least two years gets a special supplement of at least 8%. On top of that comes a foreign daily allowance according to the length of the trip. The daily allowance is tax-free up to the maximum set by the Finnish Tax Administration, so it is a favourable component of earnings in net terms. Supplements and allowances for drivers at Posti and its partners are set by the communications and logistics sector collective agreement, so check them with Posti or the unions that signed the agreement. When you invoice your own work or subcontracting, the RAHTIS API specifications help you feed job data and allowances straight into your invoicing system, so the paper notebook of who owes what becomes unnecessary.

The HGV collective agreement has no separate border-crossing allowance; if an employer pays one, it has been agreed in the employment contract and is taxable pay. Parking charges and road tolls are not usually part of the driver's pay, but they must be included in the employer's total costs when pricing international haulage.

How does HGV driver pay vary by region and by employer?

The biggest pay differences don't come from regional boundaries but from the employer's size and contractual basis. At large operators such as Posti, the collective agreement pay scale is usually the base, with company-specific benefits added on top, whereas in small firms pay is often negotiated directly around the collective agreement minimum.

Regionally, pay in Uusimaa and Pirkanmaa is typically higher than in eastern and northern Finland, but the difference is often smaller than the difference in housing costs. Urban multi-drop and refuse collection work can pay more than long-haul work, where daily allowances make up part of the difference.

When looking at employers, check three things: does the company pay the collective agreement's general supplements in full, is overtime paid or does it go unpaid, and how regularly does the monthly pay include a performance-related element. The same driver doing the same work at two different companies can see a difference of several hundred euros in monthly pay.

Competition for drivers is fiercest in growth centres, where employers have to raise pay to keep up. An experienced driver can negotiate a better package at a small firm where the employer can't replace them quickly. Besides the Helsinki region, pay in port towns such as Kotka and Hamina is often above the local average, because export and import traffic constantly needs new drivers.

How does HGV driver pay compare with other jobs in transport?

In Finland, an HGV driver's pay is typically close to that of a bus driver or delivery driver, while taxi drivers and van drivers often earn less. The differences are largely explained by the collective agreements: on the HGV side, years of experience and further training raise pay predictably, whereas in lighter distribution pay is often hourly without the same experience ladder.

A maintenance worker or warehouse operative usually earns less than an experienced HGV driver, but office roles such as transport manager or invoicing specialist can exceed a driver's basic pay. The driver's advantage lies in supplements and allowances, which can lift total pay well above the basic hourly rate.

When comparing roles, always calculate net pay in the same way. The Finnish Tax Administration's tax card calculator (vero.fi) gives a comparable tax rate for different gross salaries.

The comparison should also take account of the physical strain and irregular working hours typical of HGV driving. A delivery driver may get the same gross pay, but the work may be more physically demanding and involve more contact with customers. A long-haul driver, on the other hand, spends weeks away from home, which affects net pay once you take daily allowances and any other tax-free allowances into account. Comparing occupations is therefore multi-dimensional, and the monthly total alone doesn't tell the whole story.

Worked example: a driver's monthly gross and net pay

Take a hypothetical semi-trailer driver with five years' experience. The minimum under the collective agreement table is about €2,900 a month for them, but the employment contract sets €3,200. On top of that comes performance pay, for example 300 kilometres at €0.10 per kilometre, i.e. €30, plus 10 hours of overtime at a 50% enhancement, about €280. Supplements and allowances bring gross pay to around €3,500.

Deducted from gross pay are the employee pension contribution (7.30% in 2026 for all ages), the unemployment insurance contribution (0.89%), the health insurance daily allowance contribution (0.88%) and tax withheld according to the tax card. A rough rule of thumb: €3,500 gross comes to about €2,550–2,650 net, depending on the municipality, church tax and deductions.

The cost to the employer is higher: the employer's share of the pension contribution, the health insurance contribution and unemployment, accident and group life insurance add roughly 20–25% on top of gross pay, so a salary of €3,500 costs the employer about €4,300.

The calculation is indicative. The exact figures depend on the agreement's pay table, the amount of supplements and the driver's tax rate, so do your own calculation with your own figures before submitting a quote.

If the driver regularly works weekends, the Sunday supplement can raise monthly pay significantly. Under the collective agreement, Sunday work is paid at a 100% enhancement, so a 10-hour Sunday shift adds about €170–200 gross, depending on average hourly earnings. Similarly, the night work supplement, paid for hours between 22:00 and 06:00, adds 20% to the table rate, which makes long night shifts a considerable boost to pay. When you're calculating pay for a quote, ask the driver how many weekend and night shifts they're prepared to do, so you can arrive at a realistic gross figure.

FAQ

Does an HGV driver have guaranteed pay if there is less work?

Yes, a driver on a period wage has guaranteed pay under the collective agreement: if working hours in a two-week period fall below those agreed in the employment contract for a reason on the employer's side, pay is still paid up to the agreed number of hours. The table rate is a floor below which pay cannot be agreed, even if the amount of work varies. Part-time and hourly paid arrangements follow different rules, so the type of employment contract is what decides.

How is a driver paid for overtime under the collective agreement?

Overtime is compensated with an enhancement under the collective agreement that increases with the number of overtime hours: 50% for the first 12 hours over the 80 hours of a two-week period, and 100% after that. The enhancement is calculated from average hourly earnings and added to gross pay as taxable income. Monthly pay can rise noticeably if overtime builds up regularly: in the worked example, 10 hours of overtime raised gross pay by about €280.

Does the employer pay for a driver's Driver CPC training?

Under the HGV collective agreement, the employer pays the cost of obtaining and renewing the certificates and cards required in the job, such as the ADR certificate, the cost of the Driver CPC entry in the licence after periodic training, and the driver card, if the driver needs them in the job. The initial Driver CPC is usually obtained before employment. If employment ends for a reason on the driver's side soon after the purchase, the driver may have to repay part of the cost.

Does pay rise if the driver also drives demanding vehicles or does ADR work?

Often, but not automatically. An ADR certificate and the ability to drive more demanding vehicles make the driver fit for work that would otherwise go unfilled, so market pressure and collective agreement supplements push pay up. A heavier combination means a higher pay group, years of service move the driver into higher pay rows, and the agreement's 5% ADR and special supplements are paid separately for certain demanding transport.

kuormien-etsiminen-puheluiden-sijaan-rah.title: Finding loads on a freight exchange instead of by phone
kuormien-etsiminen-puheluiden-sijaan-rah.description: Find loads on a freight exchange instead of by phone: post your availability, search loads with filters and save hours of dispatch work every day.
kuormien-etsiminen-puheluiden-sijaan-rah.html:
Key takeaways

  • A freight exchange replaces phone calls: you post your availability and route, browse open loads and submit quotes with a single login.
  • Fill in your company details, vehicles, drivers' qualifications and payment terms in your profile before your first search.
  • On a platform, the job details, consignment note and payment tracking sit in the same view, so dispatch shifts from chasing information to making decisions.
  • The phone remains the fastest tool in urgent situations and with regular customers.
  • Check the other party's reliability through their business ID, company email address and the exchange's payment history data before accepting a job.

You can find loads on a freight exchange instead of by phone: you upload your availability and route to the platform, browse open loads along your route and bid for them with a single login. This guide compares a day on the phone with a day on the platform side by side, and gives you checklists for the profile, availability and route settings worth sorting out before your first search.

Why does finding loads by phone still take hours?

When you're the dispatcher, the bookkeeper and the drivers' boss all at once, searching by phone eats the hours: you ring brokers one by one, listen to prices, jot jobs down on a scrap of paper and hope someone rings back. The same empty leg you could fill in ten minutes takes half a day.

The hidden costs of phone-based searching in a 1–12 lorry firm

The hidden costs aren't the per-minute call charges but the interrupted work: every call breaks off invoicing, checking CMR consignment notes or planning the next job. The note on a scrap of paper saying "who pays and when" gets forgotten precisely when you need the money most.

In a three-lorry business, a single dispatch run can mean 15–20 calls a day just to fill empty legs. Each call lasts three to five minutes on average, but the real cost is the context switch: when you go back to invoicing after a call, it takes fifteen minutes to get back up to speed. Ten calls a day in practice means an hour and a half of fragmented working time that vanishes from the diary without anyone noticing.

In a one-person business it's worse: when you're driving yourself and making calls during breaks, searching by phone eats into driving time. A break that should be a rest turns into a stressful round of calls with uncertain results. Voicemail is the most common answer, and leaving a call-back request means waiting around, which only adds to fatigue.

Freight exchanges are built for exactly this: Teleroute describes how its service works as shippers publishing loads and hauliers finding them using search criteria, with no phone call (Teleroute). RAHTIS starts from the same problem at the smaller end: you publish the job once and follow it step by step (RAHTIS – Veokorraldus ja veobörs).

How does a freight exchange find a load for your lorry?

A freight exchange works as a two-way marketplace: shippers publish loads, and hauliers find them with filters or by posting their own empty legs. The system matches the two sides automatically when the details fit. The same logic applies in RAHTIS (RAHTIS – Transportledning och lastbörs): a published load is visible to those searching, and you follow the job step by step.

Search filters: origin, destination, date and vehicle type

The search is based on four fields. Origin and destination define your route, the date tells when the lorry is free, and the vehicle type (refrigerated, trailer, container chassis) weeds out loads your vehicle isn't suited to. The more precisely these are filled in on your profile, the fewer matches you get that you have to turn down.

In practice the chain of filters works like this: first you choose the origin area, for example "Helsinki + 150 km". Then you add a destination filter, such as "Tampere or Turku". The third filter is the date: "loading Monday morning, delivery Tuesday". The fourth is the vehicle type: "semi-trailer, 13.6 metres, tail lift". The system only shows the loads that pass all four filters. If you leave one field empty, you get dozens of matches that don't suit your vehicle, and you waste time scrolling through them.

Posting an offer vs searching actively

In an active search you browse the loads on offer yourself and submit quotes. By posting your empty leg, you tell the other side where you're heading and when, and the load can come to you. In practice the two complement each other: searching fills the lorry today, and a posted empty leg finds the return load for tomorrow.

What information do you need to prepare before you start searching for loads online?

An exchange search only works first time if your profile, vehicle details and route settings are in order before you open your first request for quotation. An incomplete profile shows up as a bidder nobody picks.

Profile checklist

  • Company details: business ID (Y-tunnus), VAT number, insurance and CMR liability details
  • Vehicles: lorries, trailers, payload, lifting equipment, number of lashing straps
  • Drivers: licence categories, ADR qualification, languages spoken
  • Payment terms and invoicing details ready in advance, so they aren't up for negotiation on every job

Many exchanges show the other party's credit rating and reviews before you quote. Trans.eu's documentation covers, among other things, members' ratings and payment history (Trans.eu Help Center). It's worth gathering the same information about your own customers: in RAHTIS (RAHTIS – Kuljetusten hallinta ja rahtipörssi) you can track not only the job status but also who pays what.

Availability and route settings checklist

SettingWhat to prepare
Origin areasHome town + 100–200 km radius
Empty-leg daysCalendar for the next 2 weeks
Route preferencesAreas to avoid, your preferred routes
Return load conditionsMinimum rate, maximum length, unloading time
Vehicle availabilityFree lorry + trailer, loading time
Pricing guidelinesMinimum rate per km, separate surcharges

Once these are filled in, a quote is a click, not a phone call.

A day on the phone vs a day on the platform: the dispatch workflow side by side

Morning: finding loads and quoting

On a phone day, the morning goes on calls: nobody can see who has loads on offer, so the enquiries go one after another. On a platform day, you open the freight exchange, filter routes and loading times, and see the available loads at a glance. Submitting a quote takes a couple of clicks, and the reply arrives as a notification without the phone ringing while you're driving.

Daytime: confirmations, consignment note, driver details

This is where the difference is greatest. In the phone model, the booking, load details and consignment note files live in different places: text messages, email and a scrap of paper. On a platform, the same job appears as a single whole: the driver sees the addresses, times and consignment note directly on their phone, and you follow the status without ringing to ask "where are you?".

When loads, drivers and documents are in the same system, dispatch shifts from chasing information to making decisions: you choose the next load, and the system passes the information on. In RAHTIS, the consignment note, confirmation and status tracking sit in the same view, so in a four-lorry business you no longer leaf through scraps of paper to see who pays and what's still open. RAHTIS doesn't pull loads from other exchanges, but you can enter your own customers' jobs, including ones agreed elsewhere, in the same system alongside jobs from RAHTIS's own offer desk. The Latvian-language RAHTIS page (RAHTIS – Transporta vadība un kravu birža) explains how your own customers and offer-desk jobs are handled in one place. An honest note: if there aren't enough loads on the platform for a particular route, you'll still have to make calls or check another exchange, so the phone won't disappear entirely.

Evening: invoicing and payment tracking

On a phone day, the evening goes on matching consignment notes with quote notes to raise invoices. On a platform, the end of a job prompts for the POD, and the invoice goes out from the same chain. Payment tracking is visible in the system, so you no longer need a "who owes what" list in a paper notebook.

What are the risks of giving up the phone, and how do you vet the other party?

A phone call is the traditional way to "sniff out" whether a client is reliable, but systematic checks can replace it: online, a fraudster leaves a trail, as long as you note the details down before accepting the job.

Counterparty checklist

Before accepting a load from a freight exchange, check at least: the company's official name and business ID, the client's contact details on a company email address (not a Gmail address), payment history from the exchange's rating points, and whether the client is a verified member. Trans.eu and TIMOCOM both offer members' credit ratings and payment behaviour data for exactly this purpose (Trans.eu credit information service). Keep the list and fill it in for every new client, even if the load is urgent.

Payment terms and advance payments

The biggest risk isn't a wrong address but money: is payment at 30 days or 60, and who pays if the goods arrive but the invoice isn't paid? Agree payment terms in writing before loading, and beware of cash-in-advance requests, which are a common scam. In RAHTIS, the job details, consignment note and invoicing run through the same step-by-step view, so the agreement and documents stay paired (RAHTIS – Transportmanagement und Frachtenbörse).

When is the phone still the better option, even if you use a freight exchange?

The phone beats the platform when time is short. If the lorry is standing empty and a load has to be found within the hour, a direct call to a shipper you know or to other hauliers working the area is often the fastest way to get a load moving.

The second situation is an urgent or unusual load. If the loading changes mid-day, a trailer is missing or the delivery time falls through, it's sorted on the phone in seconds. Writing a message and waiting for a reply takes the same minutes.

The third reason is relationships. Your regular customers and most important shippers are used to hearing from you, and direct contact maintains trust when jobs from the freight exchange alone aren't enough to fill the week.

So in practice: the exchange handles searching and paperwork, the phone handles urgency and relationships.

How do you start searching for loads digitally when you have no history on the platform yet?

A new account is a blank sheet, but the first job comes sooner if your profile doesn't look anonymous. Fill in your company details, registration numbers, number of drivers and insurance details straight away, and upload a sample CMR or two from previous deliveries. Respond to your first quotes within a few minutes: on platforms, response time is visible to the other side, and a quick acknowledgement makes up for a missing review history.

Start with small jobs in your local area, even if the margin is thin. The first successful jobs earn the reviews that open up better-paid routes. Be as careful as you would on the phone: confirm the loading time in writing, ask for a signed consignment note and send the POD straight away.

In small hauliers' experience, it's precisely this combination, load search, POD and invoicing in the same workflow, that makes the switch worthwhile once the paper notebook and separate logins start to become a burden (Reddit discussion of a small haulier's TMS experience).

Which tools for a small haulage business: exchanges and TMS in one package?

For a small business, tools fall into two camps: freight exchanges such as Trans.eu, TIMOCOM and Teleroute handle finding loads and filling empty trucks, while a TMS handles dispatch, consignment notes and invoicing. Many run them side by side: the exchange login in one window, a scrap of paper in another, email in a third.

What RAHTIS is suited to and where it falls short

RAHTIS combines both: it is a TMS with its own offer desk, where the shipper publishes the job once and follows the work step by step, while the haulier fills empty legs and keeps the whole fleet in one place. It does not merge loads from other exchanges. It works from a single lorry upwards, and the notebook and carrying paper CMRs back to the office are replaced by a workflow found in a single view.

To be honest, RAHTIS doesn't solve everything. It doesn't replace accounting software or a bank connection, and it doesn't show loads from other exchanges. If you need a wide international load supply or advanced reporting for a larger fleet, a traditional exchange and a bigger TMS may suit you better. RAHTIS is designed for one to twelve lorries.

FAQ

Is using a freight exchange chargeable for a small firm, and how does pricing usually work?

Most exchanges charge a monthly or annual subscription that varies with membership size and features. Some charge separately for each confirmed job. Compare pricing based on your own volumes: for one to three lorries a lighter subscription is often enough, and trial periods help you test whether searching pays off before you commit.

Can I combine several exchanges (e.g. Teleroute, TIMOCOM, Trans.eu) into one search without separate logins?

Usually not directly: the exchanges are separate systems, each with its own login and its own filters. In practice, small hauliers keep one or two exchanges open side by side and enter the agreed jobs in a TMS, where they appear in one view. RAHTIS doesn't connect external exchanges, but in it your own customers' jobs and jobs from RAHTIS's own offer desk run under the same workflow.

How is the CMR consignment note handled when the load comes through an exchange?

The consignment note details come with the job information, but signing still takes place at the loading and delivery points. In digital workflows, the driver photographs the signed CMR on a phone and sends the POD to the system immediately after delivery. The paper CMR is still the most common; a fully electronic e-CMR is valid only for carriage between countries that have joined the e-CMR protocol. The most important thing is that the consignment note and the other job details stay in the same chain.

How quickly are loads usually found once a listing is published on the platform?

On popular routes with standard vehicles, offers start coming in within hours, sometimes minutes. With a less common vehicle type or in a remote area, a listing may go days without a match. The quality of the listing directly affects the result: precise availability times, route and vehicle details produce matches faster than a vague listing nobody dares take on.

Do I need a separate TMS, or is a freight exchange account enough?

It depends on how much other work falls outside the exchange. An exchange account handles finding loads, but dispatch, consignment notes, payment tracking and invoicing remain separate tasks. If you run one to twelve lorries and want jobs, documents and invoicing in one view, a TMS adds value. For occasional work with a single lorry, an exchange account may be enough to start with.

miten-laatia-rahtitarjous-nopeasti-asiak.title: How to put together a haulage quote for a customer quickly
miten-laatia-rahtitarjous-nopeasti-asiak.description: Build a haulage quote in minutes from seven fields: route, load, vehicle, price, validity, payment terms and contact details. Send it while still on the call.
miten-laatia-rahtitarjous-nopeasti-asiak.html:
Key takeaways

  • Build your haulage quote from seven fields: company details, route, load details, vehicle type, price with justification, validity period and payment terms.
  • Unless a return load is confirmed, price in empty running using the kilometres for both directions, and tell the customer so plainly.
  • Always state the validity period, for example seven days; otherwise the quote stays open forever and the price of fuel may change.
  • Justify the price with the route, vehicle type and schedule rather than discounts, and most price haggling stops of its own accord.
  • A freight exchange gives you ready-made load details and a guide to the going rate, to which you add your own margin; RAHTIS keeps the job, the CMR and the invoice in one workflow.

Put together a haulage quote in minutes by filling in seven fields: company details, route, vehicle type, price and its justification, validity period, payment terms and contact details. With the structure ready as a template, the quote goes to the customer while you are still on the phone, not a day later after being scribbled in a notebook. This guide shows how to do it in practice, field by field. If you want a broader overview of transport management and the freight exchange, take a look at RAHTIS – Transport management and freight exchange: loose trailers, containers and express deliveries.

How do you put together a haulage quote for a customer quickly?

In five minutes, if the information is to hand and you know the structure by heart: origin and destination, type of load, weight and volume, schedule, price and payment terms. Write these seven lines in the same order every time and the quote takes shape during the call rather than afterwards in a notebook.

Base the price on your own costs per kilometre and per hour. You can follow how those costs change in the road haulage cost index published by Statistics Finland, which the industry association SKAL (Finnish Transport and Logistics) helped to develop. Once the basis is clear, the quote can be justified straight away. In RAHTIS (rahtis.eu/fi) you can see the profitability of each vehicle: job revenue minus fuel, driver pay and other costs.

Speed comes from repetition. If you always use the same template, nobody needs to do creative writing in the middle of a busy call. Start the call by asking about the route and the load, after which the price is the only open variable. Enter the answers straight into the ready-made fields and send the message as soon as the call ends.

What information must a haulage quote contain?

Company details and the customer

Start the quote with your company details: name, Business ID, address and a contact person with phone number. Do the same for the customer, so that the documents later match the consignment note and the invoice. Without a Business ID the customer cannot check who they are handing their load to.
