A missing Business ID causes invoicing delays and possible mix-ups if there are several companies with the same name. Make sure the contact person is the one who actually makes the decisions, not someone who just passes messages on. This shortens the approval process considerably.

Route, vehicle type and load details

This is the heart of the quote. Write down the details that determine the price and prevent misunderstandings about the load:

FieldExampleWhy it matters
Origin and destinationVantaa → TampereDistance determines the price and the empty running
Load8 Euro pallets, 6,000 kgDetermines the vehicle type
Vehicle typeSemi-trailer, drawbar trailer, tankerWrong type = cancellation
ScheduleCollection Thursday 8–12, delivery FridayUrgency costs extra
Additional servicesUnloading, loading, temperature monitoringA hidden cost if forgotten

If the load needs a specialist vehicle or ADR certification, say so plainly in the quote. Fewer questions later.

Giving the load dimensions in metres and kilograms is more precise than a pallet count alone. For example, "8 pallets, 120×80×200 cm, 6,000 kg in total" gives the driver confidence that the load will fit and stay within the weight limits. If you leave out the dimensions, the customer may assume standard-size pallets when the load is in fact out of gauge.

Validity period and payment terms

Without a validity period the quote stays open forever, and the price of fuel may change before the customer replies. State, for example, "valid for 7 days", or tie the price to a specific departure date. Payment terms belong in the quote from the start: 14 days net is common, and if the customer insists on 30 days, agree it before the job, not when you send the invoice. The RAHTIS API documentation (https://www.rahtis.eu/fi/api-docs) shows how a shipper's system passes the order details to RAHTIS without retyping.

The validity period protects you against swings in market prices, especially fuel. If you tie the price to a specific departure date, the customer understands that delays may lead to a new quote. Stating the payment terms in the quote prevents surprises at invoicing and gives the customer a chance to comment on the terms before the job starts.

How do you price a haulage job in minutes?

Fixed price or hourly rate

Choose the model according to the nature of the job. A fixed price suits regular runs where the route and the type of work are known in advance. An hourly rate makes sense when the work includes unloading, waiting or several drops that you cannot estimate beforehand.

The advantage of a fixed price is predictability for the customer: they know the exact sum in advance and need not fear unexpected costs. The advantage of an hourly rate is on your side: if unloading drags on or the customer is late, you invoice for the work done. Many hauliers use a hybrid: a fixed price for the basic job and an hourly rate for extra work, such as waiting beyond the agreed time.

Empty running and return loads

Let us work through an example you can apply directly to your own jobs. Start from a rate per kilometre that covers fuel, the driver's wages, insurance and vehicle wear, and add your margin. If the customer's job is 300 km but there is no confirmed return load for the journey home, price it on 600 kilometres, i.e. both directions. This is fair, because an empty kilometre costs you almost as much as a loaded one.

Tell the customer plainly that the price includes the empty leg; that way the justification is ready and neither side has to guess. If you get a return load from the freight exchange or from your own customers, you can take the empty running out and offer a more competitive price. In RAHTIS you see board jobs near your drop-off and can offer the spare capacity of a lorry already on the road (sign up: https://www.rahtis.eu/et/apply), so a return load can cover part of the journey before the quote goes out.

A concrete example: the rate is €1.20 per kilometre and the margin is 15 per cent. A one-way 300 km job with no return load costs 600 km × €1.20 × 1.15 = €828. If you find a return load, the price drops to 300 km × €1.20 × 1.15 = €414. That €414 difference is your room to negotiate while still keeping your margin.

Which extra costs to include

Include a waiting time agreement (e.g. first hour free, hourly rate after that), ferry and road tolls, a fuel surcharge and handling of the CMR consignment note. Traficom (the Finnish Transport and Communications Agency) provides guidance on consignment note and CMR requirements in road transport (Traficom), so make sure your extra charges also cover the documentation, whether electronic or on paper.

Forgetting extra costs is the most common reason a profitable job turns into a loss-maker. For example, occasional waiting at the delivery point can stretch to hours, and if you have not agreed compensation, you are doing it in your own time. Always state the waiting terms in the quote: the first hour is included in the price, after that €45–60 per hour.

How do you justify the price to the customer without haggling?

A good quote justifies the price with the route, vehicle type and schedule, not with discounts. When the quote shows the kilometres, the nature of the route (for example a one-way run with no return load), the type of vehicle needed and the collection and delivery times, the customer can see where the money goes. Empty running and the lack of a return route are real costs, and showing them openly stops most price haggling.

Also state what is included: the consignment note (CMR), waiting time terms and payment terms. When everything is in writing, the negotiation moves from details to the overall price, which you have already justified.

The same principle works for your own customers and for jobs from the freight exchange. Once a quote has been built properly, the next one goes out as a copy. Keep a reusable quote template for your own routes; you can join RAHTIS at https://www.rahtis.eu/fi/apply, from a single lorry upwards.

Justification matters even more when you are competing with larger operators. Big companies can offer a low rate per kilometre, but they carry overheads and delays. Your advantage is speed and flexibility. When you base the price realistically on costs and show the calculation openly, a small haulier can win a tender against a bigger operator, because the customer understands how the price is made up and trusts it.

How do you send the quote and follow up the reply?

Email works for regular customers, but the message easily gets lost in the customer's inbox. Freight exchange messaging is the fastest way to reach those looking for transport: Teleroute, TIMOCOM and Trans.eu, for example, handle the quote and the reply in the same system, so you have a written record of the price and terms (how a freight exchange works).

Choose the channel to suit the job: email for a regular customer, the freight exchange for an empty leg, RAHTIS when you want everything in one place. In RAHTIS the shipper publishes the job once, carriers reply directly with offers and the transport progresses step by step in the same view: https://www.rahtis.eu/lt/apply.

Follow-up is the part that a notebook-and-spreadsheet setup loses. Set a reminder for 24 hours later: if there is no reply, call or send a follow-up message. Log every quote you send and its status (pending, rejected, accepted), so you can see each week which customers and which routes actually pay.

Following up quotes is a numbers game. If you send ten quotes a week and three are left hanging without a reply, you are losing potential turnover. A simple spreadsheet with columns for customer, route, price, date sent and status is enough to get started. When you see, for example, that 80 per cent of your quotes on the Helsinki–Turku route are accepted, you can focus more on it.

How does a freight exchange speed up the quoting process?

What freight exchanges offer for quoting

A freight exchange gives you ready-made load details that you would otherwise collect by phone and write in a notebook: origin and destination, date, trailer type, weight and load description. When a customer asks for a quote, you check the price level for a comparable route on the exchange and add your own margin on top. TIMOCOM and Trans.eu, for example, provide route-level price data or a price forecast, and you decide whether to go below or above it.

The exchange also shortens negotiation. When the customer sees that there is demand on the route, your price is easier to accept without a long tussle.

Seeing the market rate gives you a realistic idea of the prices other operators are working at. If your own price is clearly above the market, you can either lower it or justify the difference: faster delivery, fewer delays or better customer service. If your price is below the market, you can raise your margin without losing the customer.

RAHTIS on routes and empty legs

In RAHTIS the whole chain is in one place: the shipper publishes a load or a trailer swap once, you see empty legs and return loads on your own route, and quote directly on the basis of the same information. Once the job is accepted, it carries on as a transport, a consignment note and an invoice without you moving data between the exchange, a spreadsheet and a notebook.

An honest limitation: RAHTIS is not yet as large an international marketplace as the established exchanges, so for finding loads abroad you may need another exchange alongside it.

How does RAHTIS handle the quote and the transport in one place?

RAHTIS brings together the same steps that a haulier with four lorries described on Reddit: separate freight exchange logins, an outdated TMS and a paper notebook of who owes what (Reddit thread on a small haulier's working day). In RAHTIS the quote is made once, the customer accepts it and the same job carries on through the workflow without copy-pasting.

While the job is under way, the driver and the shipper follow its status step by step, the driver scans the consignment note (CMR) into the system with the app and, after the POD, the invoice is recorded on the same job, where its due date is tracked. You do not need to move data separately from a quote spreadsheet to invoicing software and a notebook.

To be honest, RAHTIS does not replace everything: its offer desk is not a marketplace open to everyone like Trans.eu or Teleroute; a job goes to approved, suitable vehicles in the area, and it does not have the range of enterprise add-ons that McLeod or Turvo offer. RAHTIS is designed for small hauliers, from a single lorry upwards, and its strength is precisely that the quote, the transport and the invoice live in the same workflow instead of in three different programs.

Joining up the workflow saves time, but even more important is the reduction in errors. When you move data by hand from the quote to the consignment note and from there to the invoice, every transfer is a chance to type the wrong address, weight or price. In a single system the data stays unchanged from start to finish, and the customer receives the correct invoice at the correct address.

What are the most common mistakes in a haulage quote and how do you avoid them?

The first mistake is a missing validity period. Without a date the quote lives forever, and the customer may come back three weeks later demanding the same price even though fuel prices have changed. Always add a line saying "quote valid for 7 days" or similar.

The second mistake is a vague vehicle type. "Lorry" does not tell anyone whether the job suits a semi-trailer, a swap body or a van. If the customer assumes something else and you send the wrong vehicle, the empty running is at your expense. State the type, volume and payload.

The third mistake is forgetting the payment terms. An agreement noted in a paper notebook without terms means that who owes what is left to your memory. State the payment period, for example 14 days net, and whether you charge interest on late payment.

These three lines take a minute but save negotiation and debt-chasing later.

The fourth mistake is missing detail in the load description. "Pallets" is not enough, as pallets can come in different sizes and contain different goods. State the number of pallets, the dimensions and the weight, so the driver knows what they are collecting and what space the load will fit in. The fifth mistake is forgetting additional services: if the customer expects unloading and you have priced only the transport, the job becomes a loss-maker.

FAQ

Can I send a haulage quote directly to a freight exchange without a customer of my own?

Yes, you can. Freight exchanges such as Teleroute, TIMOCOM and Trans.eu list open loads that you can respond to directly in the system without an existing customer relationship. The exchange gives you the details ready-made: route, date, vehicle type, weight and load description. You add your own margin and submit the quote. This works particularly well for filling empty legs.

What should I do if the customer asks for a discount on the quote?

If the quote justifies the price with the route, vehicle type, kilometres and schedule, most price haggling stops of its own accord. When the customer sees where the money goes, the negotiation moves to the overall price. If a discount is still requested, see whether a return load is available: it lets you take out the empty running, making the price genuinely more competitive without the deal becoming a loss.

How long is a haulage quote valid by default?

There should be no default: always state the validity period, for example seven days. Without a date the quote remains open forever, and the customer may come back weeks later demanding the same price even though fuel has gone up. Alternatively, you can tie the price to a specific departure date, so the schedule sets the validity for you.

Do I need a separate TMS if I only send a few quotes a week?

Not necessarily. A notebook and a spreadsheet work until the quote, the consignment note and the invoice live in different places and the data has to be moved by hand. For a small haulier, from a single lorry upwards, RAHTIS handles the quote, the transport, the CMR and the invoice in one workflow without copy-pasting. Once the quote template has been built, the next quote goes out as a copy in minutes.

miten-loittaa-palautuskuorma-tyhjelle-au.title: How to find a return load for an empty lorry
miten-loittaa-palautuskuorma-tyhjelle-au.description: How to find a return load for an empty lorry: channels in order of priority, a margin decision tree and a routine that replaces hit-and-miss load hunting.
miten-loittaa-palautuskuorma-tyhjelle-au.html:
Key takeaways

  • Look for a return load in a fixed order: your own customers first, then freight exchanges along the route, and terminals and ports last.
  • Compare every load with the cost of running empty: the freight rate minus fuel, tolls and extra working hours decides whether the load is worth taking.
  • Before quoting, check four points: route, timing, equipment and payment terms; if one fails, running home empty is often the cheaper option.
  • Write your offer precisely: equipment, available time, route, price and driver details, so the shipper replies to you.
  • Check the payment period and the payment default register before committing; late payment interest is governed by the Finnish Interest Act and compensation for collection costs by the Debt Collection Act.

Check your channels in a fixed order: your own customers first, then freight exchanges along your route, then other hauliers in the same area. Assess each load with a decision tree: route, timing, equipment and payment terms. This article gives you both in concrete terms, plus a routine that replaces hit-and-miss hunting.

What is a return load and why is an empty lorry a cost risk?

A return load, or backhaul, is freight you take on for the journey home when your own customer's job or a freight exchange job ends in the wrong place. Empty running means the same journey with no load and no income. Freight exchanges such as Trans.eu and Teleroute list these return loads all the time, and RAHTIS shows on its own offer desk the jobs near the place where each of your vehicles frees up, with those heading towards home first (https://www.rahtis.eu/fi).

Empty running is not just fuel: it is lost margin

An empty lorry has the same cost structure as a loaded one: fuel, the driver's wages, insurance, tyres and depreciation all run, but no money comes in. In European road haulage roughly a fifth of vehicle-kilometres are driven empty, which is capacity wasted outright (Eurostat, Road freight transport statistics).

When you run 300 kilometres empty, you do not just lose fuel. You lose the amount the return load would have brought in, less fuel and tolls. That is why looking for return loads should be a routine, not hit-and-miss hunting.

Which channels should you search for return loads first, and in what order?

It pays to dig for return loads in a set order: your own customers first, then regular partners, then freight exchanges and terminals last. The order is based on where you get the best price and the least risk relative to the time spent searching.

1. Your own customers and regular partners

Call or message the customers and subcontracting partners whose routes cross the route of your empty lorry. You already know how they pay and what equipment they need, so the negotiation takes a minute. Ask in particular about regular loads on set weekdays: one fixed return load a week is worth more than a one-off load.

2. Freight exchanges and load boards

If your own network turns up nothing, open the freight exchanges. Those used in Finland and Northern Europe include Teleroute, TIMOCOM and Trans.eu; an option that combines transport management with its own offer desk is RAHTIS (https://www.rahtis.eu/sv). The biggest difference between the channels is how quickly you see new loads along your route.

ChannelSearch based onMain benefitsDrawbacks
Own customersPhone and emailPrice, reliable payment termsLimited volume, relies on memory
Freight exchangeRoute and equipment searchLarge number of loads, speedPrice competition, unknown counterparty
TerminalOn site or by phoneLoose trailer and port loads close byUncertain schedules, tight pricing

3. Terminals, ports and loose trailer traffic

Last of all, check the terminals and ports along the route: loose trailer and container loads often only appear on the day. These carry the highest risk, because waiting times and payment terms vary, so take them only when the other channels have come up empty.

How do route and timing affect which loads are worth offering to carry?

The direction of the route, when loads are posted and how flexible the load is decide which return loads are realistically available. The same lorry gets different results on a different day and on a different corridor.

Route direction and the rhythm of port traffic

Empty running is most likely in the direction where the least freight moves. Loose trailers leaving ports and industrial hubs head inland on weekday mornings, so an empty lorry at a port in the afternoon is competing for very few loads. The opposite direction, from rural areas to the hubs, often offers more jobs but lower rates. Equipment narrows the choice: a reefer load will not be offered to a flatbed, and a required loading time rules out long repositioning runs.

Timing: when loads are posted and when they disappear

Freight exchanges such as Teleroute and TIMOCOM post loads around the clock, but in practice new offers tend to appear in the mornings and afternoons, and urgent ones are gone within hours. If your lorry will be empty at 12 noon tomorrow, offer to take loads whose collection time is flexible, and keep your phone free for the morning posting window. Jobs published in RAHTIS are visible step by step, so you can follow the shipper's schedule changes without calling; the terms of use state that the shipper may cancel an assignment before it is completed and that the haulier is notified of the cancellation (https://www.rahtis.eu/fi/kayttoehdot). Speed of response often matters more than price.

How do you decide whether to take a return load or run home empty?

An empty journey home always costs money: fuel, time and wear accumulate even though there is no income. A return load is almost always worth taking if it covers the variable costs and leaves even a small margin. The sum is simple: the freight rate offered minus fuel, tolls and extra working hours. If what is left is more than the cost of running empty, the load wins.

Decision tree: four questions before you quote

Before quoting, go through four points in this order. The first is the route: does the load take you towards your next job or your home base, or do you have to go 200 km out of your way, making the actual journey longer? The second is timing: can loading and unloading be done before the job you have already agreed, and is there enough buffer for delays? The third is equipment: do the trailer type, lifting gear or heating meet the load's requirements, or would you need extra kit you do not otherwise carry? The fourth is payment terms: ask about the payment period straight away, and if it is 60 days or more, price the delay in or do not quote. If any of the four fails, running home empty is often cheaper than taking a bad load.

Checklist: equipment, weight, time, payment terms

Before quoting, check: the total weight and floor area of the load against your own equipment, the loading and unloading times (unpaid waiting hours can eat the margin), tolls and ferry fares on the route, and the consignment note details (the CMR in international transport) in advance. Also bear in mind the risk that there will be no next load ready at the delivery point.

All in all, the decision is the same every time: work out the margin, compare it with the cost of running empty and decide within five minutes. RAHTIS shows the route and timing of a job and the shipper's payment history in the same view, so comparing is quicker than leafing through a notebook and separate exchange logins (https://www.rahtis.eu/et). The system does not make the decision for you, but it removes the searching, which is often the reason bad loads are taken in a rush.

What should you put in a load offer to get a reply?

An offer that gets a reply contains five points: equipment (e.g. crane or refrigerated equipment, payload), availability window in hours, route from collection to delivery and return, price and driver details. Write the price clearly: is it fixed or negotiable, and does it include waiting time?

Add one line that makes the biggest difference: "Available [date, time] on [town]–[town], equipment [specify], price [€]." A vague "we have space" is ignored, because the shipper is comparing dozens of offers within minutes.

Driver details and liability issues are best agreed in writing at the offer stage, since in international transport the entries in the consignment note are evidence of the terms of the contract of carriage, and the carrier's liability is determined by the CMR Convention (Articles 17–29 of the CMR Convention). In RAHTIS the offer and the job details travel in the same system, so they do not have to be copied onto paper; the features are listed in more detail in the product description.

How do you avoid the payment and liability risks of return loads?

A return load from a freight exchange often comes from an unknown shipper, so check their ability to pay before you commit. Ask directly about the payment period and, if necessary, ask for payment in advance on the first job. In Finland, late payment interest is governed by the Interest Act (korkolaki) (Finlex, Interest Act), and in business-to-business transactions the creditor is also entitled to a fixed €40 compensation for collection costs under the Debt Collection Act (perintälaki), so collecting overdue freight charges is not merely a matter for negotiation. Keep a record of each customer's payment times so you notice who repeatedly pays late.

Payment terms and credit information

The Finnish Trade Register shows that a company exists, but payment default information should be checked separately in a payment default register before a larger job. A security deposit or the shipper's ratings on the exchange (e.g. Trans.eu or TIMOCOM) gives an indication of how the shipper pays, but it does not replace your own judgement. Running home empty is sometimes cheaper than freight paid 60 days late.

CMR and liability for the load

Fill in the CMR consignment note carefully: a checked number of packages and reservations about the apparent condition of the goods and their packaging protect you in the event of damage. Under the CMR Convention, the carrier's liability is limited to 8.33 SDR per kilogram of gross weight of the goods lost or damaged (Article 23), and the carrier is relieved of liability if, for example, the damage is caused by the sender's fault or defective packing (Article 17); any defects you notice should be recorded as reservations on the document itself. A paper notebook is not enough as evidence if a dispute arises only weeks later.

How do you turn finding return loads into a regular routine rather than hit-and-miss hunting?

Hit-and-miss hunting means you open the exchange only when the lorry is already empty and the phone is ringing. A routine means that fleet status, alerts and the order of work are ready before you need them. Three steps are enough.

Recording fleet status in advance

Every morning, write down which lorry is where, where it is heading back to, when it will be free and what equipment it has (trailer, crane, temperature requirement). This takes five minutes and is the foundation of the whole routine, because without it you do not know what return load you are actually looking for. A paper notebook will do, but it is worth having the same information on your phone as well.

Alerts and filters on the exchange

Do not browse the freight exchange by hand. Set filters for your usual routes: origin, destination direction, date and equipment requirement, and switch on alerts for new postings. When an offer comes in, reply quickly with a complete offer whose structure is already ready from previous jobs.

One tool instead of several exchanges

Several separate exchange and TMS logins are exactly the mess that eats up a one-person planner's day. In RAHTIS a job is recorded once and followed step by step, and consignment notes and payment tracking for invoices are handled in the same place. To be honest, RAHTIS does not bring external freight exchanges together in one view: it has its own offer desk where shippers publish jobs, so browsing other exchanges remains your responsibility. The routine stays the same though: record your fleet, let the alerts do the work for you and reply quickly.

FAQ

The return load does not cover the whole journey – is it still worth taking?

Often, yes. Work out the margin for the whole journey: the freight rate offered minus fuel, tolls and extra working hours, and compare the result with the cost of the empty kilometres. If a part-journey load covers the variable costs and leaves even a small margin, it beats running empty. The exception is a detour that lengthens the overall journey too much.

How long before an empty run should you start looking for a return load?

As soon as you know when the lorry will be free and what the return route is, which is often a day or two before the empty run. Loads appear on the exchanges in the mornings and afternoons, and urgent ones are gone within hours. Set up filters and alerts in advance so that you see new loads straight away without constant browsing.

Can a return load be priced lower than normal freight, and how do I justify the price?

Yes, it can, because the lorry is heading back anyway. Justify the offer by the fact that the load fits a route and time already planned: collection and delivery fit the agreed times, the equipment is the right type and there is no extra mileage. State the price precisely and say whether waiting time is included, so that the shipper can compare easily.

What do I do if the shipper of a return load does not pay?

Ask about the payment period at the offer stage and keep a record of customers' payment times. In Finland, late payment interest on overdue freight charges is based on the Interest Act and compensation for collection costs on the Debt Collection Act, so collection is not merely a matter for negotiation. For larger jobs, check the payment default register in advance; if the payment period is 60 days or more, price the delay in or do not quote.

Do I need a separate contract or a CMR for a return load taken from an exchange?

The CMR Convention applies to international road carriage where the places of collection and delivery are in two different states, at least one of which is a contracting state; in that case a CMR consignment note is needed. Domestic carriage in Finland is governed by the Road Transport Contracts Act (tiekuljetussopimuslaki), under which a consignment note is made out unless the sender and the carrier agree otherwise. Fill in the consignment note carefully: a checked number of packages and reservations about the apparent condition of the goods protect you if there is damage. Driver details and liability issues are best agreed in writing at the offer stage, since the liability rules are binding. Each exchange's terms of use supplement the contract but do not replace the entries in the consignment note.

odotusajan-kirjaus-satulastauksessa-kulj.title: Recording waiting time during trailer swaps: a guide for drivers
odotusajan-kirjaus-satulastauksessa-kulj.description: Recording waiting time during trailer swaps: required fields, sample entries and tips to make the record stand up to payroll checks and inspection.
odotusajan-kirjaus-satulastauksessa-kulj.html:
Key takeaways

  • Waiting during a trailer swap is working time when the driver has to stay on site at the employer's disposal; if they are free to leave the truck, it is availability or waiting time that does not count as working time.
  • An accepted entry includes the start and end time, the location, the type of task and a reference such as the consignment note number.
  • The most common reasons for rejection are a missing vehicle registration, vague timings, no reason given, a conflict with the digital tachograph and a late retrospective entry.
  • Record waiting time for the same period as the digital tachograph records it, and attach a time-stamped photo of the consignment note.
  • The same driver entry serves both as working time for payroll and as the basis for a surcharge on the freight invoice.

The driver records waiting time during a trailer swap as working time by noting the start and end time, the location of the terminal or port, the nature of the task (trailer swap, container swap or waiting for the load) and a reference such as the consignment note number. This guide shows step by step how to make the entry, what a sample entry that stands up to payroll and working time inspection looks like, and on what grounds a waiting time entry is rejected. Recording waiting time during trailer swaps is closely regulated, and done properly it protects both the driver's pay and the employer's invoicing.

When is waiting time during a trailer swap working time?

Often, but not always. When a driver is swapping a trailer or container at a terminal or port and has to wait for loading, unloading or for the replacement unit to become available, the wait is working time if they have to stay on site at the employer's disposal, even though the vehicle is not moving and the driver is not doing physical work. Under section 3 of the Finnish Working Hours Act (872/2019), working time is time spent working and time during which the employee is obliged to be present at the workplace at the employer's disposal (Finnish Occupational Safety and Health Administration). The collective agreement for the truck sector makes this more specific: if the driver has to move the truck repeatedly on the orders of the loader or unloader, the time is working time, but if they are free to leave the truck, the wait is paid as waiting-time pay and does not count as working time (section 11, point 12).

The practical significance of this rule is considerable. If the driver has stayed at the terminal for their daily rest but is woken in the middle of it to move the truck when the trailer becomes available, that rest is no longer uninterrupted. The rest period is then broken and cannot count as daily rest, and the driver is back on working time. This means that recording waiting time during trailer swaps is not a mere formality: it determines whether the rest is considered complete or not. Without an entry, the driver and the employer risk misreading the situation and breaching the working time rules.

When waiting time counts as working time and when it does not

Waiting counts as working time when the trailer swap is part of a task assigned by the employer and the driver has to stay on site. If, on the other hand, the driver waits at the terminal on their own initiative without an assignment, or is outside working hours, the time is not recorded. In borderline cases, what matters is whether the driver had to stay on site or was free to use their time as they wished. The entry can be made by hand or per vehicle in a system such as RAHTIS, where the stages of a job run from the driver all the way to invoicing.

In practice the difference is clear: if the transport planner has told the driver to go to the terminal and wait for a trailer swap, the waiting is working time from the outset. If, instead, the driver decides to stop at the terminal to wait for the next job without any specific instruction, the time cannot be recorded as working time. Likewise, if the driver has said they are reachable but is free to leave the vehicle and use their own time, this is a period of availability, which does not count as working time, even though it may be paid for.

What information must a waiting time entry include?

A rejected waiting time entry is almost always an incomplete one: it lacks the time, the place or the reason. The payroll administrator cannot accept a line saying "at terminal 2 h", because it does not show whether it was waiting for a trailer swap or some other delay.

To make the entry complete, the driver needs to know exactly which fields the payroll administrator and the inspector expect to see. The table below lists the required fields; if any is missing, the entry is rejected automatically. These fields must be filled in for every waiting time entry, whether a paper form, email or a transport management system is used.

Required fields

FieldExample
Start date and time14/3 at 09:15
End time14/3 at 11:40
LocationTerminal, street address or port
TaskTrailer swap: changing trailers
Order or job referenceReference to the consignment note or CMR consignment note

Supporting details that speed up approval

A screenshot or time-stamped photo of the consignment note shortens the back-and-forth, as does the name of the consignee or the terminal supervisor. If the wait was caused by a queue, record your arrival time and the time your turn came separately. When the driver records these straight away during the job, the transport planner does not have to fill in details afterwards, and the entry goes to payroll and invoicing as it stands. In RAHTIS the driver confirms arrival and completion of the stop on their phone, and the entries and photos are sent even from areas without coverage as soon as the connection returns: see rahtis.eu/et.

Step by step: how the driver records waiting time during a trailer swap

Before arriving at the terminal

Record a time stamp as soon as you set off: take a photo or send a message on your phone showing your departure time and estimated arrival time at the terminal. Make sure the job instructions or consignment note include the customer's contact details so you can report a delay or an early arrival. If the load or trailer is not ready as agreed, report it before you arrive, so the reason for the wait can be verified from the start.

On arrival and when the wait begins

On arrival, record two things: the time and the place. In practice a time-stamped photo of the gate display, the gate sign or the yard, or a location-based entry in the app, is enough. Also record who is receiving you: the terminal name, gate number and any acknowledgement of your arrival. Tell reception you have arrived and ask them to confirm that the load or trailer is not ready, because it is exactly this confirmation that separates an accepted waiting time entry from a rejected one.

Directive 2002/15/EC distinguishes between working time and periods of availability. Waiting for loading or unloading also counts as working time when the driver has to stay at their workstation and the foreseeable duration of the wait is not known in advance. A period of availability, which does not count as working time, is a wait during which the driver is not required to remain at their workstation and whose foreseeable duration is known in advance (Article 3 of the directive on EUR-Lex). So record the start of the wait as soon as reception tells you the load is not there, and note whether you were told in advance how long the wait would be: do not wait to see whether it sorts itself out within the hour. Try recording waiting time in RAHTIS yourself: https://www.rahtis.eu/sv.

When the wait ends and recording what follows

Once the trailer has been swapped or the load secured, note the end time of the wait and continue the journey on the same entry. Finally, record the trailer or container number, the consignment note number and any acknowledgement from reception. The entry then forms a continuous chain: arrival, start of waiting, end of waiting and onward journey, all on the same job.

Sample entries: a trailer swap and waiting for a load

Example 1: trailer swap in the terminal yard

An accepted entry might look like this: "10/3, 09:15–10:40, trailer swap, terminal yard, Vantaa. Trailer change: empty trailer collected from the yard, loaded trailer dropped in its place, tractor unit and trailer recoupled. Witness: terminal shift supervisor." Record the time of arrival, not just the time the swap started.

Example 2: waiting at the gate before collecting a container

Another example: "10/3, 12:00 arrived at port gate, collection from the gate began at 13:30, container secured at 14:10. Reason for waiting: container had not yet been grounded." Here the waiting time spent at the gate is 1 h 30 min, and the entry shows the reason, so the person invoicing can claim compensation from the customer.

In both cases it is worth attaching a time-stamped photo of the gate display or the consignment note. When the same entry feeds directly into the job stages in RAHTIS, the driver does not copy information by hand, and the payroll administrator sees the waiting time in the same view as the rest of the job's records (https://www.rahtis.eu/lv).

The most common reasons for rejection in payroll

The most common reason for rejection is a missing vehicle or trailer registration: without a registration number, the payroll administrator cannot match the entry to the driving log record. The second is vague timing, such as just "all morning" with no start and end time. The third is a missing reason: an entry that only says "waiting terminal" does not show whether it was queuing because the load was being prepared or getting ready for the trailer swap.

The fourth reason is a conflict with the digital tachograph. If the tachograph shows rest for the same period for which the driver is claiming waiting time as working time, the payroll administrator will reject the entry unless it is a precisely defined exception. Working time is supervised by the occupational safety and health authority (since the start of 2026, the Finnish Licensing and Supervision Agency), and driving and rest times by the police at roadside checks. In either kind of inspection, discrepancies between the working time records and the tachograph must be explainable, so it is worth adding an explanation when the entry is made.

The fifth reason is a late retrospective entry made weeks afterwards. Avoid all five by recording the waiting time on the same day and adding the trailer swap details: terminal, container number and customer name. In RAHTIS the same entry is attached directly to the job, so invoicing and payroll see the same information without a separate email.

How does the entry stand up to a working time inspection?

The authorities compare waiting time entries with two sources: the driver's working time records and the vehicle's digital tachograph. Questions arise if the tachograph shows a stop during the trailer swap but nothing has been entered in the working time records, or the recorded time differs from the tachograph by hours.

Reconciling the digital tachograph and the manual entry

Record waiting time for the same period as the digital tachograph records. If the trailer swap started at 10:15 and ended at 12:45, the same times go into the working time records, not rounded hours. Explain in the entry why the vehicle was stationary: for example "queuing at terminal, container swap, collecting consignment note".

If the entry and the tachograph do not match, correct both on the same day and record the reason for the correction. Entries rejected in payroll are often ones where the driver's paper note and the system's time stamps differ with no explanation. When the entry, the tachograph and the payroll records tell the same story, the inspection goes through without questions.

The inspector may also ask for evidence that the wait was caused by the customer or the terminal and not by the driver's own delay. That is why photos of gate displays, emails from the sender or terminal receipts are worth their weight in gold. If the waiting time was interrupted by a break or rest, the inspector will want to see that the break was taken in accordance with the rules and that there are no gaps in the working time records. From the inspector's point of view, recording waiting time during trailer swaps is most reliable when every stop is explained and the driving schedule is consistent from departure to destination.

How does the transport planner handle waiting time entries in payroll?

In a small firm, the transport planner and the payroll administrator are often the same person, so it pays to process a waiting time entry as soon as the driver's record comes in. First check that the entry has a start and end time, the name of the terminal or port and the reason for waiting. If any of these is missing, ask for it to be completed the same day, not at the end of the payroll run.

Waiting time in customer invoicing and the freight rate

On the pay side, waiting time is recorded either as working time or as waiting time under the collective agreement, according to the driver's employment contract and the sector's terms. On the invoicing side the basis is different: the transport contract sets out which waiting time is charged as a surcharge and on what basis, for example at an hourly rate after a period of free waiting time. So agree with the customer in advance when free waiting time ends and how waiting is documented; information on the sector's terms of carriage is available, for example, from the haulage operators' association (SKAL).

In practice, then, the same entry is used twice: as working time for payroll and as a surcharge on the freight invoice. When both are based on the same driver entry, the figures also match at inspection.

How does RAHTIS support recording and invoicing waiting time?

RAHTIS is built so that the driver confirms arrival at each stop and completion of the stop on their phone: time stamps, locations, photos and notes are saved in the same workflow that the shipper follows step by step. The entry does not stay on paper or in a separate app; the transport planner sees it immediately and it travels on with the job. Waiting time at a stop is counted from arrival to confirmation. When the job is completed, the waiting time details are part of the same package as the consignment note and the POD, so invoicing is based on saved records rather than memory. This removes the typical problem of waiting time only coming to light when someone asks about it after the invoice has gone out.

Where RAHTIS does not help (yet)

RAHTIS does not know your customer-specific waiting time terms, so check the basis for the surcharge in your own transport contract. Nor does the system replace the tachograph or your payroll system; it produces entries that you transfer to your own payroll.

FAQ

Does the customer pay for waiting time if the trailer swap is delayed for reasons on the terminal's side?

Often, yes, but the basis lies in the contract, not in the driver's entry. The transport contract usually sets a period of free waiting time, after which the right to a surcharge arises. Record the reason for the delay, the start and end time and the order reference, so that invoicing can base the surcharge on saved data rather than memory.

Is the digital tachograph enough as evidence of waiting time, or is a separate entry needed?

A separate entry is needed. The digital tachograph shows that the vehicle was stationary, but not the reason or the task. The inspector will have questions if the stop on the tachograph and the working time records do not match. Record the same times, the location, the type of swap and a reference to the consignment note, so that any discrepancy can be explained afterwards.

What do I do if the terminal will not give arrival or release times in writing?

Record the times yourself on the same day and add your own evidence: a time-stamped photo of the consignment note, the name of the consignee or terminal supervisor and the container number. If the wait was caused by a queue, note your arrival time and the time your turn came separately. These supporting details speed up approval even when the terminal confirms nothing in writing.

Is waiting time during a trailer swap recorded as working time for the driver of the vehicle or for the driver doing the swap?

The entry goes into the working time records of the driver who was at the employer's disposal during the wait. If the driver of the replacement vehicle waits on site as instructed, the time is their working time. What decides it is not the vehicle's registration number but who was instructed to be there and whose free time the wait restricted.

How much waiting time is paid to the driver in full, and when is it treated as a break?

No general limit for full payment can be given without an employment contract or the sector's terms: on the pay side, your own contract terms decide. On the tachograph, a long stationary period is easily recorded as rest, so that the working time claim and the tachograph data conflict. Record the start and end of the wait accurately and explain in the entry in advance how breaks fit in.

pienen-kuljetusfirman-ajopaivakirja-sahk.title: An electronic driving log for a small haulage firm's drivers
pienen-kuljetusfirman-ajopaivakirja-sahk.description: An electronic driving log for a small haulage firm's drivers: up and running in six weeks, with data going straight to invoicing and no IT budget.
pienen-kuljetusfirman-ajopaivakirja-sahk.html:
Key takeaways

  • The law does not require paper: an electronic driving log is acceptable as long as the data is complete, reliable and can be checked afterwards.
  • A realistic budget for a firm with 1–10 vehicles is from tens to hundreds of euros a month, and per-vehicle pricing is usually the fairest model.
  • The logging app must work offline, open with a single tap and take less than a minute, or paper will be back in the cab.
  • Six weeks is enough to move from paper to electronic: selection and pilot, two weeks of running both in parallel, then retiring paper.
  • The same electronic entry serves the driving log, the consignment note, invoicing and payroll without copying.

A small haulage firm introduces an electronic driving log by choosing a phone-based logging app, making sure the data meets the statutory requirements, training drivers to log their own journeys and linking the data directly to invoicing and payroll. This guide shows step by step how a firm with 1–12 lorries makes the switch without an IT budget and without finally ditching paper until the electronic version has been proven to work.

Why should a small haulage firm digitise its driving log?

When you are the firm's transport planner, bookkeeper and safety manager all at once, every paper driving log is work you will have to sort out yourself later. An electronic driving log moves the recording to the driver at the moment the journey happens, and the data is ready at the same time for invoicing, payroll and working time monitoring.

Where the paper log breaks down in practice

On paper the handwriting is illegible, hours are missing or the sheet stays in the cab for a week. The requirements for drivers' logs and working time records are laid down in law, and the Finnish Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment's guidance on working hours requires that the data can be verified afterwards. When the paper is poor, you end up correcting it in the evenings.

Time saved by linking dispatch and invoicing

When journeys, consignment note data and paid hours live in the same system, you do not copy anything twice. RAHTIS (rahtis.eu/fi) combines job tracking, driver shifts and payment tracking for invoices in one place, so the invoice can be made out from the recorded journeys instead of a paper log. The driver report also serves payroll without a separate home-made Excel set-up.

What does the law require of a driving log, and is an electronic version accepted?

Working time legislation and the driver's log

Driving and rest times are recorded by the vehicle's tachograph and on the driver card, but the employer must also keep working time records, which also cover work other than driving, such as loading and waiting. The driving log supplements this: it documents the route, load and mode of transport of each individual job. The law does not specify whether records are kept on paper or electronically, as long as the data is complete, reliable and can be checked afterwards. An electronic driving log is therefore acceptable if it produces the same information as the paper version.

Evidential value and archiving of electronic data

Evidential value is decisive in disputes: a customer questions the delivery time or a shipper questions the content of the consignment note. An electronic log contains a time stamp, the driver's identifier and an unalterable history, which is clearer evidence than paper. Retention obligations are worth checking with your own accountant, but in practice the data has to be kept on file for several years. In RAHTIS the journey data, consignment note and POD are linked to the same job, so the evidence is in one place rather than in separate folders (https://www.rahtis.eu/et). Remember that it must also be possible to show the driver's signature and the vehicle identifier afterwards.

What does an electronic driving log cost a small firm?

A realistic budget for a firm with 1–10 vehicles is from tens to hundreds of euros a month. The cost is made up of the software licence, the drivers' phones and your own time: installation, training and changing habits often cost more than the licences.

Pricing models: per vehicle, per user, fixed

ModelYou payBest suited toRisk
Per vehicleFixed sum / lorry / monthPredictable cost when drivers changeIdle months still cost money if the fleet shrinks
Per userSum / user / monthSmall fleet, many people loggingCost rises as you take on more staff
Fixed packageContract price / monthEstablished fleet and staffOversized if the firm shrinks

In a small firm, per vehicle is usually the fairest: the fleet is what earns the money. RAHTIS pricing follows this principle and suits firms from a single lorry upwards (https://www.rahtis.eu/lv).

Hidden costs: training, devices, integrations

Three items are often left out of the budget. Training drivers takes working days, and every new person logging needs to be inducted again. Devices: if logging is done on the driver's own phone, the cost is zero; company tablets cost €200–400 each. Integrations with invoicing and payroll are free when built in, but expensive when custom-made.

Remember the archiving obligation too: under Article 10 of Regulation (EC) No 561/2006 on driving and rest times, tachograph and driver card data must be downloaded regularly (the driver card at least every 28 days and the vehicle unit every 90 days, Commission Regulation (EU) No 581/2010) and kept for at least 12 months, and under Directive 2002/15/EC working time records must be kept for at least two years. So choose a service you can also get your data out of after the contract ends (EU Regulation 561/2006, EUR-Lex).

How do you choose an electronic driving log without an IT department?

Selection criteria for a small firm

When you are the transport planner, invoicing clerk and safety manager yourself, choose a solution against five criteria: can you use it on a phone without training, do you see entries in real time, does the data go straight to invoicing, does it work without a separate server, and is the pricing per vehicle rather than per user? Test each candidate on one real job, not a demo: log one loose trailer move, one consignment note and one empty run from start to finish. If installation needs a consultant or hours of learning, give it a miss.

Where RAHTIS meets these criteria and where it does not

RAHTIS is designed for firms from a single lorry upwards: the driver logs the shift and the stages of each job on a phone, and the same data is visible to you and ready for invoicing without copying from paper. Combining its own offer desk with transport management removes separate logins and paper notes about who owes what. You can apply at https://www.rahtis.eu/sv/apply.

To be honest: RAHTIS does not replace the statutory tachograph and driver card data or their download, and it is not a fleet maintenance system. If all you need is software to download and archive tachograph data, other tools will do.

How do you get drivers on board with the new way of logging journeys?

Mobile logging that copes with terminal routines

Logging is done on a phone, with gloves on, dirty screens and a poor signal. The solution must work offline, open with a single tap and ask only for the essential fields: origin, destination, load and job status. If logging takes more than a minute, it will not get done and paper will go back in the pocket.

Allow drivers their own way of working too: one logs at every stop, another at the end of the day. What matters most is that the data is created out on the road, not afterwards in the office from memory.

Ground rules for the transition period

Run both in parallel for two weeks: paper and electronic logging at the same time. This gives you comparison data and drivers learn without pressure. Agree on one rule: notes may be written on paper, but the official record is electronic, and missing entries are sorted out the same day, not a week later.

Remember the archiving obligation: in Finland electronic documents must be kept for the period laid down in the Accounting Act, and their evidential value requires the data to be unalterable and traceable (Vero.fi, the Finnish Tax Administration, on keeping electronic records). Once logging is in order, the same data is ready in RAHTIS for invoicing, and you can look for jobs for free vehicles on the RAHTIS offer desk; you can join via the application page.

How does driving log data get to invoicing and payroll?

Journey data to the consignment note and the invoice

When journey logging is electronic, the same entry can work in three places: as the driver's log, as an attachment to the consignment note and as the basis for invoicing. In practice the driver logs the job, the kilometres and waiting times, and the system links them to the order. In RAHTIS the consignment note and journey data are in the same workflow, so the invoice can be raised directly from the logged journey without copying from paper into Excel.

An honest limitation: RAHTIS does not send freight invoices through an e-invoicing operator. You make out the invoice in your own invoicing or financial management software and mark it on the job in RAHTIS, where the payment status and reminders are then handled. That is still quicker than typing it up from paper notes.

Working time and payroll

The same entry also works as a working time report. The driver's journeys, breaks and other work are saved with time stamps, and at the end of the month you send a ready-made report to payroll instead of a stack of paper slips. Digital logging is also more accurate: checks based on the vehicle's speed data reveal missing entries that on paper only come to light at inspection.

If you use separate payroll software, check before choosing which file format you can use to transfer working time data into it.

How do you move from paper to electronic step by step?

Six weeks is enough if the job is split into three two-week blocks: selection and pilot, parallel running and finally retiring paper. The aim is that no job goes unlogged by falling into a gap between the two systems during the transition.

Weeks 1–2: selection and pilot

Choose a solution using the criteria described earlier and put one driver on trial. Only one lorry's journeys are logged electronically; paper is not removed yet. At the same time, check the guidance from the industry association SKAL so the data you record is correct from the start: keeping a driving log. In week 2, go over with the pilot driver what worked and what felt like pointless tapping.

Weeks 3–4: parallel running

All vehicles now log both on paper and electronically. This is the most time-consuming phase, but it exposes the situations where the app does not fit the real work: waiting for loading, no signal in the yard, the change of day falling in the middle of a job. Compare the paper and electronic versions daily and fix logging habits immediately rather than collecting corrections on a list.

Weeks 5–6: retiring paper for good

The paper version stays in the vehicle as a backup, but it is no longer filled in. Drivers log only electronically, and you check the entries at the end of the day before invoicing. Once two full weeks have gone by with no missing entries and invoices have been produced from the driving log data without any separate reconciling, paper can be dropped completely. Keep one completed paper form as a reference point in case the tax authority or an inspector asks questions later.

Summary: where to start today?

Pick one vehicle and one driver, and log next week electronically alongside paper. Check that the data flows straight from the consignment note to invoicing without retyping. If everything goes through, extend it to a second vehicle and drop paper altogether within a month.

RAHTIS is designed for exactly this: from a single lorry upwards, with dispatch, driver shifts and payment tracking for invoices in one place and no separate IT budget. Try it in practice and see whether it fits the way you run your jobs.

FAQ

Can the driving log still be kept on paper if drivers refuse to use a mobile app?

Yes, because the law does not prescribe the form of the records, as long as the data is complete and can be checked afterwards. Paper, however, requires constant correcting and chasing: illegible handwriting, missing hours and late forms end up being fixed by you. Two weeks of parallel running lowers the threshold, and most drivers get used to logging on a phone when it takes less than a minute and works offline.

Does an electronic driving log work without a signal at a terminal or abroad?

Yes, if you choose an app that logs offline and uploads the data later. The signal at terminals is often weak, so the log must open with a single tap and save locally on the phone. Test this during the pilot on one real job, not a demo: log one loose trailer move and one empty run from start to finish. If logging gets stuck waiting for a connection, paper will soon be back in the cab.

Does a small firm need separate driving log software, or is a TMS with logging built in enough?

A separate driving log program rarely makes sense for a firm with 1–12 lorries. It is enough for logging to be part of the same workflow as the consignment note and invoicing, so the same entry serves the driving log, the invoice and payroll without copying. Choose a solution against five criteria: phone use without training, real-time visibility, direct transfer to invoicing, no server, and per-vehicle pricing.

How long must driving log data be kept by law?

The retention period depends on the data. Under Regulation (EC) No 561/2006 on driving and rest times, data downloaded from the tachograph and driver card must be kept for at least 12 months; under Directive 2002/15/EC working time records must be kept for at least two years; and under the Finnish Accounting Act data used as invoicing vouchers must be kept for at least six years from the end of the year in which the financial year ended. Check your own situation with your accountant, and before choosing, make sure you can get all your data out of the service even after the contract ends, so that the archiving obligation does not depend on the app.

How are incorrect entries made by drivers corrected afterwards?

Agree a rule that missing or wrongly logged journeys are sorted out the same day, not a week later. In a good system a correction leaves a time-stamped trace in the unalterable history, which preserves the evidential value of the records in a dispute. Check the entries yourself at the end of the day before invoicing, so errors do not make it onto the invoice and the driver gets feedback straight away.

rahtilaskujen-hoito-ilman-jalkikaiteista.title: Freight invoicing without paperwork after the fact
rahtilaskujen-hoito-ilman-jalkikaiteista.description: Freight invoicing without paperwork after the fact: order, sign-off and POD travel in one chain, so the invoice can go out as soon as goods are delivered.
rahtilaskujen-hoito-ilman-jalkikaiteista.html:
Key takeaways

  • A paperless freight invoicing process relies on recording the job details once, with the same record flowing from the order to the consignment note, the driver's sign-off and the finished invoice.
  • An electronic freight invoice must contain the same mandatory details as a paper invoice, and in Finland invoices, as accounting vouchers, must be kept for at least six years from the end of the year in which the financial year ended.
  • The driver's mobile sign-off and the POD attachment are saved to the job at the moment of delivery, which does away with envelopes of receipts scanned after the fact and speeds up payment.
  • Freight exchange and loose trailer jobs fit into the same invoicing process when each customer receives its own invoice with its own terms and references.
  • RAHTIS does not replace accounting software: the balance sheet and annual accounts are still handled by your accountant.

You can handle freight invoices without paperwork after the fact when the consignment note details, the driver's sign-off and the POD attachment go straight from the system into the invoice: the order is created once, the driver signs off the job on a mobile and the invoice material is ready complete with attachments. This guide goes through the whole life cycle from order to archiving, including loose trailer and freight exchange jobs.

What does freight invoicing without paperwork after the fact mean?

A paperless freight invoicing process means that the job details are created once in the system and go straight from there into the invoice: the order, route, driver's sign-off, POD attachment and consignment note details in a single chain. The invoice is produced ready for the archive, and you do not have to spend an evening going through envelopes of receipts and notes.

For a small business the benefit is tangible: when dispatching, invoicing and bookkeeping are all handled by the same person, every line typed by hand takes time that is lost elsewhere. According to the Finnish Tax Administration, an electronic invoice must contain the same mandatory details as a paper invoice, so the law does not force you to use paper (Finnish Tax Administration). In RAHTIS the shipper publishes the job once and the driver signs off each stage directly, so the invoice material is ready before the lorry is back at base. In practice the process starts with the customer's job or the freight exchange job being entered once, not in three places.

The essence of going paperless is not the technology itself but joining the information flows into a single chain in which the same data is never entered twice. When the driver signs off the delivery in the mobile app, the sign-off does not disappear into an inbox waiting for a separate invoicing round; it triggers the invoice automatically. This means the invoice can be in the customer's inbox or online bank before the driver has even made it back home. With the traditional model this would be impossible, because invoicing always depends on the paper consignment note coming back and the data being entered into the system by hand. In a paperless process that delay disappears and the invoicing lead time shrinks from days to hours, which significantly improves the company's cash flow.

What requirements apply to an electronic freight invoice in Finland?

Mandatory invoice details

The Finnish VAT Act sets out what every freight invoice must contain: the names and details of the seller and the buyer, the Business ID or other identifier, the invoice number, the date, the date or period of supply, the quantity and nature of the goods or the extent and nature of the services, the VAT rate, the amount payable and the payment terms. Whether the job comes via a freight exchange or from your own customer, the same fields are filled in every time. In RAHTIS the order details (parties, route, price) and the consignment note details are already on the job, so you do not have to hunt for them on paper when making out the invoice. If you invoice abroad, for example a Swedish or German customer, the details are the same, but the language and references are worth checking at the order stage. You can try it out in practice at Application · RAHTIS.

In addition to the mandatory invoice details, the haulage sector has its own specific requirements that general invoicing software does not always cover. A freight invoice often includes a reference number linking it to a particular job or transport contract, plus a breakdown of surcharges such as waiting time, unloading delays or ADR surcharges. Itemising these by hand on a paper invoice or in general invoicing software is laborious and error-prone. When the source data comes straight from the transport management system, the breakdown is generated automatically from the prices agreed with the order and the extra events recorded during the transport. This reduces customers' questions about the content of the invoice and speeds up payment.

Archiving and retention period

Under the Finnish Accounting Act (1336/1997, chapter 2, section 10), vouchers such as invoices and other accounting material must be kept for at least six years from the end of the year in which the financial year ended, and the financial statements, the annual report and the books for at least ten years from the end of the financial year. Electronic archiving is permitted as long as the data remains unaltered and accessible throughout the retention period. In practice this means POD attachments, consignment note details and invoices can live in the same system without cardboard files. When the driver's sign-off and attachment have been linked to the job during the transport, archiving happens at the same time, and no one is left with paperwork after the fact.

For retention requirements, what matters is that the electronic archive is protected against changes and its data is traceable. The system must be able to show when the invoice was created, when the attachments were added and who signed them off. RAHTIS stores the time stamps of the job's events and who recorded them, so the audit trail is in order without a separate log book. If the tax authority asks for evidence of a particular job from three years ago, the material is in one place: the invoice entry, consignment note, POD attachment and the driver's sign-off with time stamps. In the paper world the same job might be scattered across three or four files in different offices, and some of the information could be missing or hard to read.

How do you get freight invoice data straight from the transport management system into the invoice?

Order stage: getting the job details right once

The chain starts with the order: the customer's email or a freight exchange job is turned into a transport task in the system, with the collection and delivery addresses, load description, freight rate, surcharges (such as waiting time or ADR) and payment terms. This data is saved once and reused at every stage: for the consignment note, the driver's task list and finally the invoice. Eliminating retyping is the core of the whole chain, because every line copied by hand is one more possible error on the invoice and one more reason for the customer to pay late.

In practice this means that when you enter a job in RAHTIS, the same record goes with it all the way: from the order to the consignment note details, the driver's sign-offs and on to the invoice. You do not have to dig the agreed price out of a notebook later or check scraps of paper, because everything is already in the same record. The system does not replace dispatching decisions; it simply makes sure that data entered once is not lost on its way to the invoice.

The quality of the data created at the order stage determines whether the whole chain works. If an address is incomplete or the freight rate is missing, these gaps carry through to the consignment note and the invoice, so the first entry has to be made carefully. In practice it pays to create order templates for different types of customer: a regular customer with fixed routes and prices, a freight exchange job where prices vary, and a one-off job where everything is entered by hand. Once the template is ready, the mandatory fields are filled in by default and only exceptions need manual input. This halves the time spent on orders and reduces the risk of entry errors, because the system will not let a job go forward without the mandatory details.

Consignment note details as the basis for the invoice

The consignment note (CMR) is filled in from the same record, and once the driver signs off the delivery and the POD attachment has been saved, the invoice is produced without a separate step. The invoice shows the customer details, freight rate, surcharges and attachments, all derived from the original order and the events of the transport. Retention obligations are best checked directly in official guidance, such as on the Finnish Tax Administration's website, so that archiving is done correctly from the start.

The consignment note details form the basis of the invoice because they contain what actually happened during the transport: loading and unloading times, any damage or discrepancies, and the consignee's acknowledgement. When this data comes straight from the system, the invoice is based not just on the order but on verifiable events. If the customer claims the delivery was late, the time stamp of unloading attached to the invoice shows when it actually happened. If the freight rate includes waiting time, the driver's sign-off verifies how long the wait lasted. This chain from order to consignment note to invoice is what makes freight invoicing without paperwork after the fact possible: every invoice line can be traced to a concrete event, not to a note or a receipt.

How are the driver's sign-offs and attachments added to a digital freight invoice?

POD and CMR sign-off on mobile

Straight after unloading, the driver photographs the signed CMR or consignment note on their phone and marks the load as delivered in the app. The photo, time stamp and location are saved directly to that job, so paper copies do not have to be posted back or scanned at the office in the evening. If the consignee insists on a paper acknowledgement, a photographed document is enough as an invoice attachment for most customers.

How easy the driver's mobile app is to use determines how likely the sign-off is to be done correctly and on time. If the app is slow or needs lots of fields filled in, the driver puts the sign-off off until the evening or forgets it altogether, and invoicing is delayed. The RAHTIS mobile sign-off is designed around the bare minimum: the job opens, the driver takes a photo, the consignee signs on the screen and the job is marked as complete. The location and time stamp are saved in the background with no extra step. This means the sign-off is done before the driver starts the engine at the delivery point, and the invoice material is ready straight away.

Automatically linking attachments to the invoice

When the job is marked as complete, the POD photo, the CMR sign-off and any other attachments are in the same record that the invoice is based on. The invoicing software does not have to ask for attachments separately afterwards, and they do not need to be attached by hand via email. In RAHTIS the driver's sign-off is visible to the customer step by step, and the signed CMR and unloading photos are saved to the job, where the customer can see them (https://www.rahtis.eu/lt). This removes the most common reason for late payment: the customer cannot claim that the delivery document is missing.

An honest limitation: if the customer requires the original paper CMR to be posted, a digital image only partly replaces it, and the original must still be kept.

Linking the attachments to the job means in practice that the invoice is not a stand-alone document but is based on the job record. When the invoice goes to the customer, the POD attachment, the CMR photo and any additional explanations go with it, without anyone having to put them together separately. This is a significant difference from the traditional model, where invoicing is a separate step that needs its own attachments, its own email and its own archiving. In RAHTIS these are all part of the same job: when you mark the invoice you have sent on the job, the supporting material is already in place and does not have to be put together separately.

How do loose trailer and freight exchange jobs fit into the same invoicing process?

Loose trailer work should not be a separate invoicing channel. When freight exchange jobs and your own customers go through the same system, filling empty legs and invoicing are handled without a notebook or CMR copies sent by post.

Freight exchange job details straight into the system

When you take a job from a freight exchange, the customer details, route and freight are entered once, not afterwards from a receipt. In RAHTIS the driver signs off collection and delivery, and the POD attachment and a photo of the consignment note are saved with the job. An electronic consignment note (e-CMR) can be used under the Additional Protocol to the CMR Convention only if both the country of departure and the country of destination are parties to the Protocol (UNECE e-CMR page). Finland is a party, but not all EU countries are, and an e-CMR is issued in a service designed for that purpose. The photo and on-screen sign-off stored in RAHTIS are not an e-CMR, so the paper CMR still travels with the goods.

The catch with loose trailer jobs is that customers change and invoice terms vary: one pays at 14 days, another at 30 days, a third requires its own reference number system. When this information is recorded with the job, the invoice adapts automatically to each customer's requirements without you having to remember who pays on which terms. This is particularly important when you run a mix of jobs: your own customers, jobs from Trans.eu and jobs agreed directly by phone, all in the same week. If invoicing is a separate process, you have to check each job's terms individually, which takes longer than the driving itself.

Invoicing several customers

Each customer receives its own invoice with its own terms and references, even if the jobs are in the same calendar. When the POD and consignment note are already attached, the invoice can be sent as soon as the goods are delivered, and a later empty leg that gets filled is handled in the same way. RAHTIS handles both the same way; more information and application: Application · RAHTIS.

Managing several customers requires the system to keep jobs clearly apart: who ordered it, what the route is, what the price is and when the invoice falls due. When this information is in the same calendar, you can see at a glance which invoices have been sent and which are waiting. This prevents double invoicing and forgotten jobs, which are the most common mistakes in a paper-based process. And when filling empty legs is part of the same system, invoicing the return load follows the same logic: the driver signs off collection and delivery, the POD is saved to the job and the invoice is made out on that basis.

How are archiving and inspections handled without a paper archive?

When freight invoice data, the driver's sign-offs and POD attachments build up in the same system, the archive creates itself as you work. Every job remains searchable: the consignment note details, attachments and invoice can be found by customer or registration number in seconds, with no safe or old files.

Payment tracking without a notebook

You can see the status of each invoice directly in the system: sent, paid, overdue. Instead of recording "who owes what" in a paper notebook, you mark the invoice you have sent on the job, and RAHTIS tracks due dates job by job and flags the overdue ones. Payment reminders go out without a separate Excel file, and you no longer have to collect scraps of paper for your accountant.

Effective payment tracking depends on the system knowing the status of every invoice in real time. When you mark the invoice as sent, it is open. When payment arrives, it changes to "paid". If the due date passes, the status changes to "overdue" and the system flags it without you having to go through a list by hand. This is a significant advantage over Excel-based tracking, where the status has to be updated by hand and overdue invoices can go unnoticed for weeks. In RAHTIS overdue invoices are shown with their status, and if an invoice has not been marked as paid, RAHTIS sends the customer a free payment reminder on your behalf the day after the due date and again seven days later, without you having to look up the original invoice or the customer's contact details.

Responding to inspections from a digital archive

When the tax authority or customs asks for documents, digging through years-old piles of paper becomes a search.
