You select the period and the customer, and the system lists the consignment notes, POD attachments and invoices. The same applies to disputes with customers: if the other party claims a delivery is missing, the sign-off time stamp and the POD attachment can be shown in moments. RAHTIS keeps the archive in order automatically, but final responsibility for retention obligations and tax treatment lies with you and your accountant, as with any system.

In an inspection, speed and completeness are what count. If the tax authority gives you a week to supply invoices and related documents for a three-month period, putting them together from a paper archive can take a whole day. From a digital archive the same material is put together in minutes: you select the period, filter by customer and the system lists everything, including attachments. This not only saves time but also reduces the risk of errors, because documents can get lost or mixed up when gathered by hand. What is more, the digital archive is always in the same format and in the same place, so responding to different inspectors' requests is consistent and quick.

What should you bear in mind when moving from paper to electronic freight invoices?

Making the switch in 30 days

Week 1: choose one customer and one type of job for a pilot. Week 2: enter open jobs into the system and make out the invoices from the details recorded on the job. Week 3: introduce driver sign-offs and POD attachments so the attachments are ready on the job for invoicing. Week 4: invoice the pilot customer electronically and check what is missing before moving everything else across.

The paper CMR still travels with the goods unless an e-CMR is used for the transport; for the first month it is also worth keeping the paper sign-offs as a backup. Finnish Customs and the Finnish Tax Administration may require transport documents during inspections, so check the retention periods directly on the Finnish Tax Administration's website.

A successful switch depends on the driver learning the new way quickly and the customer accepting a digital invoice without resistance. For the driver, go through the mobile sign-off steps before the first job: open the app, select the job, take a photo, ask for a signature, mark as complete. Once learnt, the whole thing takes 30 seconds. For the customer, agree in advance that the invoice will come electronically with a photographed CMR attached rather than a paper one. Most customers accept this because it speeds up their own invoice processing. If a customer insists on a paper invoice, it is worth checking whether this is a real requirement or just habit, since in most cases it is habit rather than a legal requirement.

Where RAHTIS is not (yet) a fit

RAHTIS handles a job from order to archiving in one place, and it is designed to work right down to the owner-driver with a single lorry. But to be honest: RAHTIS is not a full accounting system, so the balance sheet and annual accounts are still handled by your accountant or in accounting software. If you run international loose trailer work through several freight exchanges, ask us directly about integrations with the different platforms before committing.

How do different tools compare for paperless freight invoicing?

The choice depends on whether you need a freight exchange, a transport management system or both in one place. A table from the small haulier's point of view:

An honest weakness: RAHTIS does not replace accounting software and may not cover every exchange job if your customers require a particular system. For hauliers who rely mainly on exchanges, Teleroute or Trans.eu may be the primary place to find work, with invoicing handled on the TMS side.

Your choice of tools also depends on how many different systems you are prepared to use every day. If you find jobs on Trans.eu, run them in Transportial and invoice in Excel, you have three different systems that do not talk to each other. That means every piece of data is moved by hand at least twice, which is exactly the paperwork marathon that going paperless is meant to eliminate. The strength of RAHTIS is that it combines its own offer desk and the TMS in one place, so finding, running and invoicing a job happen in a single chain. This does not mean RAHTIS replaces jobs from other exchanges, but for jobs that come through RAHTIS the documents, invoice status and reminders are all in one place. More information and the application form are at Application · RAHTIS.

FAQ

How much time should paperless invoicing save a small firm?

This guide does not give an exact number of minutes, but the saving comes from data entered once not being copied again from the order to the consignment note and the invoice. When dispatching, invoicing and collecting POD attachments are handled in the same chain, going through and scanning envelopes of receipts in the afternoons disappears altogether, and the invoice can be sent as soon as the goods are delivered.

Is a photographed CMR enough as an invoice attachment?

For most customers it is, but not for all. If the consignee or customer requires the original paper CMR, a digital image only partly replaces it, and the original document must still be kept. The paper CMR travels with the goods in any case unless an e-CMR is used for the transport, so keep the originals, especially during the first month of the switch, and agree the method of sign-off with the customer in advance.

How long must invoices and attachments be kept?

Under the Finnish Accounting Act, vouchers such as invoices and their attachments are kept for at least six years from the end of the year in which the financial year ended, and the financial statements and the books for at least ten years from the end of the financial year. An electronic archive is acceptable as long as the data remains unaltered and accessible throughout. Final responsibility for retention obligations lies with you and your accountant, even if the system handles archiving automatically.

Does RAHTIS replace accounting software?

No. RAHTIS handles a job from order to archiving: the order, consignment note details, driver sign-offs, POD attachments, the invoice status and payment reminders. You make out the invoice in your own invoicing or accounting software, and the balance sheet and annual accounts are still handled by your accountant. So your accountant still needs their own tools, but no longer scraps of paper about jobs.

Do freight exchange jobs fit into the same invoicing process?

Yes. A job taken from an exchange is entered into the system once, with the customer, route and freight rate, and the driver signs off collection and delivery just as for your own customers. Each customer receives its own invoice with its own terms and references, even if the jobs are in the same calendar, and the POD attachment is ready on the job for invoicing.

rr-seuranta-noudosta-toimitukseen.title: Order tracking: the stages of a transport from collection to delivery
rr-seuranta-noudosta-toimitukseen.description: Order tracking shows an order's progress from collection to delivery without GPS units: customers check the status themselves, so fewer calls and notes.
rr-seuranta-noudosta-toimitukseen.html:
Key takeaways

  • Order tracking means following each order stage by stage from collection to delivery, not real-time vehicle location data.
  • Order tracking does not need GPS units, so for a small fleet it is a cheaper and lighter option.
  • Five pieces of information are enough for the customer: status, schedule, exceptions, consignment note number and POD.
  • In loose trailer and container work, the swap is recorded as a separate event so tracking does not break off mid-journey.
  • The biggest problem when introducing it is a status that is not updated, which is solved by making an update a single tap.

Order tracking means following each order as the transport moves through clear statuses: collection, loading, swap, delivery and confirmation of the signed consignment note (POD). This guide shows how to set up the workflow so the customer can see the situation themselves and you save on phone calls, notes and spreadsheets, even if you run loose trailers or swap containers.

What does order tracking mean in practice?

Order tracking means tracking per order: a single consignment is followed step by step from collection to delivery, rather than the lorry's position on a map. In other words, it is about transport events, such as loading, unloading and the consignment note coming back, not vehicle location data.

The distinction matters because many small hauliers currently track only their own lorry or phone the customer to ask about the load. With order tracking, the customer can see what stage their particular job has reached, and the driver marks the stages along the way. Behind the process is the consignment note, which in international transport is the CMR: it is not the contract itself but evidence of the contract of carriage, its terms and the receipt of the goods (Articles 4 and 9 of the CMR Convention), and liability is determined by the Convention.

In practice order tracking can work without a separate GPS system: the driver updates the status, and a system such as RAHTIS (https://www.rahtis.eu/) shows the order's progress all the way to the customer.

How does order tracking differ from real-time vehicle tracking?

Order tracking means status-based tracking: the transport progresses stage by stage from collection to delivery, and the customer can see where their own consignment is. GPS-based vehicle tracking, on the other hand, follows the lorry, not the load. The same lorry may carry three different orders in a day, in which case vehicle tracking tells you where the lorry is, but not whose consignment is on board.

For a small firm, status tracking is often enough, because it tells the customer exactly what they ask on the phone: has the load been collected, is it on its way and has it been delivered. A GPS system adds devices, monthly fees and maintenance, the benefit of which is small for a small fleet.

Order tracking (per order)GPS tracking (per vehicle)
What is trackedAn individual consignmentThe vehicle
Customer visibilityTheir own order, stage by stagePosition of the whole lorry
Needs a deviceNoYes
Best suited toFirms with 1–12 vehiclesLarge fleets

In RAHTIS, order tracking is built straight into the order: you record the stages yourself or the driver marks them, with no separate GPS system. The terms of use describe what the haulier reports to the customer about exceptions, and accurate stage recording also protects you in disputes (https://www.rahtis.eu/en/terms).

When GPS tracking is still needed

GPS tracking is worthwhile if your customer requires real-time lorry location written into the contract, if you run vehicle operating hours or service intervals from the system, or if your fleet is spread across several drivers and you want a fleet manager's view. Theft risk and mandatory monitoring of drivers' working time can also justify a device. In other cases, status tracking meets the customer's needs more cheaply and with less hassle.

What information should you show the customer in order tracking?

The customer needs five things: the current status (collected, in transit, delivered), the estimated schedule, exceptions such as a delay or rerouting, the consignment note number and the POD once the signed delivery note has reached the system. This is enough to eliminate almost every customer service call: when the customer can see the status themselves, they do not ring to ask "where's the lorry?".

Avoid showing the driver's personal details, precise real-time coordinates, freight rates or other customers on the same route. When the vehicle is driven by an identifiable driver, its location data is that driver's personal data, so passing it on is restricted by the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR, Regulation (EU) 2016/679).

In practice you share a link with the customer that shows only that order's details. In RAHTIS this works by the order progressing from collection to delivery and the customer sees the stages with time stamps via a tracking link, without logging in; the API documentation describes how status data can be shared with the customer's own systems (https://www.rahtis.eu/en/api-docs). An honest limitation: RAHTIS does not show a map accurate to the minute – tracking is based on status updates, which is enough for most loose trailer and job-by-job transport.

How are one-off jobs, such as loose trailer and container transport, tracked stage by stage?

Order tracking for loose trailer and container transport is built on four stages: publication, collection, swap and delivery. Each stage is updated as soon as the driver or the transport planner records the event, so the customer can see the situation without phone calls.

Stage 1: publishing and accepting the task

The job is published once, either on the freight exchange or directly to the customer: collection point, destination, vehicle requirement and schedule. Once accepted, the task gets its own reference, around which all later information builds up. A task published in RAHTIS goes straight into your own workflow, so there is no need for separate exchange records or copying into a spreadsheet.

Stage 2: collection and load confirmation

The driver records arrival at the collection point, and loading is confirmed either in the app or with the consignment note details. At this stage it is worth recording the container or trailer number, because it is the only sure way to identify the right unit when the same equipment is used on several jobs. An incorrect container number is the most common reason tracking shows the details of the wrong unit.

Stage 3: swaps and intermediate statuses

In container and loose trailer traffic the load often changes vehicle mid-journey: at a port, a terminal or a partner's yard. The swap is recorded as a separate event, so the time stamps are kept and the customer can see what stage the load is at even when the vehicle changes. Without recording these intermediate stages, tracking breaks off at exactly the points where customers ask most often.

Stage 4: delivery and POD

Delivery is confirmed with a POD: a receipt, signature or photo is attached directly to the task. RAHTIS combines the consignment note, POD and payment tracking for the invoice in the same record: once you mark the invoice on the job, RAHTIS tracks the due date and reminds the customer about an unpaid invoice. Through the API (https://www.rahtis.eu/fi/api-docs) the status can also be passed on to the customer's own system.

How is tracking information shared with the customer automatically?

There are three practical ways: a shared tracking link, email notifications when the status changes and API integration. For most firms with 1–12 vehicles, the first two are enough.

Shared link vs. email notifications

A shared link is the simplest way: once the order is in RAHTIS, you send the customer a link through which they can see the status from collection to delivery. You do not call, the customer does not call you, and you can send the link once and forget about it. Email notifications work when the customer cannot be bothered to click anything: the system sends a message automatically when the status changes, for example "collected" or "delivered".

A shared link has one honest limitation: the customer sees the status only when you update it. If you forget to mark the collection as done, the customer sees out-of-date information. That is why the status is best updated on the phone while on the road, not in a notebook at home in the evening.

API integration

API integration means tracking data goes straight into the customer's own system without emails or links. It is mainly relevant when your customer is large and needs the data in its own system. RAHTIS has an open, free REST API for shippers, with webhooks that report changes in order status (for example order.taken, order.started and order.closed); the documentation is at /api-docs. Even so, an integration is rarely the first step for a small haulier, so it is worth coming back to it when a larger customer asks for it.

Freight exchanges such as Teleroute and Trans.eu are first and foremost places where loads and capacity meet, and their tracking features vary depending on the service and the tools the customer uses. That is why final order tracking and customer communication are best kept in your own systems, not behind an exchange login.

What are the most common tracking problems and how are they solved?

The biggest problem is the driver not updating the status. The solution is to make updating so easy that it needs no call to the transport planner: a single tap on the mobile says that the lorry is at the collection point, loaded or unloaded. When the status is updated from the road, dispatch can see the situation without notes.

The second problem is an exception that goes unreported: a delay, damage or a wrong address. When the order is tracked stage by stage from collection to delivery, the exception is recorded on the same order with a time stamp, so you can tell the customer straight away rather than when they ring.

The third classic is the paper consignment note going missing. The solution is to capture the consignment note and POD digitally the moment delivery is completed and attach them to the order. RAHTIS itself describes how the driver receives the job and status updates directly on their phone and the documents are saved in the system (source).

The fourth problem is the customer ringing with the question "where's the lorry?". When the order status and documents can be shared as a link, you can answer by looking at your own screen. To be honest: if the driver still does not update the status, no system will fix that, so learning the routine is part of getting started.

How do you introduce order tracking as part of transport management?

The first week in practice

Day one: add your own vehicles and drivers to RAHTIS. Day two: take one real job from the freight exchange and run it through the system from collection to POD, without duplicating it on paper. Day three: send the customer the first tracking link and ask whether it looks like what they need. Rest of the week: move the remaining active jobs into the system and deliberately put the notebook aside. If something breaks, fix it in the system rather than going back to the old way.

In a small firm the responsibilities are clear: whoever accepts the job marks its status. The driver updates collection and delivery; you confirm the consignment note and invoicing. One rule is enough: the status changes only in the system, not by agreeing over the phone to do it "later".

Where RAHTIS is enough and where it is not

RAHTIS is enough for what most firms with 1–12 vehicles need order tracking for: the order is tracked stage by stage from collection to delivery, the customer sees the status of their own job without calling, and filling empty legs happens in the same place as dispatch. It does not replace a GPS tracker fitted to the vehicle, so real-time map position and vehicle data come from elsewhere if you want them. Nor is it a full accounting program, although payment tracking for invoices is covered. An honest test: if your customers demand minute-by-minute real-time location or ERP integrations, you need a bigger system alongside it. If what you need is for jobs to progress visibly without phone calls, this is enough.

FAQ

How much does order tracking cost a small haulage firm?

The cost depends on the system, but order-based tracking is typically much cheaper than a GPS solution fitted to the vehicle, because it needs no devices, installation or maintenance. In RAHTIS, tracking is part of the order workflow, so there is no separate tracking charge. When comparing, also count the time saved: fewer calls and notes mean fewer working hours.

Can order tracking be done without a driver app?

Yes, but it shifts the work to the transport planner. Someone has to update the statuses, and if the driver does not do it from their phone, you mark collections, swaps and deliveries yourself based on reports from the road. This works with a small number of jobs, but some of the benefit is lost: statuses lag and the customer's visibility suffers. In practice an app for the driver is the simplest way to keep the information up to date.

Does order tracking also work for one-off jobs taken from a freight exchange?

Yes, and that is where it is most useful. A job taken from a freight exchange gets its own reference, around which collection, load confirmation, any swap and delivery with POD build up. A task published in RAHTIS goes straight into your own workflow without separate records or copying into a spreadsheet. The customer sees the stages of their own consignment even if the same lorry carries several different loads in the course of the day.

How are the POD and consignment note made part of tracking?

The delivery stage is confirmed with a POD: a receipt, signature or photo is attached directly to the order the moment the delivery is completed. That way the paper consignment note does not go missing, and the consignment note, POD and payment tracking for the invoice stay in the same record. Payment reminders go out automatically if an invoice you have marked falls overdue, and the documents can be shared with the customer as a link without chasing email attachments afterwards.

Does order tracking need a separate GPS tracker in the vehicle?

No. Order tracking is based on stage updates recorded by the driver or transport planner along the way, so nothing is fitted to the vehicle. A GPS unit is only worthwhile if your customers require real-time lorry location in the contract, you need maintenance or working time data, or your fleet is so spread out that a fleet manager's view is essential. For most firms with 1–12 vehicles, status information is enough for their customers.

trucking-dispatch-beginners-guide-small-.title: Trucking Dispatch: A Beginner's Guide for Small Carriers
trucking-dispatch-beginners-guide-small-.description: Trucking dispatch explained step by step for 1-12 truck carriers: fill empty trucks, handle CMR and PODs, and decide between a dispatcher, software, or DIY.
trucking-dispatch-beginners-guide-small-.html:
Key takeaways

  • Trucking dispatch is the daily loop of finding loads, confirming rates, assigning drivers, and collecting CMR notes and PODs so you get paid.
  • A hired dispatcher usually takes a percentage of each load's revenue, which can eat most of your margin on thin domestic rates.
  • One person can dispatch 4-12 trucks in roughly one to two hours daily if load boards, dispatch, and invoicing are consolidated in one place.
  • Two fixed check-ins per driver, at loading and delivery, are the practical baseline; other calls should be exception-driven.
  • Free tools and spreadsheets cover job lists but usually stop at rate confirmations, CMR paperwork, POD collection, and invoicing.

Trucking dispatch is the daily work of finding loads on a freight exchange, confirming rates, assigning them to your drivers, checking in on progress, and collecting the CMR notes and PODs so you get paid. This guide walks through one full dispatch day step by step, then helps you decide whether to hire a dispatcher, use software, or keep doing it yourself.

What does a trucking dispatcher actually do day to day?

A dispatcher fills empty trucks, keeps drivers moving, and turns completed jobs into paid invoices. In a 1-12 truck company, that person is often you, doing it between driving, quoting, and chasing paperwork.

The morning: filling empty trucks from the load board

The day starts with the freight exchange or load board: matching trucks that would otherwise run empty (tyhjäajo) against loads that pay well and end somewhere useful for a return load. That means several logins, comparing rates, and booking keikka before drivers finish their morning coffee.

The middle of the day: driver communication and check calls

Once trucks roll, dispatch is answering calls: delays at the terminal, a changed loading time, a detour. Each change means updating the schedule, telling the shipper, and sometimes rebooking a slot. It is reactive work, and it eats the hours you planned for selling.

The end of the day: paperwork, PODs, and who owes what

Evenings go to CMR notes, PODs, and the notebook tracking who owes what. One 4-truck owner described exactly this mess: separate load board logins, an old TMS, and a paper notebook for receivables (Reddit thread). Tools like RAHTIS exist to collapse that loop into one place.

A real dispatch workflow, step by step

Step 1: Search the freight exchange for a return load

Your morning starts with the freight exchange, not your email. You filter by the lane your truck will be empty on, check the weight and trailer type the cargo needs, and shortlist two or three offers worth a call. If you run your own clients, you first check which keikka is already booked, then search the rahtipörssi only for the gap that would otherwise be tyhjäajo. The goal is simple: never let a truck leave a region without a return load confirmed.

Step 2: Quote, agree the price, and get the rate confirmation

You quote based on the lane, the loading windows, and what the customer accepted last time. Once the price is agreed, get it in writing, whether that is a rate confirmation from a broker or an accepted offer on the exchange. A verbal "yes, we'll load you at 14:00" is not a rate confirmation. This document is what your invoice rests on later.

Step 3: Send the job to the driver and set check-in times

Pass the driver the essentials: pickup address, time window, cargo details, contact number, and CMR requirements. Set fixed check-in times, typically at loading and at delivery, so you are not chasing updates by phone all day. Write the check-ins into your dispatch sheet so a missed call is visible within the hour.

Step 4: Handle exceptions: delays, trailer swaps, terminal queues

The plan breaks at the terminal queue, the late shipper, or the trailer that suddenly needs swapping. Your job is to rebook the delivery window, tell the customer before they ask, and log what changed. A dispatcher who documents exceptions calmly is the reason customers come back.

Step 5: Close the job: CMR, POD, invoice, and tracking payment

The job is not done at delivery. You collect the signed CMR and POD, match them to the rate confirmation, invoice, and then track days-to-payment until the money lands. That last stretch, chasing paperwork and unpaid invoices from a paper notebook, is exactly what RAHTIS replaces: publish once, follow the job step by step, and keep CMR, POD, and invoice tied to the same job. If your setup still lives in separate logins and a notebook, that is the loop worth breaking, and you can start by applying at https://www.rahtis.eu/en/apply. Honest caveat: RAHTIS covers dispatch and documents, not accounting, so your bookkeeping stays wherever it is today.

What trucking dispatch terminology do beginners need to know?

Load board, freight exchange, rahtipörssi: same thing, different words

A load board is a marketplace where shippers and forwarders post loads and carriers post available trucks. In Northern Europe the same service is called a freight exchange or rahtipörssi, and the big ones are Teleroute, TIMOCOM and Trans.eu, each requiring its own login (https://www.teleroute.com). Irtoperä means a semitrailer hauled without its own tractor: the shipper or port hands you a loaded trailer and you supply only the tractor and driver. A keikka is a single job.

Rate confirmation, CMR note, POD

TermWhat it isWho issues it
Rate confirmationAgreed price and terms for a loadBroker or shipper
CMR note / rahtikirjaTransport document that travels with the cargo and evidences the contract of carriageSender and carrier; the driver signs for the carrier
PODProof of delivery, signed on arrivalReceiver

Empty running, irtoperä, tyhjäajo, backhaul

Tyhjäajo is a truck driving empty after a drop-off. Dispatchers search the exchange for a return load or backhaul to cover those kilometres; an irtoperä trailer heading your way can be that backhaul, since the tractor going home empty only has to hook it up. RAHTIS (rahtis.eu) puts its own load board, dispatch board and CMR paperwork in one place; it does not pull in loads from other exchanges, so those still need their own logins.

Should a small carrier hire a dispatcher, use dispatch software, or do it themselves?

What hiring a dispatcher costs and when it makes sense

A hired dispatcher is usually paid a percentage of each load's revenue, so on thin Finnish domestic rates that cut can eat most of your margin on irtoperä work. It makes sense when you are sitting in the cab all day and genuinely cannot search the rahtipörssi or answer driver calls. If you are already office-based part of the day, paying someone to do what you could do yourself is hard to justify.

What dispatch software must do for a 1-12 truck fleet

At your size, the software replaces the notebook, not a person. It must handle load searching and booking, driver assignment, CMR paperwork, and tracking who owes what, without per-user pricing that punishes a one-man dispatch office. Tools like Transportial or Trans.eu cover parts of this; a full workflow in one place is what RAHTIS is built for, from published job to paid invoice. Honest limitation: RAHTIS will not negotiate your rates or chase a broker by phone, so you still do the talking.

The honest case for doing it yourself with the right tools

Dispatching your own trucks keeps the margin and builds your customer base directly. The workload is real, roughly an hour or two daily on planning and paperwork, but software that consolidates load boards, dispatch, and invoicing makes that manageable for one person. Start by doing it yourself; hire help only when trucks are sitting idle because you cannot answer the phone.

How does dispatching differ for hotshot trucking versus full-size semi fleets?

Hotshot is the American term for a pickup and gooseneck trailer running smaller, urgent loads. In Finland and Northern Europe the closest equivalent is the van or light truck chasing small part loads and short keikka off the rahtipörssi.

Smaller loads, faster turns

A hotshot dispatcher books more, shorter jobs per day, so the phone work and paperwork multiply even though revenue per load is smaller. Empty running hurts more too: with a light trailer, a return load matters on nearly every trip, not just occasionally. Each international job still needs a CMR note: the UNECE CMR Convention applies to international road carriage for reward regardless of vehicle size, while domestic jobs in Finland run on an ordinary rahtikirja under the Finnish Road Transport Contracts Act (tiekuljetussopimuslaki).

What carries over to any fleet size

The core loop is identical: search the load board, agree the rate, dispatch, track, invoice. RAHTIS handles that loop the same way whether you run one van or twelve semis; on fast-turn freight, expect more calls whatever tool you use.

What does free trucking dispatch software include, and when is it not enough?

What free tiers and spreadsheets actually cover

A spreadsheet or notebook can hold load details, driver names, and who owes what. That is exactly what the 4-truck owner on Reddit described: separate load board logins, an old TMS, and a paper notebook for receivables (Reddit thread). Free tiers of dispatch tools usually add job lists and basic status tracking. That covers the first half of a dispatch day, not the paperwork half.

Where free tools break: per-user pricing, load boards, invoicing

Free tools stop where the money moves. Rate confirmations, CMR notes, POD collection, and invoicing usually sit behind paid plans, and per-user pricing hurts when you are the dispatcher, accountant, and safety guy in one. Load boards also stay separate: you still log into Teleroute, TIMOCOM, or Trans.eu to find irtoperä and backhaul loads, then retype the job into your dispatch sheet.

Running RAHTIS through the same criteria, including its limits

RAHTIS bundles a freight exchange (rahtipörssi) with a TMS, so shippers publish once and carriers fill empty trucks and dispatch in one place, from one truck up. It handles the publish-search-dispatch-invoice loop. Its limits: it will not replace your accounting software, and if your clients load you through other exchanges, those still need their own logins.

How do you train to become a trucking dispatcher without prior experience?

Trucking dispatch classes and courses: what they teach

Paid dispatch courses typically cover load board searching, rate confirmation basics, broker communication, and paperwork like the CMR note. They are useful if you have never touched a freight exchange or a rahtipörssi listing. What they cannot teach is your own lanes, your own drivers, and your own customers, which is where most of the real learning happens anyway.

Learning on your own fleet: a 30-day plan

Week 1: document every job you run, from search to POD, on paper. Week 2: move that paper into one place, replacing the notebook with a spreadsheet or a TMS so who-owes-what stops living in your head. Week 3: standardise check-in times with drivers and file every rate con and rahtikirja the same way. Week 4: review the month, find the slowest step, and fix only that one.

FAQ

How do dispatchers get paid and what does that mean for your margins?

Most hired dispatchers take a percentage of each load's revenue. On thin Finnish domestic rates, especially irtoperä work, that cut can consume most of your margin. If you are office-based part of the day, paying someone to search the rahtipörssi and answer driver calls is hard to justify; hire help only when trucks sit idle because you cannot answer the phone.

Can one person realistically dispatch 4-12 trucks while doing accounting and safety?

Yes, with the right tools. Dispatching your own fleet takes roughly an hour or two daily on planning and paperwork, and software that consolidates load boards, dispatch, and invoicing makes that manageable for one person. The realistic limit is phone time: one person can plan the day, but exceptions at terminals are what stretch the hours.

Do I need a trucking dispatch course before dispatching my own trucks?

Not necessarily. Paid courses teach load board searching, rate confirmations, and paperwork like the CMR note, which helps if you have never touched a freight exchange. They cannot teach your own lanes, drivers, and customers. A 30-day plan on your own fleet, documenting every job from search to POD, covers most of the real learning.

What is the difference between a freight exchange and a TMS?

A freight exchange, or rahtipörssi, is a marketplace where shippers post loads and carriers post available trucks; Teleroute, TIMOCOM, and Trans.eu are examples. A TMS is your internal system for running jobs: driver assignment, CMR paperwork, and tracking who owes what. Most small carriers juggle both separately; some tools now bundle them in one place.

How many check calls should a dispatcher make per driver per day?

Two fixed check-ins per driver is the practical baseline: one at loading and one at delivery. Write them into your dispatch sheet so a missed call is visible within the hour. Beyond that, calls should be exception-driven, triggered by delays, terminal queues, or trailer swaps, rather than chasing updates by phone all day.
